Mountain Lion Is the Ultimate Underrated Game Meat. Here’s How to Prepare It

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, luke Ellsbury and his 16-year-old daughter had chased the lion for miles through a foot of snow in some of northwest Wyoming’s harshest country. Their bluetick-English coonhounds finally treed the cat on the far side of a steep ridge, about 7 miles from their truck. By the time they tagged the lion, they’d already been running for well over half the day, and they still had to skin and field dress it.

“There was no good horse trail or anything to travel in and out,” Ellsbury claims. “Just getting to a lion is a lot of work.”.

Sources indicate that at that point, some lion hunters may have chosen to take the skull and cape and leave the meat, a practice that’s legal in some states like Wyoming and one that’s at the moment being leveraged to ban “trophy” mountain lion hunting in Colorado. Anti-hunters there are trying to persuade the voting public that hunters don’t eat mountain lion meat.

It has been revealed that but Ellsbury, like plenty of cougar hunters, wanted the meat from his mountain lion. So, he and his daughter and two friends carefully removed the animal’s backstraps and quarters and packed them out, making the long haul back on that cold January day and reaching their truck after dark. Lion meat, Ellsbury claims, is worth the work. Two years later, he’s still savoring the remaining packages of that lion’s meat. He made burnt ends out of it recently. “I’ve eaten my fair share of lion, and I really like it,” he says. “It’s pretty versatile and mild tasting.”.

Industry observers note that ellsbury, a large carnivore biologist for the Wyoming Game and Fish Department, longtime houndsman, and former guide, doesn’t blame people for being gun shy about eating mountain lion. It is a cat, after all. But he and others insist it’s worth trying. And not unlike other wild game, from moose to bighorn sheep and chukars to sandhill cranes, mountain lion meat is best consumed while keeping a few best practices in mind. Here’s how to prepare and cook mountain lion meat.

Sources indicate that yes. Although mountain lion meat certainly isn’t as popular as wild game like whitetail deer or wild turkey, it is edible, tasty, and safe to eat when prepared properly. The meat from mountain lions and other predators, like black bears, has long carried a stigma because these critters eat other animals, which brings unfounded concerns about taste and safety. In reality, mountain lion meat tastes great, it’s lean, and relatively easy to cook, says Luke Worthington, a Wyoming hunter, guide, and founder of the Wyoming Houndsmen Association.

“It tastes a lot like pork,” Worthington tells Outdoor Life. “I do the old shake and bake with it, where I cube it up and put it in shake and bake and fry it.”.

Recent findings suggest that and that stigma around mountain lions has changed dramatically over the last 15 to 20 years. Worthington notes his clients are becoming more interested in hauling out lion meat to take home. He credits a growing movement focused on eating other, more nontraditional types of wild game.

In a recent development, “I tell people, ‘This is good meat and edible meat, and it’s worth it. If you kill an animal, it’s worth taking the meat,’” he claims. “The least you can do is try it.”.

Most people who’ve eaten lion say the meat tastes much like a lean pork, with a mild or almost sweet flavor that is well suited to picking up other flavors in marinades, rubs, or sauces.

Ellsbury also notes that while the fat from a deer or elk can be waxy and unpleasant tasting, lion fat — like bear fat — can be quite good. He likens lion fat to pork fat, although the two animals have vastly different quantities. (Lions are much leaner.).

A common concern that many people have with lion and bear meat is trichinosis, a food-borne disease caused by a parasitic worm that lives in meat-eating animals. The worm doesn’t seem to bother mountain lions, but it does affect humans and can be fatal if left untreated. Historically, most people contracted trichinosis from eating undercooked or raw pork, but advances in commercial food and farming regulations have largely lowered the risk, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. There is still a risk with meat from mountain lions, wild boar, and bears, but it’s minimal: the CDC reports that the U.S. only sees about 15 confirmed cases per year.

In a recent development, while the risk of contracting trichinosis to humans is low, it still exists. That means hunters need to be sure they kill those parasitic larvae before eating.

Read Next: 6 Wild-Game Rituals That Are About Much More Than the Meat.

According to recent reports, to safely prepare mountain lion meat, don’t cook it rare or medium-rare. Instead, cook it thoroughly to an internal temperature of 165 degrees Fahrenheit. The CDC also notes that “Curing (salting), drying, smoking, or microwaving meat alone does not consistently kill infective worms. Homemade jerky and sausage were the cause of many cases of [trichinosis] reported to CDC in the past.”.

Because most lion hunters want the cape, Worthington recommends carefully skinning the animal before beginning to remove meat. From there, butchering a mountain lion is similar to quartering and butchering an ungulate. Just be sure to field dress your lion as rapidly as possible. Because lions eat other animals, their guts can cause the meat to spoil quicker than a deer’s, Worthington says.

For hunters who are unable to pack out an animal whole, consider the gutless method and remove the front and hind quarters, backstraps, and edible portions of the neck.

It has been revealed that worthington cautions that, depending on the size of the cat, the front shoulders may not offer much meat, and the backstraps are often about as round as a hefty bratwurst. But he states they’re still worth saving to cook later.

Recent findings suggest that dan Thompson, Wyoming Game and Fish Department’s large carnivore section supervisor, cautions hunters to avoid a lion’s anal glands when skinning and field dressing the animal. The glands, used by cats and dogs to mark their territory, are pungent and can ruin the meat if punctured.

To prevent accidental infection from trichinosis, wear disposable gloves when handling the lion and meat, and wash your hands thoroughly when you’re finished.

It has been revealed that consider dividing meat into roasts, steaks, and ground burger. Ellsbury and Thompson both recommend slow cooking roasts in a crock pot with carnitas seasonings to make tender tacos, or with barbecue seasonings to create pulled lion sandwiches.

In a recent development, you can also marinate and grill steaks. But while you need to make sure the internal temperature reaches 165, be careful not to overcook lion meat as it can easily dry out and become tough.

Recent findings suggest that if you’re looking to impress someone who might be skeptical of mountain lion meat, Thompson recommends this recipe for pork stuffed mushrooms by Steph Gaudreau. As with other recipes, you can easily substitute ground lion meat for ground pork.

The Savage Model 99 Is Still One of the Greatest Lever Action Rifles of All Time

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that we may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›.

In a recent development, in the early years of the twentieth century whitetail populations were making a comeback and deer hunting was a growing sport. Lever action rifles ruled the woods for at least the first half of the century and beyond. Even in my early years of hunting in the late sixties, lever actions seemed to fill the gun rack in every deer camp. The most popular was the Winchester Model 94, usually in .30-30, and this rifle dominated the deer woods.

Recent findings suggest that while the 94 was the gun for the masses, the gun guys, the hunters who “knew stuff” had a different pick. The Savage Model 99 rifle was often their choice. While the tube magazine on the Winchester and Marlin lever actions limited the rifles to use with blunt nose bullets, with its rotary box magazine the Savage 1899 could use pointed bullets for a ballistic advantage. It was also strong enough to handle powerful cartridges using that newfangled smokeless powder.

The lever action Model 99 featured an internal hammer and many advanced features like a cocking indicator and even a counter to show the number of cartridges in the magazine. It was simply a more sophisticated design than the other lever actions. The introduction of the .250 Savage cartridge for the Model 1899 in 1915 ushered a new world of deer cartridges. At the time most cartridges barely broke the 2,000 ft/s barrier, but this one hit 3,000 ft/s with an 87-grain bullet. The savviest hunters recognized the advantage over the big, slow, hard kicking, straight walled black powder cartridges that were still in vogue at that time.

Industry observers note that five years later in 1920, Savage changed the name to the Model 99 and introduced the .300 Savage, a cartridge that at the time matched the ballistics of the .30-06. With these advanced cartridges the Savage Model 99 rifle became the thinking man’s deer rifle.

In a recent development, prior to WWI bolt action rifles were almost unheard of for deer hunting and the Savage Model 1899 lever action rifle led the industry in innovation and performance. Even after the war when bolt action sporting rifles began to emerge into the market, the Savage remained one of the most popular hunting rifles on earth.

Industry observers note that so how did this rifle come to be? As with many of our great firearms in history it was because of one visionary, Arthur William Savage.

Sources indicate that savage was born in Kingston, Jamaica on May 13, 1857. He received an education in the United States and in England, which was probably designed to have him follow in his father’s footsteps and become a government bureaucrat.

But Savage wanted adventure, so as soon as they handed him his diploma he hightailed it for Australia to look for black opals and interesting experiences, as Teddy Roosevelt called them.

In a recent development, at some point he was captured by aborigines and held captive for a year. One version of the story claims that his captors demanded a ransom, but his family refused to pay. The historian was unable to provide details as to why, but I suspect that Christmas dinners with his family were a bit tense after his escape.

In a recent development, savage explored the wild Australian interior in a covered wagon. Later he became the owner of the largest cattle ranch down under. He married Annie Bryant while there and eventually had four sons and four daughters. After eleven years in Australia, Savage returned to Jamaica at the age of 34 to grow coffee.

Sources indicate that savage loved firearms and machinery. He was always tinkering on latest ideas. He improved the British service rifle. Among his inventions was a torpedo that he sold to the government of Brazil. He also developed the recoilless rifle and the detachable rifle magazine. Savage soon recognized that the future was in America, not Jamaica.

It has been revealed that he traveled to Newly introduced York where he took a job managing the Utica Belt Line railroad in Utica, NY. In his spare time he developed a hammerless, lever-action rifle. He patented the design in 1893 with an unwavering belief that this gun would lead the way into a new world of firearms. With a few investors, he founded Savage Arms in 1894.

It has been revealed that it took courage to open a gun manufacturer in a field that was dominated by Winchester, Remington, and Colt, but Savage recognized that the newly invented smokeless powder was about to change the rifle world and that the low-pressure, big-bore, rifle cartridges were going to become obsolete. Europe was already using smokeless powder in some cartridges and here in America in 1892, the Army had adopted the .30-40 Krag as our first smokeless powder cartridge. Some sporting rifles were chambered for this latest cartridge and Savage could see the future was with small bore, high velocity smokeless powder cartridges.

The first Savage rifle was the Model 1892, although it never got into production. Savage built it to compete for a military contract, which ultimately went to the .30-40 Krag bolt action. Savage continued to work on the design and it evolved into the Model 1895. That rifle won a contract to supply rifles for the New York National Guard. But politics prevailed, as it always has and probably always will in NY, so the contract was cancelled. The poor soldiers were sent off to fight in the Spanish-American war with obsolete single-shot trapdoor Springfield rifles.

According to recent reports, with the Model 1895 rifle Savage also introduced a new cartridge, the .303 Savage, a bottle-necked, .30-caliber (.311 diameter bullet) cartridge designed for smokeless powder. Savage created the cartridge with a military contract in mind, but that never developed so he turned to the sporting rifle market.

In a recent development, the Model 1895 rifle, which was reported to have been built by Marlin Firearms Manufacturer for Savage, was revolutionary as it was designed to use modern, bottle-necked, smokeless powder cartridges and could handle pointed bullets. The new, smaller .303 Savage cartridge had to compete with the physically larger and more popular cartridges of the day, like the .45-70 Government. At the time the public still equated killing power with physical size and convincing them that technology would allow this diminutive cartridge to perform better than those claiming brute size as their biggest asset would define the struggle for success.

Recent findings suggest that proving he understood marketing as well as design, Savage started running testimonials in his catalog about the effectiveness of the newly introduced cartridge. In those days the catalog not only displayed the products, but it was a source of information for hunters and gun owners in the era before internet, television, or radio. Savage recognized that and ran first person accounts of one-shot kills with the .303 Savage on moose, deer, caribou, sheep and even grizzly bears. But the clincher was from an Alaska resident who killed a whale with a single shot from the .303 Savage.

The Model 1895 evolved into the Model 1899 rifle. That went on to become of the most successful hunting rifles in history. On March 22, 1960 Savage presented the NRA with the one millionth rifle made. No one is quite sure about the total sales number, but it would continue to be made for 38 more years.

A little known fact is that Savage did much of the development work on his early rifles using the machinery at the Remington factory. It’s noted that he offered his lever action design to Remington.

Industry observers note that remington and Winchester were owned by the same company at the time and it’s thought that Remington was being locked out of the lever action market by upper management. Winchester didn’t want the competition. It’s what led to Remington developing their semi-auto and pump action line of hunting rifles.

But if you think about it, if those in charge had a little more foresight and had allowed Remington to dip a toe into the lever action market the Model 99 would have had the Remington name on it and Savage Arms might never have existed.

Industry observers note that savage was a restless soul and in 1904 he sold his interest in the tech giant to a group of businessmen and headed west to California. There he started the Savage Tire Company, which grew to employ as many as 2,000 people at one time. It’s mentioned that he invented the radial tire. Later he would have citrus groves, drill for oil and mine for gold. He died in 1938 at the age of 81. His was a life well lived and his lasting legacy would be the Model 99 rifle.

Savage Arms of course continued on without Arthur Savage and by the 1920s it became the largest firearms company in the free world.

In what was probably the start of a Savage tradition, the Model 1899 and 99 rifles were made in a dizzying number of models and configurations. At one time there were more than 700 SKUs of the Savage Model 110 rifle. I am not sure the Model 99 matched that, but it sure tried. Entire books have been written about the various models of this rifle.

Industry observers note that there were octagon and half octagon barrels. Carbines and rifles with barrel lengths from 20 inches to 26 inches. The military musket had a 28-inch barrel. The 1895 had a 30-inch tube. There was even a model with a .410 shotgun barrel. Some had a saddle ring and others had deluxe wood. Still others had deluxe wood and fancy engraving. Some rifles had cut checkering and many had no checkering at all. In later years as they tried to cut production costs and ultimately ruined the rifle, some of those stocks had pressed in rifling. Some 99s had straight levers and grips, but most had curved levers with a pistol grip. The forends ranged from Schnabel to a plane Jane straight forend. Some rifles were take-down and others were not. Some came with tang mounted peep sights and others with a very innovative scope mount. It wasn’t until 1950 that Savage started drilling and tapping the rifles at the factory for scope mounting. Some carbine models had a barrel band, but most models did not. The rotary magazine was at some point modified to remove the counting window and the traditional brass was replaced with steel. In 1965 they introduced the “C” model which featured a detachable “clip” magazine. (Yes, they called it a clip. No matter what they tell you on the internet, “clip” was a commonly used term to describe removable magazines in sporting rifles for decades.).

Recent findings suggest that the Savage Model 99 features a hammerless design with a much faster lock time than a traditional lever action. The lever is connected to the breech bolt by a long, wide, curving piece of metal. This gives the rifle a distinctive profile when the action is open. The breech block locks into the action as the lever is closed creating a strong action design that is suitable to modern high-pressure cartridges. While it’s not often noted, the Model 99 action is a controlled round feed design. That means that the extractor captures the cartridge as it exits the magazine and holds it against the bolt face during its travel into the rifle’s chamber. There is a cocking indicator in the form of a pin that sticks out of the top of the action when the gun is cocked and recedes inside when it is not.

It has been revealed that the stock is two pieces with separate forend and buttstock. The bottom of the metal action is rounded which makes this rifle a delight to carry in your hand.

The safety is a small catch on the right side of the lever. Pushed forward it locks the lever shut and prevents the rifle from firing. Pulled back it is in the fire position. This is opposite of the more common safeties seen on modern rifles where back is safe and forward is fire. Shooters were smart enough to know the difference back then. Sometime in the mid-sixties a top-tang shotgun style safety was added on some models, but the traditional style lever locking safety remained more popular.

In a recent development, the .303 Savage was the first cartridge introduced in 1895. It was more or less a ballistic twin to the .30-30 introduced the same year. These were the first sporting cartridges designed for smokeless powder and it’s debatable which one was first. The .303 Savage is a handloading-only deal now, but I have always wanted one just because. My friend Lane Pearce just bought one and called to gloat. I hate him.

The .22 Savage High Power was next. It was designed by Charles Newton and introduced in the Model 99 in 1912. It was based on the .25-35 Winchester cartridge necked down to take a .228-diameter bullet. With a 70 grain bullet and a muzzle velocity of 2,800 ft/s it was marketed for big game. In fact, Savage ran testimonials of foolish feats like a 400-pound Tiger taken by Reverend H. R. Caldwell with .22 Savage Hi-Power. Or W.M.D. Bell, the demigod of inadequate rifle cartridges, shooting a Cape buffalo with one. I am sure that probably sold some guns and no doubt got some people killed. But, the truth won out and the cartridge lost favor. Not saying I don’t want one; I do, but not for hunting big game.

Next came the Newton designed .250-3000, which is simply called the .250 Savage today. Newton designed it with a 100 grain bullet, but the marketing folks at Savage wanted that “3000” in the name and reduced the bullet weight to 87 grains to achieve that goal. Terminal performance was erratic until the ammo companies finally listened to Newton and made ammo with a 100 grain bullet. Sadly, he never saw it come to fruition as he died just before the ammo was introduced.

The .300 Savage is the flagship. It was 1920 and the war was over. The doughboys coming home had seen the .30-06 in action and they were impressed. Savage knew that the cartridge would not work in the Model 99, so they created one that would. They shortened the .30-06 case, made a short neck and a sharp shoulder so they could pack all the powder possible into the case. The result was a 150-grain bullet at 2,700 ft/s. That matched the sporting load for the .30-06 at the time. (The velocity was later increased in the .30-06 to 2,900 ft/s.) The .300 Savage soon became one of the most popular hunting cartridges and many gun makers other than Savage chambered it in their rifles. In addition to my Savage Model 99 I have a Remington Model 760 pump action and a Remington Model 722 bolt action rifle in .300 Savage, two of the more popular rifles in that cartridge.

When the military was looking for a new short action cartridge they looked at the .300 Savage. In the end they modified the case to create the 7.62 NATO which was introduced to the sporting world as the .308 Winchester. The pity is that the .308 killed off the .300 Savage. It wasn’t long before the .308 was outselling the .300 even in the Model 99. I don’t think any major rifle maker offers the .300 Savage today. Not even Savage.

It has been revealed that the Model 99 has been chambered for a lot of cartridges over its life span. See the list below. In addition to the .303 and .22 HP my bucket list includes a .358 Winchester and the very rare .284 Winchester. The trouble is, the folks I have encountered selling them are asking prices that make a gun writer question his career choices.

The cartridges chambered in the Savage Model 1899 and Savage Model 99 over the years.

The early guns were not clearly marked with model information and trying to figure out which model a gun is can drive a Baptist Deacon to a hard drink. Mine is a 99-EG as far as I can figure out. It was made in 1936 and has smooth, non-checkered wood, which adds a premium to the value. But, it hardly matters now. At some point the gun was drilled and tapped for a scope, which detracts from the collector’s value but adds to the “usability” of the rifle. There is a Weaver 1.5-4.5 Wide Angle scope on it with Weaver mounts. This TV screen scope was introduced in 1973 to compete with the Redfield Widefield scopes and it makes me think it was added to the rifle in the mid-seventies. Sling swivels have also been added and at some point a skilled craftsman repaired a cracked stock. Which means this is no collector’s rifle. That suits me fine; I bought it to hunt with, just as Arthur Savage intended.

My rifle has what I think is the 1926 style front sight ramp that is integral with the barrel. I have to wonder what that would cost to reproduce today. The rifle sold in 1939 for $47.00. So I am guessing that when mine was made three years earlier it was maybe $45.00? That barely buys a box of ammo today.

Sources indicate that it was a sad day in 1998 when I got a call from the marketing director of Savage to inform me that the Model 99 was being discontinued. I had a gun on loan for an article which with that call changed its focus. The gun was shabbily made and unlike the elegant 99s of the past, it felt like a dead fence post in my hands. The truth is, if this is all they could produce, it was time to stop. I should have bought it at the very good price he offered, but I didn’t. I returned it to Savage and mourned the end of a dynasty.

Read Next: The 300 Savage: A (Nearly) Perfect Mid-Range Hunting Cartridge.

In a recent development, savage experienced some hard times shortly after the Model 99 was dropped. Ron Colburn took over the company and made a drastic move to drop every single product except the Model 110. Everybody said he was crazy, but he saved the company. Savage today is healthy, vibrant, and is building good guns.

Once Ron’s brilliance became apparent and Savage began growing and prospering we all asked when he would bring back the Model 99.

“Never,” he noted with his Irish brogue. “It’s just too expensive to make because it requires a lot of hand fitting of parts. Besides, the market isn’t there anymore. I wish it wasn’t true, I dearly love the rifle, but that’s reality.”.

Ron never wavered from that until the day he retired.

The same question came up with the current owners during a press conference in early 2020 and the Savage folks provided the same answer almost by rote.

Most recently I contacted Jessica Treglia, Sr. Brand Manager at Savage Arms. Here is what she said:.

Industry observers note that “We have no current aims to bring back the M99. The cost to manufacture this gun would push the price above $1500 and would not be well received by our customers and thus the volume would not cover the cost to tool up to make the rifle. That said, a lever action is not in our current plan but is on the long term one. It will not, however, be a M99.”.

In a recent development, I am of the belief that this “conventional” wisdom is wrong. Much has changed since the Model 99 stopped production. The “high cost due to the labor of hand fitting the parts” is no longer an excuse.

With modern computer controlled machinery and newly introduced manufacturing techniques Savage can reduce greatly the labor cost. I am of the belief that the rifle could be made and sold at a price the market will accept.

Read Next: The Best Lever-Action Rifles.

Industry observers note that the question is simply that, the market. Is it there to support a return of the rifle? Sadly, I think the answer is no. The world has moved on. There is a bit of a nostalgic return of interest in lever-action rifles and surprisingly some movement to using them as self-defense rifles in states with harsh gun laws. But, that is aimed at the more traditional lever actions. Sure, a lot of the diehard gun guys would buy a new Model 99 if it was properly made. But, sadly, there just are not enough of us to justify the cost of bringing it back. However, with Savage’s new ownership … who knows what the future might hold.

‘My Knees Got Weak.’ Bowhunter Arrows 222-Inch Buck After Almost Leaving His Stand Twice

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (654 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that carpenter Enos Miller climbed into a 15-foot ladder stand overlooking a cut beanfield the afternoon of Nov.
  • “I had a ladder stand in a grown-up fence row along the edge of a bean field,” Miller tells Outdoor Life.
  • Reluctantly, Miller stayed on his stand despite the disruption, remaining patient and watchful.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that carpenter Enos Miller climbed into a 15-foot ladder stand overlooking a cut beanfield the afternoon of Nov. 11. It was a private farm in Northern Ohio that he’d hunted a few times.

“I had a ladder stand in a grown-up fence row along the edge of a bean field,” Miller tells Outdoor Life. “I got in the stand and started getting ready to hunt when a train suddenly appeared rolling along the tracks not too far away … I figured it would go by, but it stopped. I thought no deer was going to come by with a train nearby.”.

Reluctantly, Miller stayed on his stand despite the disruption, remaining patient and watchful. Then a woodchipper started working very close to his stand.

“I figured that was it for the hunt,” says the 35-year-old from Ashland County. “I gathered my gear for leaving the stand again. But 400 yards away on the far side of the field I spotted a deer, and through my binoculars I saw it was a nice buck.”.

“I decided to stay in my stand and just watch the deer to learn more about it and maybe hunt a different spot another day.”.

Miller monitored the giant buck for 90 minutes as it chased a half-dozen does around far across the field.

In a recent development, as evening approached, a small buck and a doe appeared on the field edge near Miller. And that seemed to get the attention of the distant buck.

Industry observers note that “The does he’d been after across the field were gone, and the substantial buck started toward me and the little buck and doe,” Miller claims. “I knew he was a good buck, but even with binoculars I couldn’t see all the kicker points. I never thought he’d come to me, but he just walked straight in.”.

Miller indicates the buck never looked at him, and when the deer stepped behind some nearby brush, he drew his compound.

“I grunted to stop him, and he looked up at me broadside at 11 yards.”.

Miller released his arrow and the buck took off. The moment was recorded on trail cam footage — the first time his camera had ever captured the buck.

The buck ran 80 yards and piled up. Miller texted his wife and brother that he’d shot a good buck, but he still didn’t realize how exceptional the deer was yet. He waited about 10 minutes before climbing down from his stand.

“When I walked up to recover him my knees got weak, I started counting points, and I thanked the Lord.”.

Soon his family arrived to load the buck into a vehicle and take photos of Miller and his huge whitetail.

The field-dressed buck weighed 190 pounds, and a taxidermist aged it at 5 1/2.

According to recent reports, two days later Miller brought his buck to Toby Hughes, a Buckmasters official who scored the nontypical 29-point deer at 222 4/8 inches. The buck has 27-inch main beams with an inside spread of 20 inches.

Miller’s deer is the 20th buck Hughes has measured at 200 inches or better this year (all but one has been taken in Ohio). Miller’s whitetail also is the 201st buck over 200 inches that Hughes has measured for Buckmasters, almost all of which came from Ohio.

Hughes is just one of over three dozen Buckmasters scorers in Ohio, so the number of bucks scoring 200 inches or more coming from the Buckeye State is truly remarkable.

Read Next: ‘Over the Moon.’ Ohio Hunter Shoots 215-Inch Buck from Her Favorite Stand on Her Birthday.

“God blessed me with this remarkable buck,” Miller claims. “I put in a lot of hours hunting. But to think I almost climbed down out of this stand twice that afternoon … There’s no doubt in my mind that God was watching out for me.”.

The 6 Best Survival Movies of All Time, Plus 2 We Hate

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1675 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that rarely do we tout ways to spend time inside on the couch.
  • Good survival movies, much like the best survival books, are hard to beat.
  • Good survival movies require a few key components.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that rarely do we tout ways to spend time inside on the couch. But we’re a versatile bunch, and everyone needs rest and relaxation every now and then. If you’re going to have a movie night, of course we’re going to recommend films with an outdoor component—particularly ones that involve a bit of a suckfest. In this sense, survival movies are always the right choice.

Good survival movies, much like the best survival books, are hard to beat. But survival movies are really easy to screw up, too. With that in mind, we had to include a couple that really missed the mark. These movies and the stories they tell are good for a lesson on what not to do and how nature doesn’t work.

Good survival movies require a few key components. Without checking these boxes, a survival movie won’t survive this room of tough critics.

Industry observers note that after mulling over the countless options, our editors picked their favorite survival movies of all time based on how realistic, engaging, and stomach-churning they are. Disclaimer: spoilers ahead.

According to recent reports, in 1972 a flight carrying 45 people, including an Uruguayan rugby team, crashed in the remote Andes mountains at high elevation, surrounded by nothing but snow, rock, and sky. After two months of facing the elements, an avalanche, and starvation, only 18 passengers survived—largely by eating the deceased members of their group. Eventually, two of the survivors set out on a journey to find help, one that would take them 38 miles over a 15,000-foot peak. Alive is based on that true story. It’s a film that makes you consider what you would do to survive, and is a great example of the most important survival asset: the will to live. —Scott Einsmann.

Based on the harrowing (and true) survival story of Yossi Ghinsberg, Jungle features Daniel Radcliffe as the adventurous backpacker, anxious to see the unseen and explore the unexplored. A shady guide offers to take him deep into the Bolivian jungle where the group is separated and Ghinsberg must find his own way out of the rainforest. Natural horrors abound and, eventually, our hero is forced to cut open his own forehead. I found the movie dark, realistic, and skin crawling. The film keeps you invested with every fresh hell Ghinsberg faces, and provokes disturbing thoughts about human nature, adventure tourism, and the lengths you might go to escape the mundane in pursuit of an authentic and extraordinary life. —Ashley Thess.

According to recent reports, the story of Hugh Glass’ 200-mile odyssey is one of the great frontier survival tales of all time. Who cares if Leonardo DiCaprio’s portrayal of the story is largely fictionalized. The film’s scenery is stunning, the action is thrilling, and the bear mauling scene is brutal and iconic. If nothing else, DiCaprio does a good job portraying how horrible the whole experience must have been. If you want a more realistic retelling of Hugh Glass’ adventure, try reading Lord Grizzly. —Alex Robinson.

Industry observers note that the Way Back is one of my favorite survival movies. It’s based on the true story of a few Soviet prisoners who escaped a Siberian Gulag and adapted from the book, The Long Walk, and follows the characters as they walk south across the Gobi desert, communist China, and ultimately arrive in India. I know how bad it hurts to trek around the mountains of Alaska for two weeks at a time with all the modern backpacker’s comforts. This is an unfathomable story of persistence and survival. —Tyler Freel.

It has been revealed that I’ve seen a number of mountaineering documentaries and docudramas (go watch The Alpinist now if you haven’t seen it yet) but the one that lives rent-free in my head is Touching the Void. It reenacts the true story of two climbers, Joe Simpson and Simon Yates, who were attempting a first ascent of the West Face of Siula Grande in Peru. They do make it to the top, but things go downhill (literally and figuratively) after that: bones are broken, storms ensue. At what appears to be the crux of the story, Yates is forced to cut the rope during a belay (lest both men be killed) and Simpson crashes through the glacier into a deep crevasse.

It has been revealed that yates, believing his partner dead, returns to their basecamp. But Simpson isn’t dead, simply too deep in the crevasse to call up to the surface for help. I won’t spoil what happens next but it’s a survival maneuver that still has me in awe 20 years later. —Laura Lancaster.

Sources indicate that based on the true story and #1 New York Times Bestseller by the same title, Unbroken follows Olympic track star Louis Zamperini as he goes from fame and glory in the 1936 Berlin games to the lowest lows a human can endure. After enlisting in the Army Air Corps at the onset of World War II, Zamperini’s plane goes down over the vast South Pacific, forcing him and two comrades, Phil and Mac, to survive for weeks in a pair of scarcely-supplied life rafts floating over shark-infested waters in enemy territory. They survive by fishing with hooks baited with seagull meat, catching rainwater, and wrestling small sharks out of the water with their bare hands. After 47 days adrift, during which time Mac dies, Zamperini and Phil aren’t exactly rescued. Instead, their salvation comes in the form of capture, imprisonment, and torture by the Japanese military.

What makes Zamperini’s story one of the best survival tales of all time? Just when the harrowing wilderness survival component comes to an end, the real hell begins. —Katie Hill.

Based on a true story, Into the Wild is one of the worst survival movies, and not least because the hero dies. From a survival standpoint, Chris McCandless was horribly unprepared to survive independently on the Alaskan landscape, and he would have probably succumbed earlier had he not found the bus. Also, he wasn’t in a very remote area. My family used the bus as our hunting camp until 1972, and would drive their pickup trucks out there. Unfortunately for McCandless, he decided to turn back too late, and unfortunately for the bus, it was forever turned into a tourist trap and, ultimately, removed from the landscape. –Tyler Freel.

This prequel to Predator is set in 1719 and only worth watching if you can suspend disbelief. Cool sci-fi movie? Definitely. Interesting characters? Sure. Accurate survival movie? Absolutely not.

The protagonist, Naru, is a Comanche teen desperate to prove herself a hunter and warrior among male peers. The script, however, has her perform all kinds of super-human stunts. Naru spooks a buck she’s trying to kill with a tomahawk and proceeds to run alongside it at top speed through the timber. While chasing the deer, Naru’s dog somehow trips a double long spring foothold trap with the tip of his tail. The running buck sounds like a galloping horse, complete with a whinny and bull elk chirps. Any outdoorsman can spot the problems. Later, Naru attempts to kill a mountain lion by using herself as live bait, a creative interpretation of big-cat hunting tactics. Worst of all, she manages to outrun and outswim a charging grizzly bear—which can cover 20 yards in a single second—while calf-deep in a river.

According to recent reports, the movie is set in the northern Great Plains but highlights sweeping landscapes of the Canadian Rockies. (Since I don’t know what kind of tech the Predator was working with, I’ll overlook how his thermal imaging was foiled by metabolization of a flower that “cools the blood,” rendering a warm human body invisible to heat signatures in mere seconds.) I can set aside realism to entertain most any sci-fi world, but this movie takes place on Planet Earth, with real wildlife and real people. Indeed, the whole plot hinges on human resourcefulness. True wilderness survival is in the details, and Prey gets them all wrong. —Natalie Krebs.

It has been revealed that research has shown that we get hooked on survival movies and reveals because we experience adrenaline-inducing situations without the negative emotions of being in immediate danger. In this sense, watching survival movies is sort of like seeing great white sharks from inside an underwater cage or soaring in a skydiving simulator. Plus, survival movies usually come with a healthy dose of character development, nail-biting action, and occasional romance.

Sources indicate that while it’s difficult to track down the first survival movie, films like The Sea Beast (1926), Five Came Back (1939), and Lifeboat (1944) are some of the earliest survival films ever made. The Sea Beast was the first movie ever based on Herman Melville’s Moby Dick. Five Came Back is about an airplane with a varied mix of passengers that crashes in the Amazon. Lifeboat is about, well, a lifeboat, and its passengers who must survive on emergency rations in the wake of a Nazi U-boat torpedoing and sinking their passenger ship.

Survival movies can teach us many lessons. We can learn from the mistakes protagonists make that land them in difficult situations and we can learn from their ingenuity that ultimately leads to their rescue. These movies also inform us how to gear up for our next adventure (or, at least, what to look for in the best survival kits). We can also consider our own actions in similar situations and learn a thing or two about our own abilities and morals. How far would you go to survive in these situations?

In a recent development, nothing compares to a really good survival movie. They can take you from the highest highs to the lowest lows and back again, all within a few hours. The next time you’re trying to choose between the same old horror flicks or true crime docs, take a walk on the wild side and pick one of our favorite survival movies instead. Ration your popcorn accordingly.

Recent findings suggest that savvy shoppers know Black Friday is the Super Bowl of savings. These days, it’s more like Black Friday Week, which gives us even more time to browse the best deals.

For skiers, there’s no better time to refresh your gear closet than November, when you start taking stock of what you own and what you need for the season. The good news is that Evo is a one-stop shop for everything from hard goods to travel bags, and the deals are plentiful. Keep reading to see what the SKI team is recommending from Evo’s big Black Friday sale.

We’ll admit it’s not the sexiest gift on anyone’s list, but Evo’s Roller Ski Bag is on sale, and it’s a no-brainer for ski travelers who want to bring their own skis and ensure they arrive safely at their destination. The bag has wheels, which is essential for hauling skis through airports and parking lots. It also holds up to two pairs of skis, poles, boots, outerwear, and accessories, all in padded, durable compartments. Internal straps keep everything in place, and the bag folds up for compact storage between trips. —Samantha Berman.

I’ve long appreciated the Arc’teryx Sentinel for its clean, understated design and thoughtful features. It’s a serious technical shell without a lot of unnecessary bells and whistles, and the weather protection is hard to beat.

Sources indicate that what I especially like is the longer, freeride-inspired silhouette, which provides plenty of coverage over my hips and works well with bibs. The fit feels streamlined without being restrictive, and I can comfortably wear a lightweight puffy underneath on colder days. When the weather turns, the three-layer GORE-TEX construction and helmet-compatible StormHood help seal out wind and snow.

The latest Sentinel has been updated with a tougher 100-denier face fabric, a refined fit, larger hand pockets, and a upcoming chest pocket. It’s also designed for moving between the resort and backcountry, which is exactly the kind of versatility I look for in a shell.

Sources indicate that the fabric is on the stiffer side, especially when latest, and takes a little time to break in. But it isn’t excessively loud or crunchy, and I appreciate that rugged feel in a jacket designed for years of hard use. The Sentinel is a significant investment, so finding one on sale makes it a lot more appealing. —Sierra Shafer.

I’m a major fan of getting dressed for skiing in the lodge instead of the parking lot, so I’m usually hauling my skis, boots, and assorted gear from the car. The Yardsale Day Bag makes that whole process a lot easier.

It has been revealed that at 30 liters, it’s roomy enough to fit everything I need without becoming a bottomless black hole. The magnetic closures, internal divider, dedicated pockets, and key ring help keep smaller items organized, while the cinch closure makes it easy to throw in bulkier gear without worrying about things falling out. There’s even a padded laptop sleeve for days when I’m working from the mountain and hoping to sneak in a few lunch laps.

One of my favorite details is the suitcase sleeve, which lets me slide the bag securely over my rolling carry-on when I travel. No more tote bag constantly slipping off my shoulder or luggage at the airport.

It’s also plenty durable. I’ve shoved it under countless lodge tables, dragged it around on trips, and even spilled what appears to have been an entire glass of red wine inside it. Most of the evidence came out in the wash, and I still reach for this bag constantly. —SS.

Industry observers note that I’m firmly in the mittens-over-gloves camp. They’re warmer, more comfortable, and I’ve been skiing in Oyuki mittens for years. Sources indicate that when I reach for an insulated jacket on a resort ski day, odds are high it’s the Halfdays Georgie puffer. The Stio Pinion Down Hooded Jacket is one of those versatile layers that earns its keep well beyond ski season. According to recent reports, I first fell for the Head Kore 94 at SKI Test, and it has swiftly become one of my favorites. Its 16-liter capacity keeps you from overstuffing it, while multiple pockets, dual water-bottle sleeves, and a durable recycled-polyester construction make it a practical choice. —SB.

In a recent development, kari Traa makes base layers for the girls who shred. I absolutely love my sets from this brand, founded by an Olympian, and I find that the capri pants never slip down, which is seriously notable when it comes to successful layering. These 100-percent merino wool pieces will keep you warm all day, and when you start to sweat, they’ll keep you dry, too. Mix and match patterns for a fun base layer that’ll last for many seasons to come. —JA.

I’ve skied almost exclusively in Le Bent socks for years, and the Compression Zero Cushion is a favorite. It took me a while to come around to compression socks, but now I appreciate the supportive fit, especially on long days in ski boots.

I prefer a really thin ski sock because I like being able to feel my boot, and Le Bent’s blend of merino wool and bamboo-derived rayon does an excellent job managing moisture. There’s a misconception that thicker socks are always warmer, but a thin, moisture-wicking sock helps keep your feet dry, which goes a long way toward keeping them warm. And in a snug ski boot, extra bulk can compromise fit and circulation.

The compression is noticeable without feeling restrictive, and the socks stay put all day. No sliding, no bunching, no annoying wrinkles inside my boots, even when I’m touring and moving around a lot more than I would on a resort day.

Industry observers note that I also appreciate the height. A Thanksgiving Blizzard Pushed Significant Mule Deer Off the Mountain — and Down to Us

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3175 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This story, “The Buck and The Great Gray Owl,” appeared in the November 1972 concern of Outdoor Life.
  • For at least a mile, I had trudged along a U.S.
  • Recent findings suggest that but following the trail wasn’t always easy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This story, “The Buck and The Great Gray Owl,” appeared in the November 1972 concern of Outdoor Life.

For at least a mile, I had trudged along a U.S. Forest Service trail to avoid hunting through the dense evergreen woods on both sides. There the trees sagged under heavy burdens of snow, and to brush against just one branch was to release a load of it down the back of my neck.

Recent findings suggest that but following the trail wasn’t always easy. In places the blaze marks were obliterated by snow that a high wind had plastered against the tree trunks, and here and there drifts were piled waist-high. Slogging through such deep wet snow can take the joy out of deer hunting, so I decided to head back for the warmth and comfort of the ranch. I elected to take a shortcut rather than to retrace my steps, and that decision proved to be a mistake.

My shortcut led down and around a slope, then crossed an old burned area, now grown up in a thicket, where the newly introduced snow covered a nightmare of crisscrossed deadfalls. Before I reached the far side of the burn, I tripped many times and was wet from chest to toes. I swore out loud the last time I fell, and in that instant three does suddenly sprung from their beds in the snow and fled downhill.

The does did not bounce away in the characteristic stiff-legged manner of mule deer. Instead they hesitated and floundered, now and then up to their bellies in the snow. I threw the rifle to my shoulder and could easily have shot all three, so slow was their progress. But the purpose of my trip was to bag one good buck, and I had a few more days to hunt.

Back in camp, I found George Smith and John Moxley propping wet boots close to a cast-iron stove to dry while a pot of coffee brewed on top.

“Did you see any game?” I asked.

“Not even a fresh track,” George answered.

“We may have started this hunt too late,” John added.

I almost had to agree with John — the three does were the only deer I had seen since arriving at George Smith’s Canyon Creek Ranch. For years George has been guiding hunters from this ranch, located in the Pioneer Mountains of the Beaverhead National Forest, about 17 miles of steep winding road from Melrose, Montana. When John and I couldn’t make our annual Western hunt in time for the October opening of the big-game season, George suggested that we hold off until the season’s last week, which would be the last week in November.

“By that time,” he had written, “the big bucks should be down low and we can have a real trophy hunt. Besides, all my guests will have gone home for Thanksgiving, so Bob and I can join you.”.

Bob is my youngest son, and he was working for the Smith family during the season as a guide and wrangler.

In a recent development, the plan sounded perfect to John and me. John is from Ohio, and I had recently moved from Ohio to Wyoming.

On a crisp bright day in November — perfect weather for substantial-game hunting — I met John at the airport in Butte, Montana. We picked up some supplies and then drove the 60 miles to Canyon Creek Ranch. We arrived well after dusk under a still-clear sky.

It has been revealed that I’d never felt more optimistic about starting a hunt. But two things did bother me. First, we did not see any deer in the headlights of our vehicle on the drive to the ranch. Second, after our arrival George mentioned seeing a great gray owl around the ranch buildings. In that region the great gray is a rare visitor, and according to George it arrives only ahead of a storm.

“The last gray owl I saw,” George recalled, “came just before the worst winter storm in my memory hit this place.”.

Sources indicate that late that night, snow began to fall and a violent wind came up. The snow didn’t stop until more than a foot of white covered the high country — about 7,000 feet at the Canyon Creek Ranch — and the temperature plunged to zero. We did very little hunting, and it was unsuccessful.

In a recent development, “The deer have either bedded down until the blast passes,” George explained, “or moved down to where the snow isn’t so deep. We’ll have to wait and see.”.

At first the waiting wasn’t too bad. I hadn’t seen Bob or George for a year, and we had plenty of stories to swap in the snug ranch atmosphere. Besides, there was a Thanksgiving banquet to cook and eat. But eventually I got restless and wanted to start hunting in spite of the conditions. The result was that we left a good many bootprints in the deep snow without covering much distance or seeing any deer or even any game sign.

Sources indicate that the morning after I saw the does, I started out early. The wind had stopped blowing, but visibility was still poor. Gray clouds hung in the canyons and close to the wooded slopes so that long-range scanning with binoculars was seldom possible. One very effective tactic for hunting in good snow cover in mountainous country is to carefully glass all slopes, particularly south slopes, for game that stands out sharply against the white. The clouds ruled out that tactic.

But the day didn’t pass without excitement. I had crossed a steep draw and, on reaching level ground on the far side, had paused to catch my breath. A moment later I heard animals crashing toward me through an evergreen thicket up ahead. My heart began to pound. I flipped off the safety on my Model 700 Remington 7 mm. Magnum and held the rifle ready. A cow moose followed by a calf stomped into the open and crossed my path without even a sidelong glance in my direction. It was quite a surprise to see them so far from more-typical moose habitat.

Bob had good news back at the ranch that night. He had scouted in another direction and found many tracks.

Recent findings suggest that “They seem to be paralleling Canyon Creek, heading down toward the old ghost camp,” Bob noted. “If the snow’s thinner, we might find them there tomorrow.”.

Recent findings suggest that the next morning was bitterly cold. We gathered in the ranch kitchen and huddled around the cook stove while George carved thick strips of bacon from a slab and mixed up a large bowl of sourdough pancake batter. It is a standard practical joke around Canyon Creek to conceal a round sheet of cardboard inside some unsuspecting diner’s pancake and then watch him try to cut it with a fork. George pulled the trick on John, and we had a good laugh before beginning a cold day.

It has been revealed that it was possible to drive our four-wheel-drive rig partway to where Bob had found sign the day before. We parked our vehicle beside a small tributary of Canyon Creek, now almost completely frozen, and followed it on foot to an open meadow bordered by a wooded slope. There we found Bob’s tracks as well as deer tracks that had been made since his reconnaissance. It was soon evident that a herd of deer had fed along the meadow’s edges; in windswept places they had pawed circular areas free of snow to get at the vegetation underneath. But apparently the deer hadn’t lingered long, and their tracks disappeared in many different directions.

“Our best bet,” George remarked, “is to go separate ways and see what we find.”.

Sources indicate that because George knew the country best, he took a more complicated route, which led through heavy cover, wound around a mountainside, and nearly dead-ended at a steep rocky cliff. He figured that game might be bedded on top or near the face of the cliff.

In a recent development, john and I proceeded together until the meandering tracks appeared to divide into two small herds. Then we separated, planning to meet late in the day on an unimproved road far below.

According to recent reports, one set of the tracks I followed was very large, and I concentrated on it. I walked parallel to the buck’s path on the downwind side while watching far ahead for a glimpse of the animal. That technique had worked well for me on other hunts, and it might work again.

It has been revealed that I was so intent on following the buck that I almost stumbled over a bedded doe. She went flying in a cloud of snow down the slope. Then, before my hands were steady again, a shot cracked in the distance. The shot spooked a second deer about 150 yards to my right. I saw the animal for only an instant and couldn’t tell whether it was my buck. But when I hurried back to the buck’s trail, I found the spot where he had suddenly shifted into high gear.

For the rest of the day I stillhunted slowly but got no action. I was optimistic, however, for at last we were in deer country.

Industry observers note that the shot I’d heard was George’s. He had broken the ice. About a mile from where he’d left John and me, he’d noticed that the tracks of the largest deer became more meandering — often an indication that a deer is seeking a good place to bed. George slowed his own pace accordingly, stopping often to scan thoroughly every bit of mountain terrain in front of him. This is the simplest and oldest of all mule-deer-hunting strategies, and once again it paid off.

Just before George reached a small draw, he stopped. Soon he saw a shape that put him on alert. On the slope slightly above him was the outline of a buck’s rack, somewhat obscured by a screen of brush. In the next moment the deer was on its feet and running. But it was slowed by snow, and it hadn’t gone more than 20 feet when George drilled a shot through the lungs. He found the animal dead 50 yards from where it had been hit.

The buck was an old, heavy five-pointer (Western count) with unusually heavy beams. It was a trophy that even an old-timer in the Montana Rockies could brag about. The buck, even when field-dressed, was a terrible weight to drag to the nearest pickup point. Without the slippery snow and all-downhill going, we would have needed a packhorse or two for the job.

According to recent reports, but the day produced more than a trophy mule deer for George. It also revealed that deer were moving from the high country into lower ranges where food was more available. The farther we had hunted that day, the more fresh tracks we had encountered. John reported jumping 12 deer from a sheltered meadow that, from the amount of tracks and digging in the snow, resembled a livestock pasture. None of the deer had the kind of rack that John was looking for, but his gloom early in the trip had been replaced by enthusiasm.

“Tomorrow,” he predicted to me, “both of us will score.”.

The next morning was overcast, and flurries of snow drifted to the ground as we huddled again around the kitchen stove. After breakfast George drove us to a spot close to where John had seen deer the day before. We had driven along that same trail several times before. Only two days before, John noted, the only track on the new snow had been made by a wandering coyote. Now deer tracks were everywhere.

George left John and me where the road forked. He would pick us up late in the afternoon at a point about two miles farther on.

According to recent reports, few thrills can match walking through woodlands that you know contain game. You are tense and excited, and it’s difficult to slow down and hunt carefully enough.

Recent findings suggest that john and I had scarcely separated when I saw deer running over an open ridge ahead and above me. I didn’t spot any antlers, but no matter. All the animals were out of range and gone before I would have had a shot.

“Slow down,” I said to myself half-aloud. But my pulse was racing.

That day I saw as many muleys as I’ve ever seen on a day’s hunt afoot. We had found a winter deer yard, and collecting venison would have been incredibly easy. But I kept hoping for the massive buck. Actually I did see two together, but they were traveling and already 400 to 500 yards away.

At dusk when I came out again on the road, weary to the bone, I still hadn’t fired a shot. The headlights of George’s vehicle were a welcome sight in the gloom. Even better was the massive buck lashed on top. John had scored, and back at the ranch he told about it.

In a recent development, early in the morning, after his eagerness had spooked a very good buck, John decided to hunt more from the seat of his pants and less by hiking all over the landscape. When he found a good sheltered place, he sat down on a deadfall. Though the mountain slope opposite him seemed empty of game, he studied it through his glasses. Soon he focused on a spike buck, bedded and almost hidden behind a juniper bush. John shifted his gaze slightly upward, and there he saw the kind of buck he wanted.

Sources indicate that the four-pointer was bedded in a cluster of trees and was in deep shadow. But his antlers, outlined against the snow, gave him away. John figured that the range was more than 500 yards — much too far to risk a shot — but that by making good use of the cover on his side of the mountain he could cut the distance in half. He made the stalk successfully, and one shot from his Model 700 Remington .30/06 anchored the buck.

That left one day — the last day of the open season — for me to score.

Perhaps because of the intense cold in the bunkhouse the next morning, the alarm clock didn’t work and George had to awaken me.

“Look out the window,” he called, “and over toward Canyon Creek.”.

Recent findings suggest that there, in the crown of a dead spruce splintered long ago by lightning, sat the great gray owl. Probably another storm was on its way. As a result I wolfed my breakfast and, though I should have known better, got hooked on one of George’s cardboard pancakes.

Industry observers note that george drove me close to the deer yard we had found, and from there I started out on foot. It was not a pleasant morning to be afield. Scattered snow flurries were being driven by a wild bitter wind, which was rapidly obliterating deer tracks and which made cautious hunting — stopping often to scan the slopes — very difficult. I had to keep moving to keep warm. By mid-morning I had found very few fresh tracks and had seen no deer. I figured that all or at least most of the deer had already moved to even lower elevations ahead of the new storm. My chances looked very poor.

At noon I found some deadfalls on the edge of a dense spruce thicket that furnished a fairly good windbreak, and I sat down to munch a sandwich and a candy bar. The place also gave me a good view, between snow squalls, of distant, partly timbered mountainsides. Through binoculars I examined the wooded slopes, concentrating on those farthest away. As I glassed, I caught a slight movement much closer. Refocusing the glasses, I saw a forkhorn traveling slowly down the hill below me. He was less than 200 yards away, and though the crosswind wasn’t the best for shooting, it would not give me away.

Industry observers note that I decided I would have to take the forkhorn or get nothing at all. Slowly I raised my rifle and found a rest for it on the deadfall. The shot would have been easy, but as I was about to squeeze off, a second forkhorn strolled out into the open. Then, right behind him, came a third buck.

Recent findings suggest that at first I could see only the body of the third buck in my scope. But that was enough to tell me he was substantial. As I watched, the buck changed direction and was hidden from view again. Should I take a chance and play the waiting game, or shoot one of the forkhorns, still in sight?

The significant buck resolved my indecision when he appeared again. This time I could see his splendid rack. My 7 mm. was sighted-in for 200 yards, so I held the crosshairs on the point of the shoulder, adjusted for windage, and squeezed. The deer lurched forward, out of view; I didn’t know whether I’d connected.

I hurried down the steep slope and waded through a deep drift in a gully. I found the buck lying dead against a tree trunk. He was a fine four-pointer and as heavy a mule deer as I’ve ever bagged.

That evening the great gray owl proved to be an accurate prophet. Another storm pounded the Rockies and plastered the high country with another layer of snow. But back at the ranch, I barely noticed it.

“The idea of the late hunt,” John remarked, “was sure a great one.”.

According to recent reports, A Montana nonresident significant-game license costs $151. A deer-only license, which entitles the holder to one deer in a specified district, is $35, plus $1 for a conservation license. This year the general season on deer in Montana runs from October 22 to November 26. But prospective hunters should write the Montana Fish and Game Department, Helena, Montana 59601, for a copy of the detailed hunting regulations.

According to recent reports, the tag end of the season can be a good time for any big-game hunt. Almost everywhere in the West, the odds for connecting with a trophy head may be improved then, simply because the animals are not so high and are easier to find. Of course, there are unseasonably warm years when animals are not driven downward by deep snow until after the season ends. Remember too that late-season hunting can be very rugged — and occasionally impossible. It’s wise to know bad-weather and snow-survival techniques. But these are the chances a sportsman must take. And for my money, the rewards are worth the gamble.

Winter Bivy Sack Guide (2026)

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1459 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sectionhiker

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Winter bivy sacks were first developed as solo shelters for mountaineering and climbing where participants were interested in lightweight and highly compressible camping gear.
  • Winter bivy sacks are different from three-season bivy sacks, which are often used in conjunction with a tarp for insect and splashback protection, where rain hitting the ground can bounce back and wet your quilt or sleeping bag.
  • Recent findings suggest that the biggest advantage of a winter bivy sack is that you can use it anywhere you want to stop and sleep.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Winter bivy sacks were first developed as solo shelters for mountaineering and climbing where participants were interested in lightweight and highly compressible camping gear. Bivy Sacks are also an attractive option for backpacking hunters, backcountry skiers, and winter backpackers who want the lightest and smallest shelter they can carry for overnight or emergency use.

Winter bivy sacks are different from three-season bivy sacks, which are often used in conjunction with a tarp for insect and splashback protection, where rain hitting the ground can bounce back and wet your quilt or sleeping bag. In contrast, a winter bivy sack is intended as a standalone shelter or used with a snow shelter such as a trench or snow cave. Winter bivy sacks tend to be much higher in volume to hold winter-weight sleeping bags without compressing the insulation and work best in dry and cold conditions where precipitation is in the form of snow.

Recent findings suggest that the biggest advantage of a winter bivy sack is that you can use it anywhere you want to stop and sleep. Most models don’t require tent stakes or poles, and they pack down very small, which is great when you want to keep your winter gear lightweight and compact. Most winter bivy sacks use waterproof/breathable top fabrics to reduce internal condensation and waterproof base fabrics to keep your sleeping bag and pad dry. Insect netting is also available in some cold weather bivy sacks and can be useful when they’re used in spring conditions when bugs begin to emerge,.

There are many advantages to sleeping in a waterproof bivy sack over a tent. It is easy to find a place to put a bivy sack at night since it only requires as much space as your sleeping pad and sleeping bag. Simply unroll your bivy sack, slip your sleeping pad and sleeping bag inside, and crawl in. This makes them suitable for sleeping on narrow mountain ledges or in forested glades where there’s just enough space to lie between two trees.

There are no tent stakes to freeze into the ground so you can get inside without delay and get warm. Being waterproof, you don’t have to lie on top of a groundsheet either, since the bottom of a waterproof bivy sack is designed to keep you dry. Bivy sacks also add a few degrees of insulation to your sleep system and make great emergency shelters for solo winter hikers, provided you carry a sleeping pad and enough insulation to get through the night.

Bivy sacks are much more confining than tents, with only enough space for you and a few small personal items. You can’t really do anything inside one except listen to podcasts or go to sleep. It’s awkward to change out of your wet clothes or put on dry clothes inside, depending on the type of bivy sack you have; it can be damn hard to put on your boots, even to go for a pee at night. There’s no place to store your backpack, and the rest of your gear will be fully exposed at night without any cover.

Industry observers note that bivy sacks are also more prone to internal condensation than a tent, even when manufactured with waterproof breathable materials. You’re best off keeping them open or unzipped at night to reduce the temperature difference between the inside of the bivy and the outside, which causes condensation. Tent condensation occurs for the same reason, but tents have better ventilation and more volume, so it’s easier to keep your sleeping bag dry when it occurs.

Industry observers note that despite these disadvantages, I have friends who swear by their winter bivy sacks because they’re so fast to deploy compared to a tent or tarp. I’ve used winter bivy sacks and can appreciate their strengths, but winter nights last a very long time, and it’s nice to have a little extra space to change your clothes or sleep with your gear inside your tent. Whichever you choose depends on what you’re trying to accomplish.

There are three types of winter bivy sacks to choose from:.

There are two types of hooped bivy sacks: those with front entrances that you slide into feet first and those that you can enter from the side. Both come with one more short fiberglass or carbon fiber rods that give shape to the hood and prevent it from collapsing onto your head or torso.

The head-end of a hooped front entrance bivy is usually screened with a solid cover that can be zippered closed for warmth or to block wind or rain. This design provides good ventilation for your head and helps to expel the water vapor in your breath. The Outdoor Research Helium UL Bivy is a good example of the front entry hooped design.

Side-entry hooped bivy sacks usually have a zipper along one side so you can easily get in and out of them. This design is also easier to vent because you can roll up the top cover in dry weather to reduce internal condensation. The Outdoor Research Alpine XT Bivy is a good example of a hooped bivy with a side entrance.

Sources indicate that the simplest and lightest-weight winter bivy sacks are little more than sleeping bag covers. Some have drawstrings that you can pull closed over your head; some have shaped mummy-style hoods or simple slits above the face for ventilation. While not as livable or as well-ventilated as the hooped bivy sack designs described above, they do the job if you want a highly compressible, ultralight weather protection for your sleep system.

There are multiple features and trade-offs to consider when choosing a winter bivy sack.

Sources indicate that A waterproof/breathable top fabric is vital for venting water vapor and reducing internal condensation that can make your sleeping bag wet. However, unlike rain jackets, most bivy sack manufacturers do not list the laboratory measurements used to rate waterproofing (hydrostatic head, abbreviated “HH”) or breathability (movable water transmission rate, abbreviated “MVTR”). That can make performance comparisons between different bivy sacks difficult.

Sources indicate that if headroom matters, consider a bivy shelter with a hooped design. These bivy sacks come with a flexible pole that slides into the hood to create more volume around your face and shoulders. The tradeoff is that they tend to be heavier than more minimal bivy sacks.

According to recent reports, winter bivy sacks tend to be high volume to fit bulky winter sleeping bags and inflatable pads with a high R-value. When choosing a bivy sack you want to ensure that there is enough room for your sleeping bag insulation to fully loft and that it’s not compressed by having too tight a fit.

It’s much easier to get in and out of a bivy sack that has a zipper along the side than one that only has a “hatch” at the head end, to crawl in and out of. You’ll stay drier if the ground is covered in snow and it’s much easier to put on and take off your shoes.

Industry observers note that if you initiative to bivy in early spring when biting insects emerge, make sure to get a winter bivy sack with a mesh panel over the face so you can sleep without insects biting your face at night. If you only plan to sleep in a bivy sack in winter or in snow caves, a mesh panel will be less important. For warmer weather use, I’d encourage you to invest in an ultralight bivy sack or bug shelter rather than a winter bivy sack, since they’re much cooler to use. See our 10 Best Backpacking Bug Shelters for our recommended three-season bivy sacks.

Don’t forget to consider the weight of the bivy sack and its packed size, since one of the chief benefits of using a bivy sack is gear weight and size reduction. There’s often a tradeoff between features and weight/size, but some winter bivy sacks are surprisingly lightweight and compressible.

Industry observers note that when in doubt, order a bivy sack (check the retailer’s return policy) and lie in it at home to see if it fits. This will probably tell you a lot more about whether it will work for you than comparing the specs of multiple models listed online. Check that you can fit your sleeping pad and sleeping bag inside, and that the footbox is large enough for your feet.

Industry observers note that there is a class of emergency bivy sacks that are only intended for emergency use such as the SOL Escape Lite Bivy. These are made with thin reflective aluminized fabric and lack the durability or breathability of the multiuse bivy sacks listed above.

From Gangs to Grizzlies

  • A grizzly cub, massive as an overgrown Saint Bernard.
  • “Hey, bear,” I shouted, my voice cracking.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, one summer evening, I was hiking a trail near Marias Pass in Glacier National Park, returning to the car after a few hours of wildlife photography at a lake— nothing but deer and mosquitoes to show for it—when I noticed something blondish-brown moving toward me. It barely registered. I felt relaxed, though, truthfully, I’m never fully relaxed.

And then we were on top of each other.

A grizzly cub, massive as an overgrown Saint Bernard. I was fascinated—until reality hit. The mother wouldn’t be far behind.

“Hey, bear,” I shouted, my voice cracking. The cub woofed an alarm and took off to my left, a dark blur swallowed by the forest.

Recent findings suggest that I turned toward the trail ahead. And—boom—there she was. Running at me, big and fast and flat to the ground.

I grabbed the bear spray strapped to my chest, fumbled the can free, and held it out like a pistol. She closed in. I could see the whites.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We are well into deer season now, and bucks are definitely feeling the pressure. If you’re like the rest of us, you’re probably seeing daylight movement start to decrease on your trail cameras, or maybe it’s already dropped off. I’m right there with you. The places that I hunt see plenty of pressure, even though they’re on private ground. This week on the podcast, I’m talking to our gear editor, Scott Einsmann, who just came back from an incredibly unique experience: He was hunting almost completely unpressured mature bucks in the Midwest. Scott shares what that experience was like, what he learned from it, and how it can help him — and you — back in the real world of deer hunting. —Alex Robinson, editor-in-chief.

Listen to this episode on Apple, Spotify, or wherever you get your podcasts.

Alex Robinson: Hey, Scott, thanks for joining the Outdoor Life Podcast. I want to talk to you about your favorite thing in the world, which is bowhunting for whitetail deer.

Scott Einsmann: Awesome. Let’s do it. I just came off the most amazing week of bowhunting for whitetails.

Alex: Yeah. We’re coming up on the holiday season, and you have a good redemption story, and everybody loves a good redemption story around the holidays. So to start this off, explain the property that you’re able to hunt in Illinois. What’s it like, and how did you weasel your way into getting bowhunting access to this place?

According to recent reports, scott: It’s 800 acres in southern Illinois, and what makes it a really good 800 acres is, one, it has topography, and it also has large wood blocks in it, and it’s surrounded by major ag fields. So once all the crops are cut, all the deer get sucked right into this property. For that reason, it’s just insane hunting. There are really good deer. There’s not a 200-incher on it, but there are a ton of 130- to 150-inch deer, and a ton of really good 8-points — some really cool deer. Last year, some big 6-points were killed, which is always fun. Alex: So talk about whose property it is and how you’re able to get on it, because you’re not a multimillionaire property owner.

Alex: A lot of these properties are either owned or leased by — you know, it’s the stuff that everybody dreams about hunting, but not everybody really gets access to.

In a recent development, scott: Yes. And I did inquire with the farm manager there: How does someone get a lease in this area? You really just have to know the local farmers, because a lot of them have been burned by people leasing their property and not treating it right. So you really have to have someone to vouch for you and then be part of the community.

Luckily, I know someone. Levi Morgan and Andy Morgan have the lease for this property, and they have several leases in the area now, and they’re all pretty incredible. But this one they’ve had the longest — about three years now — and they’re really starting to dial it in and understand how the deer use it.
