#228389. Old-School Wisdom for Deer Hunting During Snowstorms

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 14m • 📚 Deep Dive (2700 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Outdoorlife ↗ Open Full Page

Old-School Wisdom for Deer Hunting During Snowstorms

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2700 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that most whitetail hunters agree that a snowfall is nice for hunting deer.
  • I used to have a recipe for deer tracks, only it wasn’t very filling.
  • Recent findings suggest that hunters tend to forget that tracks show where whitetails have been — not where they are.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that most whitetail hunters agree that a snowfall is nice for hunting deer. “Look at all the tracks you’ll see with snow covering the ground,” they chorus.

I used to have a recipe for deer tracks, only it wasn’t very filling.

Recent findings suggest that hunters tend to forget that tracks show where whitetails have been — not where they are. And tracks may not necessarily indicate where deer are likely to be again. One deer can make a lot of tracks.

But if you know how snowfall changes a whitetail’s daily routine, you are starting to understand where you will find tracks — and the deer that made them.

Let’s rehearse some basic facts.

Recent findings suggest that first, snow normally comes late in most states’ deer seasons. That means whitetails already have been harassed by other hunters. Unless you hunt private land, all deer you are likely to encounter may be wary, even downright spooky. They are moving little during daylight hours. Rutting bucks are probably limiting much of their roaming to the darkness of night.

According to recent reports, second, snowstorms — and most other storms — are accompanied by periods of intensely low barometric pressure. Whitetails tend to roam wide in search of food prior to a storm. But they hole up when snow actually starts to fall. And they stay holed up until the storm passes or at least until it eases off.

Third, while snow means hunters can see deer moving much more easily, it also works the other way around. Deer see the hunter coming a lot farther off. The fact that snow silences the woods forces deer to use their eyes more. Ever spend an hour or two watching a band of deer bedded down after a snowstorm? Their heads are lifted much more often to eyeball the surrounding terrain. Eyes must assume a vigil which ears can no longer accomplish and must provide the essential early warning. Incidentally, your own hearing abilities aren’t helped by snowfall, either. Deer that rustled the crisp frozen leaves of a frosty fall morning won’t be heard walking through a soft cover of newly introduced-fallen snow.

It has been revealed that fourth, snow changes whitetail eating habits — particularly heavy snowfall. Meadow grasses may not be pawed at again until spring. Buds, twigs and surviving leafy vegetation take its place. These plants are less nutritious for deer but they are easier to obtain. Waste grains in fields blown clear of snow may promote a concentration of feeding whitetails.

So now you are thinking that snowfall might not be such a boon to hunting?

Actually, it is — if you know how to use it to your advantage.

In a recent development, whitetails, like all wildlife, are creatures of habit. You can predict a deer’s general reaction to things that impact on its environment. Maybe your predictions won’t be precise but they can be close enough to cut down on the number of fruitless hunting efforts you make.

Pay attention to the weatherman. Be sure you are out hunting on the day before a storm is forecast to arrive. Through changes in barometric pressure, deer sense the oncoming storm. They often move out to feed as heavily as possible — even in the middle of the day — forgoing the usual bedding hours in their hasty urge to stock up before the storm. So be sure to hunt all day.

In a recent development, pre-storm is the time to concentrate on checking food sources for whitetails. Hunting pressure earlier in the season may have forced the animals to visit open grainfields only at night. If hunter numbers have dwindled — as they do in most states after the first four or five days of the season — start checking those fields again at dawn and dusk. The urge to fill up before a storm may have deer less cautious.

According to recent reports, in woodland areas, check hidden openings or meadow edges where wild herbaceous cover remains. Don’t overlook timber cuttings where saplings provide cover and the lack of an overstory promotes the undergrowth that deer savor. Try the creek bottoms where frost may not have killed the green grasses yet.

Sources indicate that in farmlands, glass the local hay fields or even vegetable patches where potatoes, sugar beets, carrots, turnips or other root-type plants have not all been harvested yet. And visit abandoned orchards where fallen fruit may provide an attraction.

According to recent reports, more than once in a late deer season afternoon, while driving the back roads of farm country near where I live, I have become aware of more and more deer suddenly appearing where few were before. The back edge of a cutover hay field will hold five or six deer, all feeding near a heavy hickory and oak woodlot. Harvested cornfields may have a few animals wandering along, plucking up the waste dumped by corn pickers before it can be plowed under.

Does tend to move farther from cover than bucks, particularly when feeding in daylight hours prior to a storm. But expect surprises. Once, while walking across a partially harvested cornfield to reach a gun blind in the woodlot beyond, I stumbled across a fine eight-point buck. This lone deer, feeding in a 12-row patch of standing corn, was fully 80 yards from the nearest heavy cover. He evidently felt safe among the withered cornstalks. And their rattling in the wind had probably masked the sound of my approach.

Industry observers note that I was so startled, in fact, that I never got off a shot from the slug-loaded 12-gauge that I was carrying. The buck wheeled and bounded away before I could shoot.

In a recent development, don’t be caught unprepared. You never know where a deer will suddenly appear. I’ve had does dart from brushy drainage ditches — deep ones that were mostly dry or had the damp patches frozen solid by late fall’s icy weather. Ditches provide perfect cover routes to reach open stretches with food. Shelterbelts do so, too.

It has been revealed that once a storm of some magnitude starts, deer simply disappear. Whitetails of both sexes will head for the thickest most protective cover around. Conifers are ideal (pine plantations or cedar swamps in the North Country). In farmlands, overgrown brushy woodlots or thick river bottom or creekbottom cover is an alternative. Here deer will lie down and, unless disturbed by a hunter wandering around in the storm, they will not get up for hours — maybe days.

Industry observers note that the hollow hair in deer’s coats provides superb insulation from the snow’s cold and dampness. Curled up into a small oval (judge for yourself how compactly a whitetail can curl up by the sizes of the beds you’ll find a day or so later) deer will ride out the storm, sometimes allowing the snowfall to almost literally cover them. They don’t seek food and they don’t move much — even to stand and stretch.

Because hunters don’t normally slog around in heavy storms, deer are usually undisturbed until the snowfall begins to lessen. If a storm lasts more than a day, deer may move around close to their bedding areas but they won’t venture far.

It is an ideal time, once the storm begins to subside, to mount a deer drive.

Pinpointing whitetail cover won’t be difficult, even with the lack of tracks on newly introduced-fallen snow. Just pick the heaviest thickest junk around. Match the size of the cover to the number of drivers and standers you have with you, and you should be able to fill several tags for your group.

There is a farmland county near my Michigan home which is a mixture of cedar swamp, brushy woodlots and grainfields, plus some pastureland. Every other season or so, myself and about five of my hunting buddies drive over there on a Saturday. At this time, we’ve all just come back from the North Country’s season opener; perhaps half of us have been fortunate enough to have scored on a buck already. The lucky ones drive for their less successful counterparts.

According to recent reports, through the years, we have secured hunting permission by telephone and by long acquaintance with the local landowners, some of whom join us for these drives. Because this area is open to the use of high-power rifles, it takes only about three or four standers to cover all downwind and sidewind exit routes in the cover we visit.

The remainder of us cast back and forth in a line — more or less — of drivers, working silently in the belief that noise startles deer even more than human scent and sends them into headlong flight. We want the whitetails to break cover in a nervous trot, glancing back over their shoulders, not fleeing at top speed.

Because the drivers move and the deer focus their attention on them, the standers get some easy shots. Standers are urged to find natural blinds that will camouflage just a bit of the brilliance of the Blaze Orange garments they wear.

Drivers wear as much Blaze Orange as possible for high visibility. They don’t carry firearms, either, on our drives.

In a recent development, such minidrives have proved extremely successful. In those years when we all fill tags up north and don’t strategy to visit this county, local landowners call us to see if we’re coming over to help them. It has become a social event. We do go, of course.

According to recent reports, well-conducted drives, frankly, are one of the best ways to kill whitetails all season long — early or late, in snow or without it. If you develop a compatible group of hunters who are all safety conscious, driving may well be the best way to hunt.

It has been revealed that for the single hunter, stillhunting in the snow can prove difficult. The muffling effect snow has on sounds is appealing to stillhunters but they should remember that whitetails bedded in snow can be extremely watchful. That’s true at least while a storm is waning or before the sun reappears with warmth enough to prompt more movement of deer. Whitetails scan their surroundings intently. And because they are not likely to be moving, spotting them will prove that much tougher.

Sources indicate that if a stillhunter is extremely patient and slow moving, maybe he has a chance. But the average hunter who enjoys some success stillhunting on bare ground may find snowy days beyond his capability.

There is another factor making things tougher: wind. Snowstorms are often accompanied by high winds, ones that don’t die off when the snow stops falling. Wind makes all wildlife nervous. Their hearing isn’t as useful. Add that problem to the noise-muffling effect snow already has and you come up with doubly watchful whitetails.

So what about doing what you sometimes hear old-timers describe? Just plant yourself on a substantial buck’s track and walk him into the ground.

Unless you are a true woodsman, which most of us have neither the time nor the inclination to be, forget it. It sounds rather romantic, as the old sporting books told it, but the method isn’t likely to be very rewarding for the hunter of average skill. Oh, it can be done. And every so often you could be lucky enough to actually walk up on a buck — if you can first figure out which tracks belong to bucks and which belong to does. No, the average lone hunter faced with a snowstorm is better off doing just what the deer do: Wait it out.

Recent findings suggest that once the storm passes, whitetails will begin to circulate once again. Hunger drives them from their beds but sunny weather after a storm seems to invigorate deer, too. No scientific facts back up this phenomenon and I claim no insight into the psychology of deer. It’s just a gut feeling I have about whitetails based on observations of the ways yearlings almost cavort after a storm passes. Young bucks, not part of the serious breeding process that is probably about over when snow begins to fall, seem to want to spar. They push each other around rather good naturedly. The older does concentrate on finding food. Now’s the time for the smart single hunter to be on his stand or in his blind.

Surprisingly, there’s little need to hurry in the morning, either. Deer must feel the cold to some degree because they seldom stir at the crack of dawn after a very cold night. That fact doesn’t mean a hunter shouldn’t be out before daybreak — as he would be earlier in the season. Some whitetails may be stirring. But many times after a storm I’ve witnessed deer waiting until the sun was shining full upon them, waiting for an hour or more after daylight, before moving out to feed. It’s as if they were lying there, soaking up the warmth of the sun.

In a recent development, as a result, deer will often be feeding — or moving to and from feeding areas — in the middle of the day after the return of good weather conditions. For the man in a blind, deer moving on snow in full daylight are easy to spot.

In a recent development, remember, also, that bedding areas on southern exposures — places where the effects of the warm sun are felt the most intensely — will be favored by deer. Anytime the temperature is under 35°, deer seem to prefer places where the sun can hit them in the morning. If it is out of prevailing winds, so much the better.

Unlike the majority of Western mule deer, which must move from higher mountain summer range to the valleys each winter, whitetails normally find everything they need to survive in a year-round home. One exception is Michigan’s Upper Peninsula where deer summering in the Lake Superior watershed tend to wander southward toward the more temperate climate of Lake Michigan in late fall and early winter, often before deer season ends. Snowfall prompts even greater movement.

In a recent development, A few of these whitetails travel quite a distance — 40 or maybe 50 miles. Some don’t move at all but take their chances in the deeper snowfall and reduced winter food conditions of the northern watershed. If you are aware of such a migration where you hunt, take advantage of it. The routes traveled are not always as predictable as the game trails muleys use to move downhill but various general routes are used year after year. Spot blinds accordingly.

It has been revealed that the best advice for winter stand hunting, I think, is to stay put and to stay as comfortable as possible. Dress to remain warm in below-freezing temperatures. Make sure that your blind is well situated and that it is constructed in such a way that it blocks out any stray winds. Get a back rest and sit on a patch of canvas or plastic to keep the snow from soaking through.

I always make sure that I have a Thermos of hot coffee, tea or cocoa handy. A blind means you can move around a little without being seen and a few gulps of warm liquid can brighten a dreary day.

Sources indicate that and be patient. Deer won’t move as often or as far in snowy weather — unless it’s a bright warm day with temperatures rising above freezing. If you are hunting alone, be prepared to wait them out. And do it in a place where they’re likely to be: near a food source or along (or in the midst of) the heavier cover where they’re certain to bed down.

Read Next: Old-School Whitetail Wisdom for Deer Hunting When the Weather Finally Turns Cold.

It has been revealed that winter hunting doesn’t have to be a case of survival against the elements. You can be comfortable and successful and see more than just tracks.

This story, “Snowstorm Whitetails,” appeared in the December 1983 concern of Outdoor Life.

#228383. Industry News: The Boyhood Deer Hunt That Turned Jim Carmichel Into a Gun Guy

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 22m • 📚 Deep Dive (4488 w)

Industry News: The Boyhood Deer Hunt That Turned Jim Carmichel Into a Gun Guy

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 22 min read (4488 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~22 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • When I was a skinny, big-footed kid in grammar school, I had the unbelievably good luck of being yanked out of school for several days to go on a deer-hunting vacation with my family.
  • Our hosts were old family friends who had struck it rich and bought an historic plantation in Virginia, complete with antebellum mansion and miles of sweet-scented hardwood forest.
  • On the day we arrived, dressed in our Sunday best, in a gleaming pickup truck, our host had shot a nice buck and it hung in the smokehouse.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When I was a skinny, big-footed kid in grammar school, I had the unbelievably good luck of being yanked out of school for several days to go on a deer-hunting vacation with my family. Nowadays, thanks to the game commission’s deer stocking and management programs, deer are plentiful in the mountains of east Tennessee, but in the 1940s they were nonexistent. That meant that going on a real deer hunt involved traveling hundreds of miles and visiting places as far removed from our farm as was the back side of the moon. It was, to my mind, an elegant adventure, sort of like going to Europe or taking an ocean cruise. Nothing could be finer. My chums were green with envy.

Our hosts were old family friends who had struck it rich and bought an historic plantation in Virginia, complete with antebellum mansion and miles of sweet-scented hardwood forest.

On the day we arrived, dressed in our Sunday best, in a gleaming pickup truck, our host had shot a nice buck and it hung in the smokehouse. I remember inspecting the animal in elaborate detail; feeling the texture of its hair, looking at its teeth and bones and, most of all, marveling at the wonder of its gracefully curved antlers.

Horns, as they grew on cows and bulls, were familiar to me. But antlers were something entirely different — harder, more graceful and certainly more dangerous looking. I nearly lost my senses when told they were shed and regrown every year. For a while I simply didn’t believe it and only gradually allowed myself to be convinced.

Recent findings suggest that and deer could jump, too, higher than a cow or even a horse. My imagination reeled with stories of these wonderful animals.

“Come on,” I said, “nothing can jump a high-wire fence.” So my host took me to a crossing place and demonstrated where the deer-tracked path led up to a fence then continued on the other side. “Wow, they really can do it. Wait till I tell Mom.”.

Next day, after breakfast of deer loin, rich gravy and biscuits, I stood in front of the gun rack, itching to get my hands on a genuine deer rifle and go hunting for these wonderful animals. Already, visions of great stags were dancing through my head.

It has been revealed that my dad took the first rifle, a Model 99 Savage in .250 caliber, and my brother selected a shortened .30/40 Krag. Why, I wondered, had he passed over a truly beautiful Model 141 Remington pump-action rifle in .30 Remington in favor of the Krag? Anyway, I liked the pump and was glad I had a chance to use it. But when I was clear of the barn lot and stopped to load the rifle, his motives became clear. Nearly all of the cartridges had a sharp indentation on the primer, meaning they had previously misfired and were now useless. Of the lot, only three had virgin primers, and these I fed into the rifle with the optimism of youth.

According to recent reports, less than an hour later, I “jumped” a deer literally in his bed. He came up so close to me that for a moment I was so startled I almost turned and ran. He was not the stag of my dreams but he did have antlers, perhaps six points, and he could be mine! At first the buck ran away so fast that it looked as though I wouldn’t have time for a shot, but then he did something that still has me wondering. After running dead away for about 100 yards, he spun around and headed right at me. Clearly, he would pass by within a few feet, and even at full tilt I’d have a fairly easy shot.

Closer he came and the rifle was at my shoulder, my teeth clinched against the fearful recoil, eye squinted over the sights.

“There he is, pull the trigger!”.

In a recent development, “Hurry, he’s getting away. Try another shot!”.

Sources indicate that then the buck whirled again and headed back at me again! He was passing by close enough to hit with a hoe handle.

Tears streamed down my cheeks. Tears of disappointment, tears of frustration and tears of anger. I’d had a better than fair chance and lost it because of grown-ups who’d palmed off a bunch of useless cartridges on me. On the way back to the house, I tried the last cartridge but like its brethren, it only clicked in dismal failure.

It started with a deer rifle that wouldn’t fire and a .22 that missed crows, and I’m still at it, studying, asking questions and, bit by bit, unraveling the puzzles.

Industry observers note that as it turned out, I was the only hunter who’d had a “shot” that day, meaning that on the following morning the gun rack was again emptied of all workable deer rifles. All that was left was a little Mossberg Model 151 Rimfire Autoloader complete with a 4X scope (don’t ask how I remember these details, how could I possibly forget?) and several boxes of Super-X ammo.

The day before, I’d passed a newly disked and seeded field of winter wheat that was covered with crows. Surely they would be there again. “If I can’t shoot a deer, at least I’ll shoot some crows,” I told myself as I lifted the .22 from the rack and pocketed a box of ammo.

The crows were there, within easy range, but my first shot kicked up dust far to the left and lower than where I’d aimed. When the crows settled back I missed again the same way. Clearly the rifle didn’t hit where the scope aimed. Why? The rest of the day, and the days following, were spent unraveling the mysteries of sight adjustment and bullet trajectory. A whole new world of excitement lay before me. So many things to learn about guns and only a lifetime to study them.

It started with a deer rifle that wouldn’t fire and a .22 that missed crows, and I’m still at it, studying, asking questions and, bit by bit, unraveling the puzzles.

A small boy can do worse than go deer hunting, even with a rifle that won’t work.

Every time I look at the 12-point whitetail mounted on my trophy room wall, I wonder if I’d do it over again if I had the chance.

Industry observers note that it was December ’77 and I was after substantial whitetails on the Guajolota (translates to female turkey) Ranch in deep south Texas. When I say big whitetails, I don’t mean just big, but big-big, Texas-big, the kind of big that makes vaqueros (cowboys) whisper “muy grande” in wide-eyed wonder. The Guajolota is a working cow ranch but, like most big spreads in south Texas, it swarms with quail and so many big-antlered whitetails that owner Jim McAllen got the idea that he could make more money “farming” deer than beef.

So true to his stock-breeding tradition (McAllen, Texas, is named after Jim’s pioneer family), he set out to make his herd of deer bigger and better by using the same selective breeding techniques proven in the development of superior beef herds. In Texas, just about everyone who hunts deer either owns land, leases hunting rights or hunts on a “pay per day” ranch. (That “per day” arrangement is not the same sort of operation as the exotic game ranches, which also flourish in Texas.) Accordingly, McAllen figured that if he could breed a “super” race of elk-headed whitetails, hunters would just naturally pay more to hunt on the Guajolota.

The first step in his program was to kill off the “culls” — bucks with skimpy antlers and a tendency to pass on this trait — and save the giant bucks for a while for breeding. The program had been in effect only a few years when I hunted the Guajolota, but signs of its success were abundant on my first morning of hunting.

Accompanied by my pal Jim Nolen, maker of the well-known Nolen knives and guided by Ed Dutch, who at that time was the ranch’s game biologist but has since become a top wildlife photographer, we hid under a mesquite tree where we could look out over a 60-yard flat of open grassland.

In a recent development, with a bit of imagination, you might call the south Texas terrain “brush country,” but it’s not the kind of brush hunting one gets in, say, Pennsylvania or Missouri. Just about everything that grows wild in that part of the Texas empire either sticks, scratches bites or poisons, so stalking deer through the cactus and catclaw isn’t all that much fun. That’s why hunting is usually done from a quick stand or from a high seat that lets you look over the thorny chaparral. Fortunately, there is a high buck-to-doe ratio that makes the bucks especially aggressive and eager to challenge other bucks for available does.

Industry observers note that the sound of these bucks doing battle is a distinctive clicking and rubbing of antlers that can be heard a pretty fair ways and has the effect of calling other bucks to join the fray. If you ever happen to come upon a couple of bucks fighting it out over some does, you’ll probably spot one or two more waiting their turn, and while the fighting is going on, a smarter-than-average Romeo may be trying to make off with the harem.

According to recent reports, many years ago, some deer hunters had the clever idea of banging a couple of deer antlers together to imitate the sounds of a fight and thereby call bucks to the gun. It worked like a charm and “rattling” up bucks has become an accepted form of the hunting arts.

In a recent development, I’ve tried rattling bucks from Maine to California but the only places I’ve had much success were in areas of dense deer population where there were plenty of aggressive bucks. South Texas is the home of rattling, with both the terrain and temperament of the bucks ideally suited for the technique. The trick, though, in addition to knowing how to rattle the antlers together, is finding a stand that gives you a fairly good view of at least an acre or so of relatively open space.

It has been revealed that some bucks apparently lose all reason at the sound of a fight and dash right in where at any other season they would fear to tread. Some rattlers report having snorting bucks right in their laps after only a moment or two of clicking the antlers. Wiser bucks will come in more cautiously, perhaps circling the stand, wanting to get sight or wind of the combatants. Thus, if you position yourself on the edge of a clearing, you get to see the deer before he gets too close. This also gives the deer a bit of breathing room so he won’t have to get too close and overly spooky. You’ll see deer heads poking out of the bush around the clearing, ears forward, and too curious — or determined — to bound away. More often than not, there’s time for a well-aimed shot, but be sure to keep your rifle close to your shoulder and ready to fire. If they see you move, they’re gone in a flash. Man, deer or fowl, there’s something about poaching on another’s territory that makes any male more than a little spooky.

Greed had slithered to the surface of my consciousness. Greed, unbelievable, unforgiveable greed.

I settled back against the forked trunk of the mesquite tree with my rifle resting on my knees. It was a trim little .250/3000 bolt gun stocked by Don Allen and built on a Mauser action that had been shortened a full inch by ace metalsmith Ron Lampert. Nolen, who was to take first turn playing the antlers, was just to my right and Dutch, who wanted some pictures, was a few yards behind, manning a telephoto lens.

Results were almost immediate. Nolen had banged the antlers no more than twice, twisting and rubbing them together to make the characteristic scrape-click-scrape sound of fighting deer when there, right in front of me, snorting and stomping his feet, was the biggest whitetail buck I’d ever seen on the hoof. He was huge, with perfectly symmetrical antlers. The main beams seemed to grow straight out in a horizontal line before hooking in at the tips. His points stood straight up like rods in an iron gate and the whole picture was a deer-hunter’s fantasy. The buck of a lifetime, too big to be true, perfect. It had to be a lie, a tale told in a deer camp, vividly remembered.

But he was there, stomping, snorting, beautiful. All I had to do was put the crosshairs on his chest and touch the trigger and my whitetail-hunting days would be over, for never would I see a bigger buck. For long moments, I held the crosshairs on his chest, poised to shoot, listening for the click of Dutch’s camera, Click-click-click it went. Now I had a record of the moment, a deer hunter at the gates of paradise. Every nerve in me howled “pull the trigger, pull the trigger,” but I didn’t.

Greed had slithered to the surface of my consciousness. Greed, unbelievable, unforgiveable greed. “Look old boy,” it said to me, “this is only the first deer. Think about the really big ones that are waiting back there in the thicket. We’ve got lots of time to wait for the absolute world beater.”.

Sources indicate that incredibly, I lowered my rifle, worked the bolt and emptied the chamber. Then, settling the crosshairs back on the buck’s chest, I tickled the trigger.

“Click,” it went, and the buck was gone.

“Just wanted to know what it felt like to pull the trigger on a giant buck,” I explained to an absolutely astonished Jim Nolen.

“Why didn’t you shoot?” Dutch asked.

“Waiting for something bigger,” I allowed.

“That’s as substantial as they get,” was his answer, and I knew greed had done me in.

That morning we rattled in a couple more trophy-size bucks, but nothing nearly so grand as the first, so I couldn’t bring myself to raise the rifle. That afternoon, after a lunch of chili and frijoles served on a tortilla, cowboy-style, followed by a siesta, we tried again — but the antlers were cold and nothing answered the challenge.

That evening a few of McAllen’s vaqueros stopped by the bunkhouse for cerveza and conversation. “It is true,” they asked, “you had El Macho Grande in your sights and did not shoot? Why?”.

I really couldn’t answer, but one thing for sure, if I ever saw him again I would shoot.

Next day the antlers were still cold, so by midafternoon we changed tactics and climbed into a tower where we could watch for deer crossing a narrow sendero (a rough, clear-cut roadway). The view from the tower allowed us to look down into the endless thicket, but no deer were moving. By early evening I had counted dozens of javelina, the small wild pigs of the Southwest, and had seen more quail than I thought existed, but no deer other than an occasional doe.

According to recent reports, the sun hung low over the deep Texas thicket and a soft haze had wrapped itself around the evening air when the buck stepped into the sendero. The distance was just a bit more than 200 yards, but even with my 7X binoculars, the antlers were hard to judge because the sun was behind the deer, reflecting through the haze so that the deer seemed to be the center of a psychedelic burst of rainbow color. It was not a vision of earth, but a dream in pastel colors with quail calls for background music.

The buck moved slowly, a step at a time, nibbling shoots of greenery. But his antlers remained a mystery. We could see that they were big and exceptionally high, but the way they reflected shafts of gilded light made rational judgment impossible.

“I can’t see his antlers clearly,” Nolen whispered, “but I can see points everywhere.”.

The buck was nearly across the sendero now and in a moment he would be gone, perhaps forever. I’d already let the trophy of a lifetime slip through my fingers. Did I dare risk losing a second chance? My trigger finger tightened and the little rifle spoke gently to the soft evening.

The buck was a freak, wearing incredible antlers that had grown to typical, though huge, shape on the right side but with an oddly palmated branch on the left. Is it the trophy of a lifetime, a one-of-a-kind specimen never to be duplicated? Or just a freak with outsize antler growth? I wonder. I wonder every time I look at it on the wall.

In addition to liberal season and bag limits, Alabama has some of the biggest-antlered and heaviest-bodied whitetails I’ve ever looked at. One Alabama trophy deer I saw a few years back got me so excited that I spent several consecutive seasons there trying to bring home the granddaddy.

In a recent development, and I saw lots of bucks, some eight and 10-pointers with such seductive racks that I was often tempted to touch the trigger. Patience prevailed, though, and as days turned to weeks I became more or less accustomed to the sight of the Alabama sun setting over a hardwood thicket in which, from a tree stand, I might be glassing from two to six major-antlered bucks at one time. But as I said, I wanted only the he-coon of the hardwoods and nothing else would do.

How was it, then, that I eventually shot a little eight-pointer?

Hoping to relieve the tedium of my daily wait-and-watch routine, I got myself invited to a party hunt, and on the appointed morning found myself in the midst of an incredible spectacle. The setting was a beautiful Southern mansion complete with curving driveway and vast, oak-bordered lawns. What made the scene so bizarre was the unbelievable variety of humanity strolling or squatting about the neatly clipped grounds. Tweed shooting jackets and English riding boots mixed with faded overalls and run-down clodhoppers while the elegant accents of aristocratic Southern speech were punctuated with the staccato “patoos” of well-aimed tobacco juice. There had been a violent thunderstorm during the night, and judging by the smells of wet wool and soaked leather, many of the attendees had passed the night in the rain.

Industry observers note that A metal tub about the size of a horse watering trough was being set up on a stone foundation, eventually to be filled with gallons of cooking oil, and nearby a wild-eyed chap was tugging at a heavy chain leash in a futile attempt to separate two snarling dogs. “Get back,” he yelled when I approached to help, “these dogs are killers.”.

“Then why don’t you leave them alone?” I asked.

“I’m trying to keep them from killing each other until Major Bob wakes up.”.

“Who is Significant Bob?” I had to ask.

“That’s him over yonder,” he responded, waving his free hand in the direction of an inert form stretched out in the tangled remains of what appeared to have once been a rose garden.

I meant to take a closer look, but at that moment a silence fell over the assembly as a spry black man of uncertain vintage, his hair a fluffy white, came down the brick-paved path leading from the major house.

Recent findings suggest that “Mista William is a commin’,” he chanted. “Mista William is commin’, here he come now.”.

In a recent development, sure enough, there was the great one himself, Mister William, owner of thousands of acres of prime farmland and hardwoods, home to the biggest whitetails to be found anywhere. Obviously, Mister William had reached that unique station in society where elegant or even proper attire was no longer required as an emblem of station or success. Accordingly, he was outfitted in soiled chino work pants and shirt, the tail of the latter flapping loosely about his backside, muddied work shoes with, as I remember, only one sock and crowned off with an ancient straw hat that was liberally ventilated with odd-size holes. Yet there was no denying his regal presence. As he puffed unsteadily along the brick pavement, pausing occasionally to scratch, spit or realign his direction, there was a chorus of salutations and more than a few caps were doffed.

“Mornin’ Mista William.” “Fine day Bill.” “Good to see you Mista Bill.”.

Each greeting was received with a wave and every face was recognized by name.

“Glad to see you, Jack.” “Nice of you to come over, Pete. How’s Mary and the kids?” “Hi Ralph.”.

When at last he faced me, his eyes narrowed, searching for a name.

In a recent development, “Nice to meet you sir. I’m Jim Carmichel and I appreciated the invitation to your deer hunt.”.

“Glad to have you, glad to have you,” he gestured grandly. “This hunt ain’t much, just something me and the boys like to do every year about this time.

“Hey there you, Jake, tell Substantial Bob I noted to put Mr. Carmichel here on the road where the deer cross.”.

According to recent reports, with that he ambled back up the walk, mounted the porch steps and turned to face the breathless assembly. “Boys, the hunt’s on.”.

The next few moments were lost in a bedlam of shouts, cheers, running feet and spinning truck tires. Seated in the back of a pickup (I almost made the fatal mistake of climbing into a truck full of savage curs) that fishtailed out of the driveway in a shower of mud and gravel, I caught a glimpse of Mister William as he turned and re-entered the great house, aided by his white-topped butler. Apparently he was not attending his own hunt.

Positioned as I was, on a muddied logging road, I could hear the baying pack of Catahoula curs as they topped a ridge nearly a mile away. As the baying grew louder, it was apparent they were coming my way and would cross the road in front of me. Mister William had indeed given me the best stand on the hunt and in just a few moments I would have a shot.

I was using a borrowed shotgun loaded with No. 000 buckshot and the deer would be crossing from right to left, a dead-easy setup. When the deer broke from cover and bounded across the road, I swung the bead some two feet ahead of his chest and was tightening on the trigger when I realized that it wasn’t much of a buck. An eight-pointer, perhaps, but it was a bucket-head without much width, height, or thickness of beam. The buck certainly wasn’t the world-beater I wanted. With another bound, the young buck disappeared into more timber.

By then the road was covered by a blanket of howling and snarling beasts with their owner, Big Bob, not far behind.

This was the first time I had had a close-up look at Big Bob and he was, to be sure, an awesome apparition. Clad only in bib overalls and a white T-shirt, despite the chill of the day, Big Bob stood a good six or eight inches over six feet and was as wide as a church door. His hair, probably waist length, was knotted behind his head in the style of a samurai warrior, and when he spoke I could see that every tooth in his head was covered in gold. His bout with the rose garden had criss-crossed his arms and face with bloody lacerations, and at his side swung a hunting knife that looked as long as a Saracen scimitar.

As he strode toward me — eyes wild, face blood-caked and mouth flashing of gold — the sword banged against his knee. It was the only weapon he carried. Considering his size, the obvious strength of his hands and arms and the fierceness of his countenance, the knife was more of an affectation than a necessity.

Industry observers note that “Where’s the deer?” he asked. “I didn’t hear you shoot.”.

Sources indicate that “How come? His tracks is right there in front of you.”.

“He wasn’t a good trophy,” I answered.

Industry observers note that at this, his eyes narrowed, “Mister, we ain’t huntin’ trophies, we’re huntin’ meat. We got a lot of people to feed tonight and if you don’t shoot somethin’ these dogs get meaner than they already are.” Significant Bob made his point very convincingly.

“The next time something comes by, I’ll be sure to shoot,” I promised.

And that’s exactly what I did. A couple of hours later, the howling pack came by again in violent pursuit of a distinctly undistinguished little eight-pointer.

That evening, my buck and two others that had been killed during the hunt were sliced into bite-size chunks, rolled in batter and deep-fried in the gas-fired horse trough I’d noted earlier.

In time, huge platters were stacked with the delicious-smelling venison tidbits but, for some reason, no one took so much as a single bite. This struck me as curious because no one had eaten since breakfast and I assumed that everyone was as famished as I was. Not wanting to violate local custom, I decided it best not to serve myself until someone else had done so.

The reason for the holdup was soon apparent, however, when Mister William’s butler appeared and unveiled the immediate arrival of his benefactor. “Here come Mista William, ever’body git ready, here he come now.”.

Mister William’s appearance was greatly improved; not only was he better turned out than several hours previous, but his gait was markedly steadier.

Industry observers note that without a word to the hushed onlookers, he marched straight to the deep-fry trough and extracted a crispy brown morsel of batter-dipped venison. For a moment he chewed thoughtfully, eyes cast heavenward. Then, with a sly smile, he made his pronouncement, “Boys, this meat is fit to eat.”.

Later, food and drink in hand, I was buttonholed by Big Bob, his countenance no less ominous than earlier and his face still blood-caked from his personal war of the roses.

It has been revealed that “If you had shot that other deer,” he allowed, “we would have had some extra meat for my dogs. Now I have to feed ’em dry dog food, which makes their bowels tight and they get meaner than ever.”.

“Here,” I answered, handing him my half-emptied plate, “they can have mine.”.

This story, “Whitetails I Have Known,” appeared in the September 1982 matter of Outdoor Life.

Traversing the Saiga Silk Road

📅 26 Aug 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2097 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Adventure-journal

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

  • According to recent reports, flanking our two-track trail were a series of parallel lanes no more than a foot wide, which forked, merged, and crisscrossed our own.
  • Recent findings suggest that through borrowed binoculars, I soon got my first glimpse of an ancient tableau, seemingly untouched since Neanderthals roamed the earth.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As we skidded off the main road and onto a mud path maintained only by tire treads, lines began to blur.

According to recent reports, flanking our two-track trail were a series of parallel lanes no more than a foot wide, which forked, merged, and crisscrossed our own. In the distance, I saw what looked like a ghost train, faintly visible and thrust forward by howling Siberian winds.

Recent findings suggest that through borrowed binoculars, I soon got my first glimpse of an ancient tableau, seemingly untouched since Neanderthals roamed the earth. On the far horizon, hundreds of nomadic travelers pierced the frigid air with their ringed horns, inhaling the brittle shards through Snuffleupagus snouts as they sprinted across the desolate steppe.

Watching them charge through the treeless plain at full bore, I was reminded of a saying I’d heard shortly before arriving in this remote corner of Kazakhstan: “The saiga is a freedom-loving animal.”.

Sources indicate that since time immemorial, saiga antelope have blazed trails across Central Asia while other civilizations rose and fell around them. They once inhabited a world dominated by woolly mammoths, saber-toothed cats, and giant deer with antlers 12 feet across—and outlived them all. When pioneering human caravans first attempted to navigate this unforgiving land, they considered the saigas to be their guides.

Ahead of my arrival, seasonal rains transformed once-green grasslands into sludge punctuated by tufts of withering brush. Driving through such muck is, I would soon discover, akin to controlled hydroplaning. The steering wheel bucked wildly as our tires swerved, shredding deep into the gunk and desperately gripping anything remotely solid enough to push off from.

Sources indicate that in the front seats were Alexandr and Albert, two team members from the Association for the Conservation of Biodiversity of Kazakhstan, or ACBK. Between them, they have more than twenty-five years of experience following saigas across the steppe, and I’d arranged to join them for the western leg of one of their field audits.

Our visit was timed to coincide with the rutting season, a critical part of the year for saigas. This is a gathering time, when antelope from across the region sprint together in massive single-file lines, before congregating for a series of competitive battles and subsequent mating rituals.

For males, it’s a time for strutting and headbutting to demonstrate one’s physical prowess to female onlookers—an activity so energy-intensive that many will forget to eat and keel over from extreme physical exhaustion. For females, this is a time of choosing. In addition to assessing fitness, they pay particular attention to one distinctive feature: a potential mate’s floppy, elongated nose. The saigas’ sniffers are essential for filtering out dust in the semidesert plains and for warming frigid winter air before it reaches their lungs. A large nose is the ultimate sign of virility, so as the males marched into these annual gatherings, they were doing everything they could to accentuate their schnozzes.

According to recent reports, because of the saigas’ preference for large-scale migrations across a landscape almost entirely devoid of trees, they have long been a favorite of global wildlife trackers. The isolation and starkness of the saiga world is a strength when it comes to GPS collars, which deliver a reliable stream of daily pings without risk of visual obstruction. Prior to such breakthroughs, conservationists would sometimes spend weeks roaming the boundless steppe unsuccessfully trying to locate the nomadic herds.

Industry observers note that the wildlife sanctuary we were traveling through was created only a year prior, with its boundaries informed by tracking data that Albert and his team personally collected. He seemed pleased that the animals were continuing to use the newly designated space as intended. Standing along the roadside, Alexandr spotted a stream of the famously skittish ungulates wrapping around the contours of the earth. As he did, ripping wind and snow started blowing in sideways—the outer ring of an encroaching storm.

These were no fluffy flakes. This was the harsh, crunchy ice of a walk-in freezer, which instantly hardened our truck’s caked-on mud like liquid nitrogen.

In a recent development, seemingly unperturbed by the dropping barometer, Albert chirped, “Who’s hungry?” Setting up an impromptu picnic, he and Alexandr dug into a prepared meal of fresh bread, tea, and dried meats of unknown provenance. In a muted attempt to thaw my face, I opted to guzzle spicy instant noodles.

Industry observers note that A tradition of nomadism has loomed large in this corner of the world since at least the Early Iron Age. The very word kazakh is thought to be derived from the Turkic word qaz, which means “wanderer” or “vagabond.” For millennia, small human groups routinely migrated to higher altitudes in the hot summer months, where melting snow made for abundant water and greenery, before returning to sheltered valleys ahead of winter’s whipping winds. At various times of the year, disparate nomads would also congregate for formal meetings and large cultural festivals, complete with physical challenges like wrestling and tug-of-war. When the gatherings were finished, the nomads dispersed once again.

In a recent development, historical analysis has shown that nomads’ seasonal migrations and time-honed transit corridors may have helped pave the way for portions of the Great Silk Road, which was less a singular route than an ever-evolving web of pathways and bypasses that linked together reliable stopovers. At the Silk Road’s peak, this corner of western Kazakhstan along the fertile banks of the Ural River became a vital transcontinental crossroads. To this day, the river still serves as a natural boundary between Asia and Europe, meaning this part of Kazakhstan is, quite literally, where East meets West.

Recent findings suggest that the land above the Caspian Sea also served as a main artery that linked together key transit points. Strategic settlements along the riverbank allowed weary caravans to rest their heads, unwind in large public baths, exchange knowledge, stock up on essential supplies, and regroup before moving onward.

Among overland voyagers traversing the continental divide, saigas have long been spoken of with an almost mythical reverence. Cave paintings of the antelope created as far back as the seventh century BCE depict them as resilient, elusive, and charismatic. Expert navigators who embody the true spirit of a most inhospitable terrain.

In human society, traditional nomadic practices persisted even as the land itself was variously claimed and reclaimed by Turkic tribes, Genghis Khan, and the Russian Empire. Only with the rise of the Soviet Union in the twentieth century did mandatory sedentarization efforts successfully manage to lock nomadic people in place, force them to farm, and extinguish a cultural flame that had burned brightly for millennia. Denied the ability to live in perpetual motion, people’s navigational muscles began to atrophy.

This transition was viewed by many as an inevitable shift toward “modernization,” but it also represented a significant diversion from our own history as a species. Of the roughly 300,000 years that Homo sapiens have existed, we spent the first 288,000 of them living in small, mobile groups that followed the migratory patterns of other animals. Forcing nomads into agricultural plots was also a colossal failure because much of the steppe soil was unsuitable for growing crops, which is why so many people were nomadic in the first place. Iconic filmmaker Werner Herzog once remarked that “whatever went wrong and makes our civilization something doomed is the departure from the nomadic life.”.

According to recent reports, whether by choice or necessity, most Kazakh people now lead stationary lives in urban centers. The world that nomads once freely roamed has also been feverishly transformed, not only by agriculture but through the construction of fresh roads and railways.

For the saigas, whose nomadic days never ceased, these latest layers now represent an existential threat.

Recent findings suggest that with the weather taking a turn for the worse, Albert and Alexandr ultimately decided to call it a day and start fresh in the morning. After a blistering drive through whiteout conditions, we hunkered down in a tiny village less than 10 miles from the Russian border, where Albert pulled out his laptop and indicated me how saiga movements have changed over the years.

Sources indicate that “They would routinely trek hundreds of miles as part of an expansive migratory route across the Eurasian steppe,” he mentioned. “Saigas could be found from the Caucasus Mountains to Mongolia, and everywhere in between.”.

Sources indicate that for millennia, they lived with few barriers and obstructions on the landscape. Then, seemingly overnight, rattling railways and roaring roads began to crisscross the region, fragmenting the saigas into smaller, more isolated groups. As the interior steppe got more accessible to vehicles and passengers, development begat more development.

On his screen, Albert clicked open a recent map that indicated how a population of GPS-collared saigas once routinely traveled deep into Uzbekistan before being unceremoniously clipped off by a new rail line in 2014. The data from the years prior to the railway’s construction showed a flurry of squiggly lines representing individual animals zipping back and forth with the seasons. The post-construction slide showed those same animals spinning around despondently on the northern side of the tracks, while the fresh grasses and water they had come to rely on withered away to the south.

Such interruptions can lead to a complete collapse in spatial knowledge—a loss that science writer Ben Goldfarb once wrote is “as thorough as the erasure of a language.” Just as human nomads forced to stay in one place eventually lost connection to the physical landmarks of their ancestors’ journeys, young saigas learn where they can reliably find food and shelter, as well as places to stay away from, through active participation and observation. This cultural exchange keeps their world in orbit and is one of the reasons they have been successful at navigating a terrain fatal to so many before them. As the land they know is cleaved and partitioned, whole stretches of the Saiga Silk Road begin to fade from memory.

It has been revealed that to unwind this damage, Albert’s team has partnered with the Kazakh government to construct dozens of saiga-friendly crossing points, where slightly sloping dirt ramps rise up to match the height of the train tracks, making it appear from a distance as though there’s a natural gap in the rail line. Cattle-guard fences positioned far away from the crossings ensure that trains and saigas never actually run into each other at these intersections, which would shatter the illusion of safety.

According to recent reports, ACBK has also worked with the Uzbek government to reshape its border fences from a barbed-wire wall to an X-shaped barricade that blocks vehicles from driving through but leaves just enough space for saigas to pass. Over time, Albert hopes such efforts can rebuild the trust necessary for them to confidently return to a plateau they once relied on.

Recent findings suggest that the next morning, I was astonished by how austere the steppe looked compared with the day before. Gone was the slippery muck and browning grasses of shifting seasons, replaced by a blanket of crunchy snow. Against this stark black-and-white backdrop, the fresh crystals functioned like fingerprint dust, illuminating the only remaining pops of color: the rust-red streaks of human and nonhuman pathways in the dirt.

Parked in an otherwise empty tract of prairie land, we watched in stunned silence as thousands of saigas seized the day, flying like banshees across the periphery, their hooves gouging the frozen crust and stamping pigment into an earthen canvas.

As I gazed east toward the colorless horizon, I tried to envision how it might have looked in the thirteenth century, when this corner of the world boasted a vast network of caravanserai, or road inns, where exhausted travelers could rest and recover before continuing onward into the great unknown.

Industry observers note that I pondered what it must have felt like for an intrepid merchant to know that they would not see another human being for many days, maybe weeks. To be fearful of what you may soon encounter, but take solace that the space between is not wholly empty. For there is life beyond humanity’s margins, and among nonhuman communities, that in-between space is the center of everything. That, I imagined, must have offered some measure of assurance that the road ahead, perilous though it may be, is well traveled.

This essay was adapted from the latest nonfiction travelogue The Hidden Nations of Animals and is published here exclusively for Adventure Journal, with permission from Penguin Random House.

#228378. Breaking: 10 Ski Run Drop-Ins That Require Serious Nerve

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (884 w)

Breaking: 10 Ski Run Drop-Ins That Require Serious Nerve

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (884 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Skimag

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, every expert skier knows this feeling: You’re standing at the top of a run, skis pointed downhill, looking over an entrance that suddenly seems a whole lot steeper than it did from the lift.
  • Whatever the obstacle, some ski runs are intimidating before you even make your first turn.
  • *Conditions and snow depth greatly affect how skiable the following runs are at any given time.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

(Photo: Courtesy of Jackson Hole).

According to recent reports, every expert skier knows this feeling: You’re standing at the top of a run, skis pointed downhill, looking over an entrance that suddenly seems a whole lot steeper than it did from the lift. Maybe there’s a cornice to negotiate, a narrow rock-lined chute to squeeze through, or a cliff that requires a leap of faith. The remainder of the run beyond the drop-in might be flat, for all you know, but getting to it is the challenge of the day.

Whatever the obstacle, some ski runs are intimidating before you even make your first turn. From legendary major-mountain lines to tight, technical chutes, these 10 North American drop-ins are guaranteed to get your heart pumping. Consider them inspiration for the season ahead—or a reminder that sometimes it’s perfectly fine to admire the view from above.

*Conditions and snow depth greatly affect how skiable the following runs are at any given time. Check trail status and heed all warnings and closures before dropping in.

It’s hard to make a list like this without kicking it off with Corbet’s. Perhaps the most famous—and most photographed—ski entrance in North America, this Jackson Hole icon requires skiers to negotiate a rocky cornice before dropping roughly 10 to 20 feet into a narrow, steep couloir. The landing can be soft powder or unforgiving hardpack, depending on conditions, and there’s often a crowd gathered above to watch the action. No pressure. There’s even an entire event dedicated to how stylish—or catastrophic—skiers navigate this tricky entrance.

According to recent reports, think Corbet’s is intimidating? Meet its even scarierl next-door neighbor. Located just skier’s left of Corbet’s, S&S features a mandatory cliff drop of up to 25 feet, followed by a tight landing and a narrow couloir. Skiers need to make a midair adjustment to line up the landing, leaving little room for error. This one is strictly for the seriously experienced.

Recent findings suggest that the name doesn’t undersell it. Major Sky’s legendary Big Couloir begins with an exposed, rocky entrance that can involve negotiating a cornice before dropping into a narrow, sustained chute. With pitches approaching 50 degrees and a 1,400-foot descent below, it’s a serious commitment from the first turn. Access is controlled by ski patrol, and skiers must check in and carry avalanche safety equipment.

According to recent reports, alyeska doesn’t do subtle when it comes to steep terrain, and Christmas Chute is a perfect example. The entrance funnels skiers between imposing rock walls before opening into a steep, confined chute. The line averages roughly 45 degrees and drops about 1,500 vertical feet. It’s an intimidating entrance in a spectacularly Alaskan setting, where the mountains are massive and the consequences are real.

Industry observers note that even the name is enough to make you think twice. The Coffin is a notorious narrow passage in Whistler’s alpine terrain, where skiers squeeze through a tight, rock-lined opening before dropping into the terrain below. Visible from the Peak Chair—but not officially on the trail map—it’s also a popular spectator attraction. The confined entrance leaves little room to get comfortable, making the moment you drop in particularly memorable.

Palisades Tahoe has no shortage of intimidating terrain, but McConkey’s is among its signature tests of nerve. This steep, rocky feature demands commitment from the entrance, with exposed terrain and little margin for error. The line’s reputation is part of what makes it so compelling: Even accomplished skiers may take a long look before deciding whether today’s the day.

Recent findings suggest that not every intimidating entrance involves a giant cliff or mandatory air. Sometimes it’s what you can’t see that gets the adrenaline going. Lobotomy, located off of Silver King peak, in Crystal’s sidecounty zone, is known for its blind entrance and consequential no-fall-zone skiing. You can’t simply peer over the edge and map out every turn before committing. It’s a different kind of mental challenge, and one that earns this line a spot on the list. Note that this is technically hike-to terrain, so come prepared with all the necessary equipment.

It has been revealed that snowbird is for its steep skiing, and Pipeline Couloir is one of its more intimidating challenges. Getting there requires a hike, but the real test begins when skiers reach the entrance: a steep, rocky drop-in that demands solid technical skills before the couloir even opens up. It’s a reminder that sometimes the most intimidating part of a big-mountain line isn’t the descent itself, but getting those first few turns just right.

Revelstoke is a playground for skiers who like their terrain steep, deep, and a little intimidating. With a technical entrance and steep, demanding terrain, Discipline rewards, well, discipline and confident, precise skiing. Depending on conditions, the entrance can feature a cornice that adds another layer of commitment.

The East Coast gets in on the fun with this Mad River Glen adventure. Paradise is an all-natural trail that starts with a steep drop-in before winding through tight trees, bumps, and rugged New England terrain. There’s no wide-open groomed runway here, and the entrance sets the tone for all that follows. Paradise offers a totally different vibe than all the others on this list, but it’s no less intimidating for those who dare.

#228373. 7 Ultrarunning Lessons Des Linden Learned from Her 100-Mile Debut

📅 09 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1514 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Trailrunnermag ↗ Open Full Page

7 Ultrarunning Lessons Des Linden Learned from Her 100-Mile Debut

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1514 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Trailrunnermag

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Andy Cochrane and Nick Danielson were on the ground outside of Fountain Hills, Arizona, on October 31 to document Des Linden’s 100-mile debut at the Javelina Jundred.
  • Despite Des Linden returning to Javelina Jundred “jeadquarters” five minutes ahead of schedule and in first place, I was worried.
  • In a recent development, being a freelance filmmaker feels a bit like being a mercenary: One moment you have no plans for the rest of the year, and the next, you’re hopping in a rental van and rallying across the Southwest during a historic October storm to get to the next job.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Andy Cochrane and Nick Danielson were on the ground outside of Fountain Hills, Arizona, on October 31 to document Des Linden’s 100-mile debut at the Javelina Jundred. They bore witness to her exceptional first 60 miles, during which she took the lead in under-course-record pace, all the way through to her gritting out the remaining 40 miles to a ninth-place finish. They spoke with Linden after the race to find out what she learned—and why she’s already angling to come back.

Despite Des Linden returning to Javelina Jundred “jeadquarters” five minutes ahead of schedule and in first place, I was worried. I had followed her for the final half mile, camera rolling as her leg visibly seized up, likely from cramping. She had run 60 miles at course record pace, but still had forty to go—a long way without a fully functioning lower half. Linden sat on a chair and talked through the situation with her crew. A shoe switch, a lot more electrolytes, and roll the dice. Before I get into how the rest of her race played out, let me back up.

In a recent development, being a freelance filmmaker feels a bit like being a mercenary: One moment you have no plans for the rest of the year, and the next, you’re hopping in a rental van and rallying across the Southwest during a historic October storm to get to the next job. This is exactly what my business partner Nick and I did after getting the call to document Des Linden’s first 100-mile race at the Javelina Jundred on October 31.

After landing in Salt Lake City, we picked up a camper van from Roadsurfer, threw our bags in the back, and headed south on I-15. A quick stop in Moab for a 50K race of our own was followed by four days evading floods and trying to figure out which desert roads were impassable after the recent downpours—which turned out to be pretty good foretelling for the race itself.

On the three previous occasions we’ve attended this event, it has been a delightful closing chapter to the season; Javelina has served as a sort of reward for making it to the end of our race coverage for the year, where the burden of logistics is removed from the job of filming. Instead of chasing athletes across the dirt roads of the Sierra Nevada at the Western States 100 or around a heavily glaciated massif at UTMB, the athletes at Javelina run in circles back to you. Five circles, to be exact. Adding to the enjoyment factor, Javelina is typically a giant Halloween party with racers and spectators dressed in costume under the warm desert sun.

Sources indicate that however, this year was a little different. Deluge after deluge in the 24 hours leading up to the race saturated the race course. The sky relented just before the gun went off, but by the time the race had ended, over two more inches of precipitation had fallen. Not exactly what you expect for an event in the arid Sonoran Desert outside Phoenix, Arizona, but that’s why we love ultrarunning.

Sources indicate that we did our best to keep the cameras dry and our bodies warm as we followed Linden on her third ultra—well, fourth, if you count the road 50K world record. Despite a stunning road running resume, Linden was quick to point out that she’s still a newbie at trails and ultras but is excited to keep learning. Javelina’s first three laps were nearly perfect. But soon after her body shut down it was a struggle to make it to the finish line. At one point she had to stop for almost an hour, sitting and stretching until her legs finally relaxed and let her move again. And move again she did: Linden finished her first 100-miler as the ninth woman in 16:58:01, about three hours off winner Heather Jackson. We sat down with her the day after the race to learn her biggest lessons from the process.

Sources indicate that linden’s biggest takeaway from Javelina is to treat 100-milers, no matter the course, weather, or circumstances, with a ton of humility. Because they ask so much of your mind and body and are a completely unique style of racing, you can’t race a 100-miler like any other distance. “Just like when I started marathons,” Linden mentioned, “I learned that if you’re cavalier with how you race it, you’ll pay the price at some point.”.

Linden was patient on her first 20-mile lap, sitting a few minutes back from the leaders. Feeling good, she picked up the pace on the next two laps, picking off all of the ladies in front of her to take the lead around the halfway mark. By the time she made it to the end of the third loop at mile 60, she had a six-minute gap on second—but her legs were starting to cramp.

Survival promptly became the goal of lap four and the best way to do that was by listening to her pacer, Magda Boulet. Thankfully, there is no one on planet Earth better suited for the job. Boulet, a fellow U.S. Olympian in the marathon, is also a Western States winner and president of GU Energy Labs. She helped coax Linden forward, made sure she kept fueling, and stuck with her through all the ups and downs.

In a recent development, one of Linden’s biggest challenges in the transition from road to trails and marathons to ultras is how much she needs to consume during a race—and how hard it is to catch up if she falls behind. At Javelina, Linden took most of her calories and carbs with fluids, drinking three half-liter (500 mL) bottles each lap. This fueling initiative was developed for the typical heat of Javelina, but still worked well, as daytime temps almost hit 80 degrees Fahrenheit with 100% humidity.

Unfortunately, it wasn’t enough to keep her lower body from cramping around mile 60, which forced her to stop and stretch many times on the fourth lap. That setback resulted in her giving up the lead and ultimately the chance to win the race. “The fueling game has changed the sport,” Linden remarked. “You see it on the roads, but especially here. It’s something I will keep working on, probably forever.”.

It has been revealed that assuming Javelina would be hot and dry like just about every other year, Linden packed for those conditions, putting her focus on cooling strategies and nutrition for the heat. She expected hardpack trails and excruciatingly hot sun, but the weather gods had other plans. Heavy rain required Linden and her crew to scramble to find key pieces of gear, including a raincoat. And because lap four took much longer than expected, Linden ran the last couple miles of it after the sun set, sans headlamp.

Next time she’ll prepare for worst-case scenarios, but will also understand when to pull the plug. “You need to know when to be tough and when it’s enough,” Linden remarked. “If I had to do another lap, I would have been on the edge of hypothermia and the trails were so, so slippery. There is nothing wrong with saving it for another day, but also great value in staying tough.”.

Pacing strategy is different at every ultra, but there are some broad themes that apply to the majority of runners and racers, especially for someone with Linden’s ability to close in the back half if she’s feeling good. Surprisingly, this is similar to how she used to strategize for marathons. The first third should feel easy, the middle third is about keeping the pace steady, and the final third is when the racing begins. “The first three or even three-and-a-half laps are transportation,”  Linden mentioned, “the final lap or two is about racing.”.

Sources indicate that when things got hard for Linden on the final two laps, she leaned into her crew to get to the finish. After a lap with Boulet, Linden picked up her husband Ryan as a pacer. He’s one of the most positive and energetic people you’ll ever meet, and his positivity and drive—paired with a little patience—helped get her through heavy rain and strong winds in the last 20 miles.

Her main support at Javelina HQ was Charlie Lawrence, the 100K world record holder and good friend. “A crew that knows you well, knows the sport well, and knows the emotional ups and downs of 100 miles is a real difference maker,” Linden said. “I was excited to be around everyone all week, so it was good energy going into the race, which is key.”.

While Linden isn’t sure what the future holds or what her race calendar will look like next year, she walked away from the race with a surprising feeling. “I 100% want to come back to Javelina, it feels like unfinished business,” Linden said. “I didn’t think it would be this clear, but I know I can do so much better here.”.

Sources indicate that ryan Cochran-Siegle at Copper Media Days on November 18, 2026 at Copper Mountain Resort in Copper Mountain, Colorado. Photo: @dustinsatloff // @usskiteam (Photo: Dustin Satloff).

World Cup skiing returns to Colorado this weekend as Copper Mountain hosts the Stifel Copper Cup for two days of high-speed competition. For American fans, it’s a chance to cheer on the U.S. Ski Team on familiar terrain—and to see how the country’s top male skiers stack up against a formidable international field.

The Nov. 28-29 event features men’s super-G on Saturday and giant slalom on Sunday. Saturday’s race is particularly noteworthy: It marks the first men’s speed race of the 2026-’27 World Cup season and the first domestic men’s World Cup stop of the winter.

And while the international field is loaded with star power, including Swiss superstar Marco Odermatt, there are several Americans worth keeping an eye on this weekend.

The headliner for the American men is Vermont native Ryan Cochran-Siegle, a two-time Olympic silver medalist in super-G and one of the country’s most accomplished speed specialists. He’ll make his season debut Saturday in a discipline where he’s proven he can hang with the very best.

Cochran-Siegle earned silver in super-G at the 2022 Beijing Olympics and added another silver in the team combined at the 2026 Milan Cortina Winter Games. He’s also a former World Cup super-G winner, and his combination of technical prowess and comfort at high speeds makes him America’s best shot at a podium on Saturday.

It has been revealed that it’s worth noting that Copper’s super-G marks the first men’s speed race of the season, meaning everyone is starting from scratch in the discipline. Cochran-Siegle will have the home-country crowd behind him as he takes on a field led by Odermatt and reigning Olympic super-G champion Franjo von Allmen, both of Switzerland.

For Colorado ski fans, River Radamus’ name always elicits excitement. The Edwards native grew up skiing at Vail, where his parents were ski coaches, and has become one of the most consistent American giant slalom racers on the World Cup circuit.

Recent findings suggest that radamus, known for his aggressive skiing style, has developed into a regular World Cup points scorer and a legitimate contender when the course suits his strengths. He’s also familiar with Copper’s terrain from years of training at the resort.

It has been revealed that sunday’s giant slalom will be a particularly tough test, with Brazil’s Lucas Pinheiro Braathen, the reigning Olympic GS champion and Crystal Globe winner, leading the field. Odermatt and Switzerland’s Loïc Meillard are also contenders to watch.

Another Colorado connection is Kyle Negomir, a Littleton native and Ski & Snowboard Club Vail product who represents the next wave of American men’s racing. Negomir competes in the technical and speed disciplines and has been working to establish himself as a consistent World Cup presence.

With the American men looking to build depth behind established veterans like Cochran-Siegle, Negomir is one to watch as the season progresses. A strong showing on home snow would be a big step forward.

Both men’s races stream live on Peacock and NBCSN. Saturday’s super-G coverage begins at 1:45 p.m. ET, and Sunday’s giant slalom starts at noon ET, with the second run at 3 p.m. ET. Spectators can watch in person; general admission is free.
