Gadgets ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Trailrunnermag ↗ Open Full Page

Watch: Jessie Diggins Explains Why Sparkles Are Her Superpower

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1662 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Trailrunnermag

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Trail Runner managing editor Abby Levene caught up with cross-country skiing superstar Jessie Diggins in Kona, Hawaii, a few days before the Ironman World Championship.
  • After retiring from cross-country skiing as the most decorated American of all time, glide off into the sunset Jessie Diggins did not.
  • Recent findings suggest that diggins, 35, raced the Broken Arrow Triple Crown in June, as has become her annual ritual.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Trail Runner managing editor Abby Levene caught up with cross-country skiing superstar Jessie Diggins in Kona, Hawaii, a few days before the Ironman World Championship. In this exclusive interview, Diggins shares how she battled through a deep low to finish (and win) her first 100-miler, the lessons from cross-country skiing that she’s applying to trail running, and why she always puts on face glitter before a race.

After retiring from cross-country skiing as the most decorated American of all time, glide off into the sunset Jessie Diggins did not. The Olympic gold medalist earned one last piece of hardware in Milan-Cortina this spring—on bruised ribs no less—hung up the skis, and dove head-first into trail running.

Recent findings suggest that diggins, 35, raced the Broken Arrow Triple Crown in June, as has become her annual ritual. She then lined up against the world’s best trail runners at Sierre-Zinal in August, won the Superior 100-miler in September, and just last weekend won the (bear with me) Trail Animals Running Club Stone Cat Trail Festival 50-miler in Massachusetts.

On paper, it’s been an effortless transition into a sport Diggins swears she is just doing for fun. But of course there is so much more to the story once you dig in. I was lucky enough to catch up with Diggins at the epicenter of yet another endurance sport—the Ironman World Championship—in Kona, Hawaii, last month. She’d just come from a snorkeling expedition trying to find a sea turtle. (So far no luck.) Gazing out onto the turquoise waves crashing into shore, we chatted about what she’s learned and loved about trail running so far. That list includes (and is not limited to) how trail running really is a team sport, achieving personal goals is bigger than the results, fueling on a “washing machine” stomach is not easy, and the power of glitter translates from snowy trails to dry ones.

It has been revealed that this interview has been edited for clarity. You can also watch some of it above.

Jessie: It was a really cool experience. It was so humbling, but so exciting to tackle a totally different challenge. I was filled with curiosity: What will this feel like? What’s going to happen to my body? What will happen inside my brain? How does this work?

Having a crew and pacers like that is very different from skiing. [In skiing] you are alone on the trail, and people can cheer for you, but you don’t actually have anyone with you on the trail. And so it was just so exciting I got to do it with a team. That was really significant for me. I’m a very team-oriented person, and I would get so excited to come into the aid station and see the crew and to get to have a pacer with me. Even when I was falling apart and couldn’t even  talk—I was at a really low point—it was just like, ‘I’m here with my team and I’m pushing my limits and I’m seeing what’s possible for me.’ And that’s so exciting.

Industry observers note that I would just tell myself ‘every step you take is a step you don’t have to take again.’ So I was just like, ‘I’m doing it. I’m slowly working towards that finish line, step by step.’ It was so funny because even when I was deeply uncomfortable, I never actually thought about quitting, which I thought I would. It was more just like I’m so uncomfortable, but I know I can if I just keep moving. Even if I’m slowing down, even if I’m not even able to run, I have to just power hike this section. I’m still moving towards my goal. I’m in the process of getting there, and that’s exciting in and of itself.

Sources indicate that I kind of wanted to set up a charcuterie board of the trail world and try different things because they were all so different, right? Broken Arrow is a huge festival and it was a multi-day thing, so oh my gosh, what is day three gonna feel like? Can I even run downhill on day three?

In a recent development, and then Sierre-Zinal is so historic, and it was such a cool course. It was beautiful, and it was like experiencing a very classic “short” trail race, right? I was like, ‘this is not short.’ It took me 3 hours, but it was so cool to experience.

And then going into the 100 miler, it was different and more of a backyard format. Or not a backyard in terms of the laps, but like there was no award ceremony. It wasn’t about winning. It was just about doing it, and I love that. That is so aligned with how I feel about racing. It’s like, ‘No, we don’t really care who wins. We just want everyone to challenge themselves and hopefully make their goal of crossing the finish line.’ And that was so cool for me.

Industry observers note that and so getting to be a part of each of these events, I got to experience so many different angles of the trail world and meet so many people. And for me, that was a big thing, too: feeling the sense of community that was around every single race and making upcoming friends and trying something new. That was very cool.

Industry observers note that no, I definitely am excited to do more. I don’t know what that’s gonna look like yet, but I feel like just getting to be involved in this world is so cool and so exciting. So, I’m sort of now in the phase of like, ‘OK, I feel like I’m bouncing back with 100. Like, my body’s coming back, and now I can start dreaming and scheming and brainstorming, like what else do I want to do? What else is out there? What excites me? What feels like the appropriate challenge for this phase of my life?’ Yeah, I’m trying to figure it all out.

I think the biggest thing was in training, like listening to my body. So I stopped wearing a heart rate monitor like five or six years ago, and it was really about being in tune and listening to my body and figuring out where I can push. What does it feel like when I’m riding that line of level three, and what are the signals in my body when I’ve gone over that line and I need to pull it back?

And so really trying to deeply understand how I feel, and I feel like that’s helped me steer away from injuries too, because I’m not relying on metrics. I want to feel how my body feels and respond to that and act on those feelings.I think that’s something I’m taking with me because I’m well aware now that running can really beat you up in a different way. Even listening to my body and learning how much can I eat while I’m running because your stomach is a washing machine and that does not happen in cross-country skiing.

Industry observers note that I think it was really exciting in my final years of cross-country skiing, learning more about high-carb fueling and having all these great products come on board. Because in a ski race, let’s say a 50-kilometer race, you come through a feed zone, but you have gloves and your hands are in poles, so you are not like ripping open a gel. You’ll end up stabbing yourself in the face. And so what you do is you tuck your poles under your armpits and you grab the feed bottle, which is usually an actual baby bottle with the lid taken off, from a coach who cannot run with you, they have to just stand there and hold it by the rim. So you grab it while you are gliding quite quickly. You down it so you get like a few good sips, and then you have to chuck the bottle on the side and keep moving. And so having really high carb drink mixes where you can, if you only can get a few mouthfuls, you need them to count, and so having these was huge. Because before it’d be like, ‘I guess we’ll boil down Coke to de-fizz it, and that’s what you can have.’ But it  just wasn’t high carb enough, and the electrolyte balance might not have been great.

According to recent reports, now there’s so many options, and that really changed the way I could race. And so now, in trail racing, there’s all these different gels. You can find the one that works for you. There’s all these different mixes. You can find the amount of salt that works for you. That’s been really cool. Being able to tailor it. I feel like 15 years ago, there weren’t that many options. Now having more options is power.

In a recent development, I do get scared. It’s funny. I just saw on the elevator this morning a woman was wearing glitter, and I was like, ‘Yes!’ That was my whole thing through my ski career. And it came out of being scared and being nervous. And I feel like people don’t always know that that’s the origin. But I would get so nervous for races, and a little bit of nerves is great. It means you care. If you’re not nervous for a race, it’s sort of like, ‘Why am I doing this?’ You know, then it’s time to maybe examine, do I really care about what I’m doing?

At the end of the day, yes, there’s a lot of pressure. There can be expectations. There can be a lot of lights. A lot of people are watching you, but you get to do this. You get to challenge yourself and see what’s possible. And that, in and of itself, is such an amazing opportunity.

#228362. The Story of the Mickey Buck, Michigan’s State-Record Nontypical Swamp Buck

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 24m • 📚 Deep Dive (4891 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Outdoorlife ↗ Open Full Page

The Story of the Mickey Buck, Michigan’s State-Record Nontypical Swamp Buck

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 24 min read (4891 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~24 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This story, “Swamped by Trophy Bucks,” appeared in the December 1980 problem of Outdoor Life.
  • According to recent reports, I’d bet 10 to 1 there are at least 20 whitetail bucks within a 50-mile radius of my home that have racks good enough to be listed in the Pope and Young or Boone and Crockett record books.
  • Sources indicate that there are millions of people in this area, but there are also farmlands and swamps that produce some of the nation’s finest trophy whitetails.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This story, “Swamped by Trophy Bucks,” appeared in the December 1980 problem of Outdoor Life. Mickey’s buck, which scored 238 2/8 according to the Boone and Crockett Club record books, remains the largest nontypical ever killed by a hunter in Michigan. It’s ranked as the No. 2 buck in the state, however, after a 246 2/8 deadhead found by Ronald A. Waldron in 2010.

According to recent reports, I’d bet 10 to 1 there are at least 20 whitetail bucks within a 50-mile radius of my home that have racks good enough to be listed in the Pope and Young or Boone and Crockett record books. I live near Bay City, Michigan, not far from the other massive cities of Flint and Saginaw and less than 100 miles from Detroit.

Sources indicate that there are millions of people in this area, but there are also farmlands and swamps that produce some of the nation’s finest trophy whitetails. They are so smart, and so used to coping with the activities of humans, that most hunters never see them.

In 1976 I shot a nontypical whitetail that scored 238⅝ points. It won the first award at the Seventeenth North American Substantial Game Awards program in 1980. It was the best nontypical whitetail taken in North America during the previous three years, and it’s the best ever taken in Michigan.

Sources indicate that I shot that buck about 9 miles from my home. There’s another buck as good or better than him even closer. He has an 18-point rack. He has outsmarted me for two years, but I think I’ll get him. There’s a 16-pointer in the same area. I’m confident I could take that buck with my rifle, but I’m determined to get him with a bow.

In a recent development, I’m 32, but I decided 10 years ago not to shoot any bucks with a rifle unless I got chances at really outstanding trophies. I have head-and-shoulder mounts of 11 of my bucks now, and a lot of them were taken with arrows.

The main reason I get massive bucks is that I hunt deer full time for two to three months every fall. All that time without earning a paycheck produces some financial problems because I work as a carpenter, but my wife Kay doesn’t say anything. We lived together for 1½ years before marrying, so she knew what she was getting into.

I used to hunt everything in season years ago, but now I concentrate exclusively on Michigan deer. I’d love to be able to hunt other major game in Western states or Alaska, but I can’t afford to. Anyway, I’m obsessed with trophy whitetail bucks. And when you hunt them as much as I do, you’re bound to learn some strange things about deer behavior. Here’s an example.

Sources indicate that in 1972 Rick Havercamp and I were bowhunting along a bank of the Saginaw River on a cold but sunny afternoon in late December. The 300-yard-wide river had recently frozen over. Rick was close to the shore, I was a few yards up the bank in some brush. Suddenly my partner stated, “Get down, there’s a whole herd of deer running out there on the ice. They might come across. Get ready, here they come!”.

According to recent reports, I looked out there and saw about 40 deer. There were at least 10 bucks, and the whole herd was coming dead on. I nocked an arrow on the string of my 70-pound Jennings compound bow, then squatted down.

Sources indicate that as the deer got close to our side of the river they began breaking through the shoreline ice. I don’t know if they saw us, but for some reason they veered to our left and crashed into a cattail marsh about 500 yards long. The going was tough for those deer. I figured if I ran along the bank at full speed I could get to the end of the marsh before the deer did, and that I could intercept them as they came out.

Industry observers note that I was puffing hard by the time I got there, but I knew right away that I was ahead of the herd. I could hear the deer breaking ice and banging through dead cattail stalks. Then the commotion suddenly stopped. About half an hour passed without my hearing a sound. I couldn’t figure out what was going on, so I walked back to confer with Rick.

According to recent reports, I met him half way around the marsh. He was as confused as I was.

“I’ll climb a tree and see what’s going on,” he mentioned.

When he got up the tree and looked, he stated, “Hard to believe. They’re all out there, standing still as statues. Some of ’em are through the ice, up to their chests in water. There’s a couple of really huge bucks. What’re we going to do?”.

“I’ll give you 10 minutes to get back to where they ran into the cattails,” I answered. “Then I’m going back to the other end and drive those deer back your way. If that ice is thick enough to support the deer it’s thick enough to hold me.”.

When I returned to the far end of the marsh I cautiously tested the ice near shore. It seemed OK, so I took off. I covered about 50 feet, then I dropped through that ice as suddenly as if I’d walked off a plank. My boots hit the mucky bottom about 3 feet down, but I was already making my move to get out of there.

In a recent development, I rolled up onto the ice at the edge of the hole I’d made, and the whole edge broke off. I was soaked by the time I made my next roll, and again the edge gave way. I broke through once more, and then I found ice that supported me. By the time I reached the shoreline I was covered with black muck and marsh weeds.

It has been revealed that I had lost all concern for deer, then I suddenly heard loud noises. It dawned on me that all those deer were crashing through the marsh again, and they were coming straight toward me. I nocked an arrow and squatted low in a kneeling position on the edge of the wall of cattails, and shook my head when I realized that, almost unbelievably, I was seconds away from having a whole herd of whitetails in my lap.

Recent findings suggest that the first deer out was a doe. She broke through the cattails about 10 feet to my left, stared wild-eyed at me, then bolted up the bank. Another doe came out just to my right and did the same thing. Now the crashing diminished. Somehow the rest of the deer had been alerted that those two does had run into something that wasn’t right.

Then I spotted movement above the cattails a few yards in front of me. A rack of antlers was moving slowly toward me. I couldn’t see any part of the buck except his 10-point rack, but it was obvious what was going on. That buck wasn’t about to run out of the marsh as the does had done. He was going to peer over the edge of the cattails to see what the problem was.

In a recent development, it seemed like that deer’s neck was stretched out 5 feet when it popped into view at a range of about 3 yards. I was already at full draw, and I drove my arrow dead center into the white spot on his throat. When I had that head mounted I told the taxidermist to mount it with the neck straight out, exactly as I’d first seen it.

Recent findings suggest that that hunt taught me one of the most vital buck-hunting lessons I’ve learned. When I broke through the ice and began floundering about, I was producing exactly the same sounds as the deer were making when they broke through. They assumed that I was a deer making my escape through that end of the marsh. So on they came, intending to use the same escape route.

Sources indicate that since a deer’s range of vision in thick cattails is only a few yards, you can actually walk or wade right up to a buck because the sounds you make won’t seem unnatural to the animal. An crucial part of the equation is that smart bucks in heavily hunted farm country soon learn to go where most hunters won’t go. Those places are swamps, the rougher the better. If you hunt whitetails, and you have thick cattail swamps in your area, you can bet that they hold a lot of deer.

One of the best bucks I’ve taken out of a cattail marsh was an 11-pointer I arrowed in 1979. Though it was a great rack, it wasn’t nearly as impressive as one belonging to another buck in the same herd. The inside spread of the 11-pointer’s antlers measures 19½ inches. I saw both bucks only moments apart, and I’d bet everything I own that the bigger buck’s antlers have a 23-inch inside spread.

It was windy and clear that day, but the 20° temperature made for colder than usual December hunting. Though there were traces of snow on the ground, there was none on trees or cattails. That called for brown camouflage outer wear, including a brown face mask. I usually wear camouflage face grease, but when it gets so cold that makeup would freeze, I wear masks.

Sources indicate that when I go with a bow I’m camouflaged completely according to weather conditions. Early in the season, when the foliage and ground is green I use green camo. Later I switch to brown. If there’s lots of snow I’m dressed in white, and so is my archery tackle.

I began that hunt by walking up to a major marsh and climbing a sloping deadfall in the oak bottomlands that edged the cattails. I immediately spotted two big racks. They seemed to be floating above the stalks only 60 yards away. I’ve seen similar sights several times. Deer will stand in water for hours without moving. You won’t see most of them because the cattails completely hide their bodies. But when you get a buck that’s not alerted — when he’s not trying to conceal his antlers — his rack will be above the marsh terrain when he’s standing.

Sources indicate that I slithered down the deadfall, then stalked along the edge of the cattails to a spot that was about even with those bucks. There I eased up another deadfall, just far enough to see one of the bucks. He was walking slowly down the marsh, but he was only about 30 yards out in the cattails. Again I began sneaking along the edge of the marsh. I wanted to get ahead of him before I began wading into the swamp.

Right then that enormous buck — the biggest one I’ve ever seen — stood up in the cattails 20 yards from me.

In a recent development, he was looking dead away, but he quickly turned his head and looked right at me. Though I was perfectly camouflaged, and still as a stone, he knew something wasn’t right. Our little game lasted at least 30 seconds. I don’t think he ever figured out what I was, but he whirled and bounded out of range before I could shoot.

According to recent reports, I stalked on for 25 yards and stepped up on another of the maze of sloping deadfalls that littered the edge of this marsh. I spotted the huge buck I’d spooked. He was more than 100 yards away, standing near the other side of the cattails and looking back. The two bucks I’d originally spotted were 40 yards straight out in front of me. They didn’t seem nervous.

Recent findings suggest that when I hunt these marshes I always wear hip boots or waders, depending on the water’s depth. I stepped into the cattails and began wading without making any attempt to conceal the sounds of my approach. When I figured I was about 20 yards from the closest and largest buck, I pulled my arrow to full draw in the compound bow and kept right on wading. At a range of about 17 yards I saw his shoulder through the maze of cattails. I picked out his heart area and drove my Bear Razorhead right into it. He bolted, but died on his feet.

In a recent development, he was looking dead away, but he quickly turned his head and looked right at me. Though I was perfectly camouflaged, and still as a stone, he knew something wasn’t right.

In a recent development, I sincerely feel that a bow in the hands of an expert is almost as deadly as a rifle. If I can get within 40 yards of a buck I can kill him because I can hit a grapefruit-size target every shot at that range. I can do that only because of dedicated practice. It’s extremely unusual if I don’t practice shooting arrows at least an hour every day.

I learned how to hunt on my own. My folks were divorced, but I lived with my mother on 15 acres of land near Kawkawlin where I live now. Even when I was a little kid I was out in the woods most of my free time, studying birds and animals and shooting arrows or my BB gun.

I shot my first buck, a spikehorn, when I was 14. I didn’t know much of anything about deer hunting then. I just blundered into the little buck in a pine plantation and knocked him flat with my grandfather’s .300 Savage.

In a recent development, though I bowhunted deer for several years I didn’t get one until I was 18. He was a five-pointer. I’ve taken bigger bucks with arrows every year since. A few years ago, when it became legal for Michigan hunters to take a deer with a bow and another with a gun, I’ve always scored on another major buck with my .30/06 sporterized Enfield.

I used that rifle to shoot an 11-pointer in his bed in 1975. Rick Havercamp was with me that day too. He’s 36, and a carpenter. We were in an area 3 miles across, that borders the Au Sable River near Cook Dam. It’s laced with beaver ponds, tag alders, and muck.

It has been revealed that you have to wear hip boots or waders to get in there, and even then you usually get wet because the mucky bottoms are so treacherous. Every year I have to chop out trails with a machete because there’s no way I could find my way in or out of that place in darkness. I throw the chopped off alder branches in muddy places that would be impassable without their support.

The middle of that place is so rough I’ve never seen another hunter in it. That’s why it draws deer like a magnet.

There had been a blizzard the day before that had left a foot of snow on the ground, but there were a million stars in a clear sky when Rick dropped me off near one edge of the swamp. His strategy was to drive around to the opposite side and hunt in from there.

I took a stand on an island, and I sat there until a forkhorn and six does browsed to within 25 feet of me. The little buck finally saw me and panicked. He charged into brush and through some skim ice, and he took the does with him. They made such a racket I decided to go stillhunting.

Because of the recent blizzard, every deer track I found was fresh. When I came upon a set of enormous tracks I began following them. I stayed on that track for five hours, taking a few steps at a time and then stopping to inspect the area ahead. I’d squat and bend to look under branches, around clumps, and behind deadfalls.

Because the snow was deep and soft my extremely slow progress was almost soundless. Once I almost walked up to a doe. When about 20 feet separated us she jumped out of her bed and crashed into a thick stand of snow-laden cedars. She produced a miniature blizzard of sun-sparkling snow when she blitzed through those trees. As time passed I jumped several deer, including an eight-pointer. It was impossible not to surprise at least some deer; there were deer tracks all over. It was a job to keep the tracks I was following separate from the rest.

Industry observers note that finally, during one of my staring-ahead sessions, I saw a brown spot 40 yards to my right. I figured it was a dead cedar stump, but I turned up my 3X-to-9X Redfield scope to full power for a closer look. I still couldn’t tell if the spot was a deer or a stump, so I inched forward a couple of yards. Another look through the scope proved nothing. I just couldn’t identify any part of a deer. Then the stump suddenly became a deer and shook snow off its body like a dog shakes off water.

I had to crawl a couple of yards to my left before a massive rack suddenly popped into focus. I broke the buck’s back with a 180-grain handloaded slug. When my rifle went off that place erupted deer. They seemed to be rushing off in all directions. Rick, who was a few hundred yards away at the time, remarked later, “After you shot I had deer running by me for five minutes.”.

A different kind of stalk produced my award-winning buck. John Miller, another hunting buddy (he’s 29 and works in construction) saw the buck just after the 1976 archery deer season opened. The buck was on a ridge eating acorns when John saw him, and he figured the buck was working toward a runway leading down into a stand of tag alders. John guessed correctly, but it was almost dark when the buck went by his stand. He missed his shot, but he sure got excited. He was waiting at my home when I returned from hunting.

“Paul, that buck is unreal,” he said. “I couldn’t get a good look at him, but he’s got a rack that’s so wide it looks preposterous. He’s got at least 12 points, maybe twice that many. The antlers are so massive I just couldn’t believe what I was looking at. I overshot him because he was closer than I thought. When my arrow hit a rock I could see sparks fly, that’s how dark it was.”.

Sources indicate that john and I were back in the area before dawn the next morning. He wanted to be on stand near the oak ridge, but I had a different idea. I figured that if the buck went into a stand of alders at night there was no way he wanted to stay in them. I assumed he would go through the alders, then cross a road and go down into a winter wheatfield that edged another stand of alders. So I went down in there and picked a stand near a runway.

I hunted that area for five straight days and never saw a deer, the worst run of bad luck I’ve ever had. Miller saw several deer every day, but no big bucks. We finally got disgusted and went to Michigan’s Upper Peninsula (U.P.) for two weeks of bowhunting.

It has been revealed that when we got back, an ironworker friend told me that his two boys jumped the giant buck in a field of weeds while they were pheasant hunting. He said the animal’s rack was so big it wouldn’t fit through a doorway. But what really shook me was that the kids had jumped the buck in the same area where I’d been hunting him. John and I were back on our stands the next morning.

It has been revealed that I hunted three days without seeing a deer, but I found a clump of tag alders and willows that were ripped and shredded from near the ground to eye level. It was by far the biggest buck rub I’ve ever seen. I wondered aloud how many points the buck must have to do that kind of damage.

The next morning I saw three does.

They went into a jungle of alders, so I decided to leave my stand and follow them. About an hour later I jumped that buck 40 yards ahead of me.

Sources indicate that when the buck leaped up his antlers slammed into a maze of branches thick enough to stop his up and forward motion. He was in a half-standing position, and he was actually trying to pull those trees out of the ground. The muscles in his hindquarters were standing out like whipcords, but my attention was riveted on his massive and almost pure white antlers. I was so startled that the whole show was over before I could nock an arrow. The buck dropped low, then bolted away.

Recent findings suggest that I saw him once more before I got him, and that time he almost ran over me. We came as close to a full-speed collision as you can get. If he had hit me he probably would have put me in the hospital, or worse.

It has been revealed that it was Halloween, cloudy and very foggy. I was on a stand in some weeds edging a drainage ditch about 6 feet deep. John got bored with the miserable, wet morning before I did, so he decided to drive a cornfield toward me. A stubblefield about 100 yards wide separated my position from the standing corn. I knew John was in the corn, but I didn’t think anything unusual was happening until he suddenly yelled, “Here he comes!”.

The muscles in his hindquarters were standing out like whipcords, but my attention was riveted on his massive and almost pure white antlers.

In a recent development, I heard the buck before I saw him. He was crashing through cornstalks and flattening them as he ran. He burst out into the stubblefield and bolted for a corner in the drainage ditch 150 yards to my left. Spray flew as he hit shallow water. Then he disappeared and everything became still. I knew there was a runway down there, and I was positive he used it to get into a thick stand of alders.

So I stood up, put my quiver on my bow, put the arrow I had nocked in the quiver, and jumped across the water in the ditch. One more step would put me on top of the ditch and on level ground. To understand what happened next you must know that the buck did not go down the runway as I assumed he would. Instead, he jumped back up on the ditch’s bank and ran straight toward me at full speed. He was not aware of my presence, and I was sure he was gone. When I took that last step out of the ditch, I popped up into his vision and route of travel at point-blank range.

The first thing I saw was the buck hunching up as he slammed on the brakes. All his legs were stiff, and he was jamming his hooves into the soft ground like spears. I could have hit him with the tip of my bow, but I was so startled, I couldn’t move. He reacted like a giant coiled spring. He seemed to bounce backward and hit the ground, bounce again as he whirled toward the ditch, then bounce across it into some willows. He was gone before I could even think about reaching for an arrow.

According to recent reports, john had watched the whole episode from 100 yards away. He was still dumfounded when he ran up to me.

Sources indicate that “I couldn’t believe what I was watching,” he said. “I saw him change course at the corner of the ditch, and I knew he was going to run right past you. I figured that buck was as good as dead. Then I saw you stand up and put your arrow back in your quiver. I just groaned when I realized what was happening.”.

Sources indicate that I kept hunting the buck for almost two weeks without seeing him again. By now it was time to head for the U.P. for the rifle season. Every fall, 13 of us hunt from a cabin there. It’s the highlight of the year for all of us. I couldn’t get that significant white-racked buck out of my mind, but I figured I’d get him in December with my bow.

I usually stay at the cabin through November, but this time I went home for Thanksgiving, mostly because it would give me three days to try for that buck with my rifle.

John Miller and I hunted the next morning in pouring rain. We went home about noon, got out of our sopping clothes, then headed out again about 4 p.m. I was about 700 yards from my stand near the winter wheatfield when I spotted something out of place in the wheat. Visibility was poor because of the rain. My first thought was that somebody had put an old junk car out there because the thing I’d spotted resembled a car bumper. I checked it out with my scope. The car bumper immediately turned into the enormous white antlers of my giant buck. I had missed seeing his body because it was dark with the rain and blended in almost perfectly with a background of wet and dark alders.

Recent findings suggest that I was in a field of weeds about 4 feet high. I immediately dropped down out of the buck’s sight. I could close the distance by 200 yards just by hunching over and running through the tall weeds to the edge of a stubblefield. The buck hadn’t moved much during the few moments it took me to reach the foot-high stubble. He appeared to be grazing without any hint of fear, so I rested a minute to control my gasping breath.

It has been revealed that then I flattened out in the mud and began crawling. I knew if I could make it through the 300 yards of stubble I’d be within a shooting range of about 200 yards.

According to recent reports, then I flattened out in the mud and began crawling. I knew if I could make it through the 300 yards of stubble I’d be within a shooting range of about 200 yards. If he detected me sooner, I’d just have to shoot when he began running.

In a recent development, I hadn’t crawled far when I found that the buck was going through a precise routine. He’d graze for a few seconds, then jerk his head up fast. He’d look straight ahead, then inspect things to his right for another few seconds, turn his head left and do the same thing, then conclude his check for danger by craning his neck around to the side and looking straight to his rear. After that he’d take two steps forward, lower his head and resume grazing. He did the same exact thing every time.

Sources indicate that I had a definite advantage now. I timed my crawling periods to start when he lowered his head, and to end just as he jerked it upright. When I got to the end of the stubble I wiped my scope clean of water and pieces of weeds and seeds. Then I waited to make one last move that would give me a wide-open shot.

When his head went down again I made a complete roll from the stubble into the very short wheat and then spread out into the typical prone shooting position. My 180-grain bullet broke his back and put him down instantly.

Read Next: The Story of the Allison Buck, and the Best Opening Morning in Ohio History.

Industry observers note that the excitement of such a stalk exhausts you as much as the exertion. By the time I ran full speed to the deer I could hardly breathe. I was gulping for air. I finally managed to tape the outside spread of the rack at 26½ inches, and then I tried counting antler points. I kept losing count, but I finally counted 31. By that time, John was running onto the scene. From over 100 yards away he yelled, “Did you get him?”.

“Yeah, I got him. I finally got him!”.

“Does he have more than 12 points?”.

“John, he’s got more than that on one side.”.

It has been revealed that when John got to me he was so happy he was laughing. I was still in a state of shock. I couldn’t think of anything appropriate to say, so I started grinning and laughing too. We stood there in the rain, staring at those fantastic antlers and laughing our tensions away.

The Killington World Cup Is Back. Here’s Why This Weekend Matters for the U.S. Women.

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

  • Sources indicate that the Stifel Killington Cup returns to Killington, Vt., Thanksgiving weekend, welcoming some of the world’s best women ski racers back to U.S.
  • It has been revealed that the two-day Stifel Killington Cup features women’s giant slalom on Saturday (Nov.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mikaela Shiffrin during Copper Media Days on November 17, 2026 at Copper Mountain in Frisco, Colorado. Photo: Matan Coll // U.S. Ski Team @matancoll (Photo: Matan Coll // U.S. Ski & Snowboard).

Sources indicate that the Stifel Killington Cup returns to Killington, Vt., Thanksgiving weekend, welcoming some of the world’s best women ski racers back to U.S. soil. For the American women, in particular, there’s plenty to be excited about.

It has been revealed that the two-day Stifel Killington Cup features women’s giant slalom on Saturday (Nov. 28), followed by slalom on Sunday (Nov. 29). It’s the first time the World Cup has visited Killington since 2024, when Mikaela Shiffrin crashed on a steep portion of the giant slalom course and suffered a deep puncture wound to the abdomen.

This time around, Shiffrin returns as a three-time Olympic gold medalist, the winningest Alpine ski racer in history, and one of the favorites in both disciplines. But she’s not the only American worth watching. A strong U.S. squad includes a rising slalom talent and an athlete who arrives in Vermont fresh off the biggest victory of her career so far.

Sources indicate that there’s no question who will draw the biggest crowd. Mikaela Shiffrin has won 110 World Cup races and three Olympic gold medals, and she has stood atop the Killington podium six times, including four consecutive slalom victories from 2016 to 2019.

She arrives in Vermont following another impressive season, highlighted by a gold medal in slalom at the 2026 Milan Cortina Olympics. She’s also coming off an impressive stretch of technical racing: Shiffrin won her last five slalom starts, including the Olympics, and has finished on the podium in 14 consecutive slaloms dating back to February 2025.

According to recent reports, sunday’s race carries particular significance. Shiffrin has indicated that she’ll be selective about her slalom appearances this season, and Killington is expected to be her first slalom start of the winter. It’s a fitting place for her return to the discipline following her 2024 crash on the final pitch before the finish line on her second run. She lost control on the steep section of the Superstar course, slid into a gate, and punctured her oblique muscles. Shiffrin underwent surgery to clean and close the wound, followed by months of rehabilitation before returning to competition in February 2025.

In addition to the physical toll of the injury, the episode shook the ski racer’s confidence, and it took time for her to get back to her competitive rhythm. But in typical Shiffrin fashion, she went on to reclaim her place atop the sport, eventually adding another Olympic slalom gold medal to her collection in 2026.

According to recent reports, if anyone can challenge Shiffrin for the spotlight, it’s Moltzan. The 32-year-old Minnesota native is coming off the best start to a World Cup season of her career, having captured her first-ever World Cup victory in the giant slalom in Sölden, Austria, on Oct. 24.

Sources indicate that moltzan’s breakthrough win was a long time coming. A consistent contender on the World Cup circuit, she has steadily established herself as one of America’s strongest technical racers. She also earned an Olympic bronze medal in the team combined at the 2026 Games, further cementing her place among the country’s top Alpine racers.

In a recent development, with confidence from her first World Cup victory and a strong history of giant slalom results, Moltzan is a legitimate podium threat on Saturday. She’ll also be one to watch in Sunday’s slalom.

Recent findings suggest that keep an eye on 25-year-old AJ Hurt, who’s emerging as another important piece of the American technical team. Hurt has been particularly impressive in slalom this season, finishing fourth at Gurgl, Austria, and 15th at Levi, Finland, earlier this month. She was the top American woman in both races.

According to recent reports, that fourth-place finish at Gurgl was especially encouraging, putting Hurt within striking distance of her first-ever World Cup podium. She’s shown the ability to ski aggressively against the world’s best, and another strong performance in Killington could be a significant step forward.

Other American technical racers, including Nina O’Brien and Katie Hensien, are also worth following as the start lists take shape. O’Brien has established herself as a strong giant slalom competitor, while Hensien brings additional technicality to the U.S. slalom squad.

Both days of racing will be broadcast live on NBC and Peacock, with first runs available on Peacock and NBCSN. Saturday’s women’s giant slalom begins at 9:30 a.m. ET, with the second run at 12:30 p.m. ET.

Sunday’s slalom starts at 10:30 a.m. ET, followed by the final run at 1 p.m. ET. For viewers who can’t tune in live, Peacock will also offer streaming access to the races.

#228357. Industry News: Ben Zartman Splices Climbing Slings In His Garage. They’re the Best I’ve Ever Used.

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1101 w)

Industry News: Ben Zartman Splices Climbing Slings In His Garage. They’re the Best I’ve Ever Used.

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1101 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Climbing

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ben Zartman at work splicing slings in his garage.
  • When Ben Zartman learned to climb near Mexico City in the early 1990s, no one he knew could afford climbing gear.
  • It has been revealed that “All of us were poor, and all the gear was imported and so expensive,” he says.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ben Zartman at work splicing slings in his garage. (Photo: Courtesy Ben Zartman).

When Ben Zartman learned to climb near Mexico City in the early 1990s, no one he knew could afford climbing gear.

It has been revealed that “All of us were poor, and all the gear was imported and so expensive,” he says. “Most of the guys at the crag were sewing their own shoes or making their own cams.” Backpacks, harnesses, quickdraws—if they could sew it themselves, they did. At the time, Zartman was in high school. He didn’t have a job, but he did have a knack for making stuff. It never occurred to him that doing so might be sketchy until he arrived in Yosemite for the first time in 1995 and partners refused to climb on his rack. They were astonished he’d made his own gear. He was astonished that they’d bought theirs.

According to recent reports, later that year, when a government shutdown forced Zartman out of Joshua Tree, he hitchhiked to San Diego and bummed a ride to Baja with some sailors. Over the next few years, he split his time between major walls and boats, getting better at both kinds of rigging all the while. Then he got married, had three daughters, and spent five years sailing around the world on a boat he’d built himself. Eventually, he got work in a rigging shop in Rhode Island. He spliced custom slings for workaday sailors, then for open-ocean racing boats.

“At one point, I was sitting in the shop, splicing these high-end Dyneema loops, and I thought, man, if I had these in Yosemite, I would have been the coolest kid at the lodge cafeteria,” he says. And he likely would have: the spliced, covered loops used in sailing are seamless: no bar tacks or stitching. Instead, one end of the loop is woven into the other like a snake eating its tail. When you pull, the ends suction against each other (Zartman compares it to a finger-trap toy), making the loop stronger under load than bartacked Dyneema.

According to recent reports, “The idea fomented for a while in my mind, and in 2021 I started reaching out to every climbing gear manufacturer I could think of,” Zartman says. Letters and samples went out to Black Diamond, Metolius, Sterling, and others, asking them if they’d be interested in partnering on a product. Hardly anyone responded.

Sources indicate that so Zartman did what he’d always done: he took the DIY approach. In 2023, he launched his organization, Zartman Rigging. He joined the UIAA, mailed in slings for lab testing, and registered for UIAA labels. Once his gear was certified, the renowned gear shop IME, in North Conway, Upcoming Hampshire, started selling it. Rock and Snow in New Paltz, New York, and IME in Salt Lake City, Utah, were next. As his following grew, so did his offerings: a featherlight personal anchor system, seamless rappel back-ups, a rope-carabiner alternative called the Dreamlink, and a tiny rappel plate designed for 6-mm cord. The ideas come from Zartman’s experience climbing Yosemite walls; the materials come from his time on boats.

In a recent development, “The research and development budget in the [sailboat] racing scene is so significant,” he says. “It’s a great place to take technology from. I’m at that edge—I make ropes for the fanciest racing boats in the world, so I’m able to bring that into the climbing world pretty quickly.”.

The results are wild. The Dreamlink has a breaking strength of 43 kN (or, rather, he tested it up to 42 kN in a UIAA lab, and that’s when it broke their machine). The seamless runners are tagged 24 kN but break at 27kN. A fancy UV coating makes them essentially sun-proof. They don’t expire like other soft goods; you only have to retire them if the core becomes exposed. I have a double-length seamless runner that I use for building anchors and extending rappels. No bartack means easy setup, it racks well, and it’s pretty light. (Most traditionally manufactured Dyneema slings are tagged at 22kN. Mammut’s 120-centimeter Contact Sling weighs 28 grams, while Zartman’s version is 32 grams, the same as Black Diamond’s Infinity Cord.).

Zartman has a strong social media fan club, but he has plenty of critics too. Mountain Project commenters, he remarked, can be particularly vicious. Many scoff at the idea of a soft shackle or a seamless runner as gimmicky or unsafe. He’s not too bothered.

“Ray Jardine got scolded by all the Valley locals when he showed up with Friends,” he says, citing the first-ever cams. When other companies started making camming devices in the ‘80s, Jardine’s critics were forced to bite their tongues. Zartman is seeing a similar arc with his own gear. Several other climbing brands have started marketing soft shackles similar to Zartman’s Dreamlink. And in 2025, Black Diamond released its Infinity Cord, a Dyneema sling that uses the same bartack-free construction as Zartman’s and the same covered-loop splicing technique that sailors have used for decades. Black Diamond called it a “breakthrough in the evolution of cordelette engineering.”.

Sources indicate that zartman claims he’s unaffected by the new competition. “If there are people copying the concept, that’s good because that means the concept is good,” he says. In the meantime, he’s keeping his head down, focused on fulfilling orders and prototyping his next batch of inventions.

It has been revealed that zartman Rigging is gaining recognition, albeit slowly. Zartman does no paid advertising; about 80 percent of his business comes from Instagram. His top-shelf pricing likely tempers growth as well. For context, a 120-centimeter Zartman Rigging sling is $63, versus $40 for Black Diamond’s Infinity Cord or $14 for a basic Dyneema Trango runner of the same length.

“Because I make everything out of the nicest materials and by hand, it’s the most expensive gear on the market. It’s a luxury brand,” he says. “Which is ironic given that I started in Mexico with my own homemade climbing shoes.”.

Still, he produces enough to keep busy. Recently, he was able to hire one of his daughters part-time to help him splice, tag, and quality-test each product. He’s now a member of the UIAA safety commission, helping the organization design fresh testing protocols around skinny ropes and other novel forms of cord. He’s shipping to Alaska and Hawaii. People have started recognizing him in gear shops and at crags. Things are taking off—despite what Mountain Projectors may say.

“To a lot of people’s surprise,” he laughs, “I’ve sold a lot of gear.”.

These Ski Resorts Let You Ski for Free on the Day You Arrive

  • Industry observers note that while free arrival-day skiing might sound too good to be true, it’s not a new concept.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that november 28, 2023; Bozeman, MT, USA; Horizon Airlines operations at Bozeman Yellowstone International Airport (BZN). Mandatory Credit: Joe Nicholson-Alaska Airlines (Photo: Courtesy of Alaska Airlines).

A ski vacation usually starts with a travel day. Between catching flights, collecting luggage, and making your way to the mountains, it’s easy to lose an entire day before you ever click into your skis. But what if you could hit the slopes the same day you land, without paying for a lift ticket?

Industry observers note that while free arrival-day skiing might sound too good to be true, it’s not a new concept. Park City, Utah, previously offered a program called Quick START, which allowed travelers flying into Salt Lake City International Airport to exchange their same-day boarding pass for a complimentary lift ticket at Park City Mountain Resort, Deer Valley Resort, or Canyons Resort. Although the program has since ended, the idea of turning a travel day into a ski day hasn’t disappeared.

Today, several ski resorts and airlines offer similar incentives. Some require flying with a specific airline, while others are available to travelers booking an eligible resort stay.

According to recent reports, through its Atmos Rewards Alpine Getaways program, Alaska Airlines partners with ski destinations across the western United States and Canada to offer travelers special perks. For the 2026–’27 season, the airline has confirmed partnerships with Crystal Mountain in Washington and Palisades Tahoe in California, with additional resorts potentially joining as the season progresses.

In previous seasons, the airline has also partnered with Alyeska Resort, Arctic Valley Ski Area, and Eaglecrest Ski Area in Alaska; Bogus Basin and Schweitzer in Idaho; Jackson Hole Mountain Resort in Wyoming; and Sun Peaks Resort in British Columbia.

Sources indicate that while some participating resorts have offered complimentary lift tickets, others have provided discounted rentals and additional perks. At Palisades Tahoe, travelers can present a same-day Alaska Airlines or Hawaiian Airlines boarding pass or proof of Atmos Rewards membership to access the resort’s offer. Details for Crystal Mountain’s 2026–2’7 promotion are still being finalized.

“Skiing is a natural fit for Alaska because we serve so many great mountain destinations across the West,” Sarah Lasky, Senior External Communications Manager at Alaska Airlines, noted.

“Through Atmos Rewards, we want to make the journey more rewarding and connect our members with the experiences they love, including making it easier to turn the day they arrive into part of the adventure,” she continued.

Travelers can find the latest participating resorts and offers on Alaska Airlines’ website.

For the 2026–’27 winter season, travelers flying into Jackson Hole Airport can receive a complimentary lift ticket at one of three nearby ski resorts, regardless of which airline they choose: Jackson Hole Mountain Resort, Snow King Mountain, or Grand Targhee Resort.

Each resort offers something slightly different. Snow King Mountain provides a full-day lift ticket, while Jackson Hole Mountain Resort and Grand Targhee offer half-day tickets. Snow King also offers night skiing on select evenings, giving travelers who arrive later in the day another opportunity to get on the mountain.

To redeem the offer, visitors must present their boarding pass or flight confirmation showing their arrival at Jackson Hole Airport, along with a matching photo ID, at the participating resort’s ticket window.

The complimentary ticket is only valid on the day of arrival, and blackout dates vary by resort.

For the 2026–’27 winter season, guests who reserve at least five nights of lodging through Big White Direct Bookings qualify for one free lift ticket on their arrival day. The offer is available for both latest and existing eligible reservations and doesn’t require flying with a particular airline. To receive the complimentary ticket, guests must present their boarding pass.

Massive White is about a 50-minute drive from Kelowna International Airport, and there is airport shuttle transportation available for those who prefer avoiding driving in the snow. For travelers arriving later in the afternoon, the resort also offers night skiing, allowing them to make use of their free ticket after dark.

Free arrival-day skiing isn’t limited to North America. In Chile, Ski Portillo offers guests the opportunity to ski on both their arrival and departure days as part of its all-inclusive vacation packages.

Located in the Andes Mountains beside Laguna del Inca, Ski Portillo operates during the Southern Hemisphere’s winter season, typically from June through September.

Unlike programs that require travelers to present an airline boarding pass, Ski Portillo includes arrival and departure day skiing in its seven-night packages and three- or four-night Mini Week stays.

Before booking, be mindful of your arrival time. Between collecting luggage, picking up rental equipment, and traveling from the airport to the resort, you may have less time on the mountain than expected. Booking an early flight can help maximize your ski day, while resorts offering night skiing may be better options for travelers arriving later.

Recent findings suggest that it’s also notable to check blackout dates and other restrictions, as some offers are only available during certain periods of the ski season. Additionally, some resorts may require reservations or specific booking arrangements to qualify for complimentary tickets.

Finally, don’t forget to keep your boarding pass. Many of these programs require proof of same-day air travel, and having everything ready when you arrive can help you get on the slopes that much faster.

There are three things that make an approach shoe “high value:” its price, versatility, and durability. At $159, La Sportiva’s all-upcoming TX1 (replacing the cult-classic TX2) is decently affordable, and was versatile enough to take testers across a range of objectives, including fifth-class ridges in the Sierras and daily crag commutes, and be worn as a slip-on between limit boulder problems. I logged dozens of scrambling pitches in my TX1s and noted no signs of premature wear along the TPU-coated polyester upper or its Vibram MegaGrip outsole.

The breathable upper and shallow dot lugs make the TX1 an excellent shoe for the fair-weather rock climber who dodges rainy forecasts and muddy approaches. Those little lugs provide just enough grip for your average walkoff, but really shine on technical, slabby approaches where surface contact is king. On the mile-long Eagle Lake Buttress Traverse (5.0), the TX1 smeared well across its opening slabs—but I wished for a taller rand while jamming hand-sized cracks.

Fit wise, all testers found the TX1 to be comfortable out of the box, thanks to a stock 4mm Ortholite Hybrid insole and a plush Air Mesh lining. (The TX1 fits a touch wider than the TX2, for those familiar.) One tester, who has a relatively narrow, low-volume foot, loved the fit of the TX1, saying its toebox felt roomy and allowed her toes “to spread and relax naturally.” My wider foot, meanwhile, had me eager to take the TX1 off after an hour-long approach. I wish this shoe came in a slightly wider last.

#228350. Escape Winter With These 6 Underrated Desert Trail Runs

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1598 w)

General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Trailrunnermag ↗ Open Full Page

Escape Winter With These 6 Underrated Desert Trail Runs

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1598 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Trailrunnermag

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission.
  • Recent findings suggest that in his research for his upcoming book, “The 50 Classic Trail Runs of America” Andy Cochrane ran hundreds of trails across the U.S.
  • With all due respect to Presidential Traverse, Teton Crest, and Wonderland, the most sought-after one-day trail running route in the U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy.

Recent findings suggest that in his research for his upcoming book, “The 50 Classic Trail Runs of America” Andy Cochrane ran hundreds of trails across the U.S. These are his six favorites across the Southwest that come into season when most of the country is hibernating.

With all due respect to Presidential Traverse, Teton Crest, and Wonderland, the most sought-after one-day trail running route in the U.S. is the Grand Canyon Rim-to-Rim-to-Rim. Every spring and fall runners flock to Arizona to test their luck on this double lap of the major ditch, despite the National Park Service strongly advising against it. (Signs around the Grand Canyon warn of heat illness, elevation, and difficult evacs.).

Sources indicate that some have called R2R2R an obsession—while I’m not sure I would personally go that far, I do see the argument. I’ve run the route three times and each trip I find myself more enamored than the last. On my last visit in 2023, a peak autumn weekend with nearly perfect temps and all the water facets still running (the NPS shuts some of them down seasonally), I saw hundreds of runners attempting R2R2R. That’s a tiny fraction of the four and a half million people who visit the park each year, but very busy for a trail run.

It has been revealed that however, that was before the closures. The North Rim of the Grand Canyon was shuttered for most of the 2025 season due to the Dragon Bravo Fire, which burned 149,000 acres and 118 buildings. Then, on August 29th, 2026, a flash flood struck Phantom Ranch at the bottom of the Grand Canyon, killing three and forcing 82 others to be evacuated by helicopter. Trail damage was widespread, taking out footbridges and much of the park’s water line. The North Kaibab Trail, parts of the Bright Angel and South Kaibab trails, and sections of the River Trail remain closed with no set date for reopening.

Recent findings suggest that it’s getting colder and darker across most of the country. That means one thing: It’s desert season. In lieu of a double dip into the Grand Canyon—and to open your mind to the endless possibilities elsewhere—I’ve compiled a list of my six favorite trails across the American Southwest. All of them are in my upcoming book, “The 50 Classic Trail Runs of America” (which you can pre-order now!). They cover six different states and four unique desert ecosystems, so there is plenty of variety to choose from.

Unlike the rocky singletrack of the Northeast, the forested trails of the upper Midwest, or the alpine ridges of the West, running across the Southwest desert is a singular experience. Limited shade, even less water, and direct solar radiation create obvious hydration challenges. The temperature swings dramatically from near freezing overnight to scorching heat midday. The trails themselves are a mix of surfaces, from soft sand to loose scree to firm slickrock, with many—including the ones listed below—being very remote.

Beyond the physical experience, running in arid environments carries a different emotion, too. I often find myself in a quiet and contemplative mental space, passing by ancient saguaros, joshua trees, and prickly pears while trying to stay alert for subtle movements of rattlesnakes, lizards, and coyotes. Running in the desert is, simultaneously, the antidote to life’s complexity and a plague of endless possibility.

There are four distinct desert ecosystems in the U.S. The northernmost is the Great Basin, which covers most of Nevada and parts of neighboring states, making it the largest desert in the country. With frigid winters, it’s filled with sagebrush instead of cacti. Just south is the Mojave, the smallest of the four, which is home to Death Valley and Joshua Tree. Further south is the Sonoran, the “green desert,” with large saguaros and rainfall in both summer and winter. Last, the Chihuahuan, covers West Texas and southern New Mexico, and is known for succulents like Agave, Yucca, and Creosote.

Industry observers note that hidden in one of North America’s most remote national parks, Big Bend, the Outer Mountain Loop is a 32-mile circuit featuring a stark ecological contrast between the Chihuahuan Desert and the high-alpine Chisos Mountains. Beginning and ending in the Chisos Basin, a sky-island that’s home to rare species like the Colima Warbler, the trail plunges down stone steps and rolls across the sun-scorched flats of the Dodson Trail before making a grueling 3,000-foot final ascent up Blue Creek Canyon. Early Spanish explorers called this isolated region El Despoblado.

Why I love it: Getting to experience both sky islands and the solitude of the Chihuahuan desert.

In a recent development, spanning 39 miles from the edge of the Navajo Nation to the Grand Canyon’s South Rim, the Little to Substantial Colorado route is the less conventional way to explore one of the country’s most popular national parks. Tracing the historic Hopi salt journeys, the route plunges down Bekihatso Wash, follows the Little Colorado to its confluence with the Colorado River, passes sacred sites, scrambles obstacles like the Papago Wall, and passes by billion-year-old rock. With a 4,700-foot grind up the New Hance Trail at the end, it’s just as challenging and rewarding as rim-to-rim-to-rim.

Why I love it: It’s so close to the most famous one day trail route in the country, but still unheard of.

Sources indicate that crossing the national park from east to west, this 37-mile rolling route passes two distinct deserts—the higher Mojave and the lower Sonora—as you wander by long shadows of Yucca brevifolia (Joshua trees) and massive, weathered granite batholiths. Championed by the activist Minerva Hamilton Hoyt after decades of cattle grazing and mining exploitation, this sandy sanctuary strips away the crowds, offering sheer solitude as runners cross ancient mountain passes, gaze down at the dark expanse of the Salton Sea, and experience a desert communion.

Why I love it: it’s the one place in America that feels straight out of a Dr. Seuss book.

Recent findings suggest that one of the most remote routes we considered for the book, this 64-mile trek traces the ridgeline of the Toiyabe Range. Like Outer Mountain, this area is a sky island, a rare ecosystem in which the valley below is a scorching hot desert, but the trail itself is a lush forest of aspen and bristlecone pines, some 3,000 years old. Despite being Nevada’s longest named trail, Toiyabe is off-trail in nature, with significant routefinding and some sections of unrunnable terrain.

Why I love it: Remote and rugged, it’s a good test of navigation and alpine movement of all sorts.

Perched above Albuquerque, this 26-mile trail follows a limestone ridge along the backbone of the Sandia Mountains, with 360-degree views of the Rio Grande Valley below. Sandia is Spanish for watermelon, named after the ridge’s unique sunset alpenglow that turns the cliffs deep pink, with green conifers on top representing the rind. The trail features wildflowers, ponderosas, spruce, and white fir, and can be accessed via an aerial tramway, providing easy access without sacrificing its rugged, aesthetic appeal.

Why I love it: Quick and easy access paired with absolutely beautiful sunsets.

Sources indicate that winding through one of Southern Utah’s most distinctive landscapes, the 30-mile Bryce Canyon Traverse links the heavily trafficked northern amphitheater where thousands of hoodoos, rock fins, and natural arches create a natural maze with the primitive Under the Rim Trail to the south. Crossing a geological marvel shaped by erosion and freeze-thaw cycles over millions of years, the traverse is the best way to see it all. Heading southbound allows runners to catch sunrise over the spires before descending into remote backcountry, which is the direction we recommend.

Why I love it: There’s no place in the world with the same density or volume of hoodoos.

Desert running presents many challenges that the Mafate X can handle. Deserts are often oven-hot, so having a woven, high-airflow upper is ideal. They are rocky and filled with pokey things, so having a taller stack with soft PEBA foam is a bonus. They are loose, so having Vibram lugs adds a level of stability and confidence. And, with uneven ground, a wide base makes your feet feel much more planted, too.

Industry observers note that on long, sweaty days, sunscreen only goes so far. I take extra precaution and wear a Tahoe sun hoody, which delivers UPF 50+ protection against harsh UV rays, paired with a light polyester-spandex knit that wicks sweat off my skin and dries swiftly. And, integrated thumbholes and a fitted hood keep my hands and neck completely covered without restricting movement.

According to recent reports, for most desert runs I recommend stashing water the day before, but if you aren’t able to, having an extra large running pack is key. Kiprun’s 10L has room for a bladder in the back and two flasks up front, which is ideal for long desert stretches. The harness keeps the pack secure and large front pockets make it easy to access your phone, electrolytes, snacks, or sunscreen on the go.

My favorite drink mix, Fuel combines essential electrolytes like sodium, potassium, and magnesium to replace minerals lost in heavy sweat. It tastes good, prevents cramps, and the added zinc supports fluid retention in hot conditions. Using a low-GI carb from beet sugar, it also provides steady energy without blood sugar spikes or crashes, which is great for longer days.
