Breaking: The Best Back-to-School Books For Every Age and Stage

📅 01 Aug 2025 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1028 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fatherly

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The time when kids go back to school is full of hope and excitement.
  • Not all great back-to-school books have to be specifically about school or jitters.
  • You might remember Amelia Bedelia as a bumbling housekeeper, but her more recent adventures as a younger woman are great for young ones.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Smart reads for a crucial time.

The time when kids go back to school is full of hope and excitement. It can also be a time of nervousness and apprehension. And, for as long as most people can remember, one of the greatest ways to cure the blues, for kids and adults, is to read a good book.

Not all great back-to-school books have to be specifically about school or jitters. But sometimes that kind of thing helps. From Pre-K kiddos to high schoolers, here’s a selection of great books that will help kids feel calmer, brighter, and more confident about heading back to the classroom.

Amelia Bedelia's First Day of School.

You might remember Amelia Bedelia as a bumbling housekeeper, but her more recent adventures as a younger woman are great for young ones. This picture book contains some of the same wordplay of the old books, with a great message.

Age: Pre-K, Kindergarten, and 1st Grade.

It has been revealed that this board book is part of Usborne’s “Very First Questions and Answers” series and, as such, addresses the basic question of why school, or some form of education and structure, is notable. Neither pandering nor confusing, this book is literally designed to explain the concept to very young school-age ones. The talking points here take some of the guesswork out of a parent’s speech, so you may want to read it swiftly to yourself before sharing with your kid.

This sweet picture book isn’t about school specifically at all. But it is a book about how kids can initiative for and manage their disappointments. The titular mouse, Clementine, worries about all sorts of things going wrong. But, the key lesson here is to plan for “Uh Ohs.” Great for parents who have anxious kids or children who feel like everything has to be perfect.

Ages: Pre-K, Kindergarten, and 1st Grade.

According to recent reports, as first chapter books go, Abby Hanlon’s brilliant Dory Fantasmagory books are really without any peers. Hilarious, heartfelt, and easily readable for kids just starting chapter books, the Dory books don’t just make kids feel better about being kids; the books actually capture the hilarious nature of little kid logic.

All of Dory’s adventures are good for back-to-school jitters, but the second book, The Real True Friend, is perhaps the best primer for meeting new kids and trying to fit in.

Judy Blume’s immortal book is technically the third in a series that began with Tales of a Fourth Grade Nothing. Focused on the trials and tribulations of 5th and 6th graders, and their changing feelings toward the world, this book has only gotten better since 1980. The humor and realism still work, over 40 years later, and the analog nature of this very recent past can be nothing but positive for modern kids.

Ages: Late Elementary school and Middle School.

Choose Your Own Adventure (Newly introduced Covers!).

According to recent reports, that’s right, the classic Choose Your Own Adventure books are back. And now, with new, slick covers for the 2020s. Why are these good for back-to-school? As nuts as some of the classic Choose Your Own Adventure books are, the thing that makes these stories so great for emerging readers is the fact that it’s totally okay to fail.

The bite-sized adventures are also great for kids who think that they don’t enjoy reading. These books are modern classics for the specific reason that kids feel like they’re in control.

According to recent reports, imagine a series sort of like Harry Potter, but instead of humans, you’re following a bunch of talking dragons. That might not fully represent Wings of Fire, but it does give you a sense of the appeal of this series. With different dragon characters that every kid can identify with, Wings of Fire is a truly inclusive series, which is impressive since most of the characters are fire-breathing reptiles.

Sometimes the best way to educate kids about the classics is to barely disguise the classics at all. The brilliant thing about George O’Connor’s Olympians graphic novel books is that these are fairly straightforward takes on classic Greek mythology. Middle-grade kids will love the awesome illustrations, but they’ll also be way ahead in history class.

In a recent development, the story of siblings finding a secret world within a normal city has become an instant classic since 2012. Not exactly coded for back-to-school, middle-grade or early middle-school kids should read the Wildwood series for one reason: Other bookworm kids will have probably read these books, too.

Ages: 5th grade, 6th grade, or Middle-School.

A graphic novel from author and illustrator Jerry Craft, New Kid is perhaps the perfect contemporary back-to-school book for older kids. Focused on a 7th grader named Jordan Banks, the book is all about feeling like an outsider, relative to both class and race. A good point of view for all kinds of kids.

If your kid likes this one, there are others in the series, including Class Act and School Trip.

Ages: Middle School and High School.

Sunrise on the Reaping (Hunger Games series).

Sources indicate that yes, after all these years, Suzanne Collins' Hunger Games universe is still relevant and great for older kids. The newest 2025 book, Sunrise on the Reaping, is the second in the Hunger Games prequels series that began with The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes in 2020. In some ways, these prequels are better than the classic Hunger Games books. But if your kiddos get hooked, the other books are waiting for them after they finish the latest ones.

The Complete Collected Poems of Maya Angelou.

Industry observers note that sometimes tweens and teens need a little bit of inspiration. And that comfort and inspiration don’t always have to come in the form of narratives. Instead, why not turn to the poetry of one of the greats? Every kid who has ever had a deep feeling about something will relate to at least one of Maya Angelou’s poems. And, in terms of centering oneself before the stress of back-to-school, nobody touches the soul quite like Angelou.

Ages: Middle School and High School.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Bonus: They’re all literally proven to be good for you, too!

It has been revealed that here’s a fun fact about your Flexible Spending Account (FSA): whatever you don’t spend by the deadline is gone. Granted, some looks give you a little grace period or rollover a small amount, but most of us are on the use-it-or-lose-it clock. And while Health Savings Account (HSA) money doesn’t expire, it’s still sitting there earmarked for your health, and the holidays are a good excuse to finally use it.

What’s great is that you can buy a lot more with it than just your basic bandages or the odd bottle of contact solution. We’re talking heating pads, period underwear, sunscreen, smart rings... even ergonomic office chairs can qualify! Some of the bigger-ticket items here (like the Lettuce Grow) may require a letter of medical necessity, but that typically just means filling out a quick online health questionnaire at checkout through a service like Truemed or Flex. Everything else you can usually just swipe your HSA/FSA card for. Of course, rules vary by plan, so check yours if you’re not sure.

Sources indicate that one notable caveat: HSA/FSA funds can only be used for you, your spouse, and your dependents. That means the following picks are perfect for treating yourself, stuffing your kids’ stockings, or, you know, finally getting your snoring partner something that’ll ultimately help you both sleep.

Here are some of our favorite items that are often covered by HSA and FSA guidelines.

Sources indicate that if you know someone who gets painful period cramps or has endometriosis or adenomyosis, these little menstrual heat pads are such a thoughtful stocking stuffer. I stick them inside the waistband of my pants, and it genuinely gets hot enough to offer relief and go wherever I go all day. They last for hours, and I just love that they let me get relief without feeling stuck to a heating pad (and therefore a wall outlet). — Katie McPherson.

Isn’t it great when really trendy, great-smelling, cute beauty products are also good for you and eligible to buy with tax-exempt money? This is the case with Touchland hand sanitizer, which is all the rage with tweens and teens, and for good reason. It’s so cute and fun that it makes keeping germs away a blast. This is so perfect for stocking stuffing. — Sarah Aswell.

Industry observers note that as someone who works from home, I’ve always struggled with back pain from sitting hunched over a laptop all day long. I never even thought to check whether an office chair could be HSA/FSA-eligible... until I found out about Branch, which is usually through Truemed. Yes, you typically need to fill out a short form to get a letter of medical necessity, but it’s so worth it if the end result is a beautiful Branch office chair with 14 points of adjustment, including lumbar support that moves up, down, in and out, with armrests that adjust five ways. It’s also nice that there are so many upholstery options (I ordered the black boucle!). — Julie Sprankles.

Ancestry DNA Origins & Traits Kit.

While not all DNA kits are eligible for HSA and FSA spending accounts, ones that give you health information are usually kosher. This one, from Ancestry, falls into that category. Have fun learning more about yourself and your past while also finding out medical information that could change your life. This is a great gift for someone who has everything. — Sarah Aswell.

One of the most popular purchases with FSA and HSA money is this heated massage gun. It feels amazing, and it makes you feel better in the long run. We like this one because it gets killer reviews and comes with an app. Again, this is a substantial-ticket item that might turn out to be a great way to spend FSA money at the end of the year. — Sarah Aswell.

I have a chronic illness that causes high inflammation, so I tend to have a lot of body pain... especially in my joints. This flexible, wearable device combines red light, infrared light, micro-vibration, and micro-magnetic pulses in one band. I’ve found that if I strap it on to whatever aches, it really seems to help ease the pain. You should be able to pay directly with your HSA/FSA card, but it’s always a good idea to check with your specific health proposal to see if you need a letter of medical necessity. — Julie Sprankles.

Recent findings suggest that supergoop is one of my favorite beauty products and by far my favorite sunscreen tech giant. They make my skin look and feel great while protecting it for the future. Many of Supergoop’s products are FSA- and HSA-eligible, including this mineral eye cream that works like a dream. But don’t sleep on many of their other products — I also love their Unseen Sunscreen for faces. — Sarah Aswell.

Geniani XL Electric Heating Pad Throw.

I am not exaggerating when I say that my life was changed by breaking down and getting an electric heating pad for my bed. It makes my sore body feel better, it prevents stiffness, and it is also just really, really nice when I have my period and I’m feeling crampy. — Sarah Aswell.

Recent findings suggest that this smart scale tracks 16 metrics, including muscle mass, body fat, and heart rate. You can pick the ones you want to show on the substantial color display and hide the rest, and it recognizes up to eight users. Plus, it syncs up with Apple Health and Google Health. Oh, and it has a few fun extra modes: Baby Mode (in case you need to check before your next pediatrician visit), Pet Mode (if your pup is on a diet), and Luggage Mode (so you know before heading to the airport). — Julie Sprankles.

Sources indicate that I’m not proud of it, but in my middle age I’ve become a pretty bad snorer. The best gift I’ve ever gotten for my partner is these Ozlo earbuds, which can’t be beat. They are really comfortable to sleep in, and the white noise makes you catch your Zs like a baby. The price is a bit splurgy, but can you put a dollar sign on deep sleep, especially if you can put it on your HSA card? — Sarah Aswell.

VisoOne Blue Light Blocking Glasses.

According to recent reports, man, do some reading about blue light glasses, and you’ll see that they have virtually no downside — especially if you wear them at night while looking at screens. It’s probably the best thing you can buy for yourself under $20 that can help you feel better and get better sleep. And VisoOne has some really cute styles, too. — Sarah Aswell.

According to recent reports, I’ve always wanted an Oura ring but held off because (a) I’m a mom and tend to buy everything for everyone else first and (b) this is more than I normally spend on myself. So I was pleasantly surprised to find out it’s HSA/FSA-eligible! The Oura Ring 4 looks like regular jewelry but tracks more than 50 metrics like sleep, stress, heart health, cycle, and more, which is hugely helpful always but especially when you’re in perimenopause like so many of us on the Scary Mommy team are. — Julie Sprankles.

Keep Going Travel Family First Aid Kit.

I love giving first-aid kits to people for the holidays, especially if someone has recently gotten a fresh car, moved into a new place, or had a new baby. We should really have more of these in more places — and my favorite one is this cute portable one by Keep Going. There are so many cute patterns, and it fits anywhere from your glove box to a tote to a diaper bag. — Sarah Aswell.

Saalt Hanky Panky Boy Short Period Underwear.

I love period undies so much! They don’t leak, they’re good for the environment, and they will save you a significant amount of money over time. My favorite pair is these boy shorts from Saalt called Hanky Panky. They have great coverage while also still managing to be cute. Most, if not all, period panties are eligible to be purchased with your HSA or FSA! — Sarah Aswell.

Caring Mill Vapor Shower Tablets.

Sources indicate that one of my favorite discoveries of 2025 was shower tablets — also known as shower steamers. You throw them onto the floor of the shower and, over the course of your rinse, they evaporate and let off fumes infused with essential oils. Certain types can help clear out your sinuses (peppermint) or relax you for bed (lavender). They’re fun and they have a purpose. I like these from Caring Mill, which is a brand specifically for people buying HSA and FSA items. — Sarah Aswell.

Neutrogena Pink Grapefruit Cleansing Wipes.

These cleansing wipes are great for everything from removing grit and makeup at night to keeping in your purse for a little refresh during the day. And they smell divine! — Sarah Aswell.

I’ve had my Lettuce Grow for over a year now, and it’s one of my most favorite things in our house! It’s like having your own personal salad bar. The Nook grows 20 plants under built-in grow lights, and they arrive pre-sprouted, so you’re harvesting about twice as fast as you would from seed. It's such a great option for families who want to get more greens on the table, and it’s HSA/FSA-eligible through Flex. — Julie Sprankles.

According to recent reports, I’ve been putting pimple patches in my daughters’ holiday stockings for a few years now, but only recently have I tried them out and discovered that they actually work and are really awesome! Many of them qualify for HSA/FSA purchases, especially if they are medicated. I love these spot patches from Curology, which contain the active ingredient hydrocolloid. — Sarah Aswell.

Cure Hydrating Electrolyte Drink Mix.

I was surprised to find that some hydration drink mixes are FSA- and HSA-approved. Which is great because sometimes when I’m feeling rundown, I just put one of these in a big glass of water and feel so much better. — Sarah Aswell.

#228234. How To Make Summer Memories That Stick

How To Make Summer Memories That Stick

📅 04 Sep 2025 | ⏱️ 5 min read (921 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fatherly

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Labor day is upon us and as I celebrate the ending of the chaotic mess that is summer for parents, I also can’t help but feel a little wistful.
  • Recent findings suggest that the answer to that, I think, is yes.
  • The “remember when” moments are a different kind of fun — Type 2 fun.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Summer’s behind us. What memories did you make?

Labor day is upon us and as I celebrate the ending of the chaotic mess that is summer for parents, I also can’t help but feel a little wistful. Did I make the most of the summer? Or, more to the point, have I made lasting memories for my kids?

Recent findings suggest that the answer to that, I think, is yes. But the memories are not found in volumes of ice cream, the rides at the county fair, the hours of pool time and picnics, or the (shockingly expensive) songs and bonding they had at camps. I believe that in the long term these simple joys will become part of a happy and balanced childhood, but they’re not the kind of thing they look back on and say, “remember when …?”.

The “remember when” moments are a different kind of fun — Type 2 fun.

As former Fatherly editor Julia Holmes explained in her wonderful essay on memory and adventures, there are varying levels of fun. “The ‘fun scale,’” she writes, “which first circulated in climbing books and media in the 1980s, divides outdoor recreation into three major categories. At one end of the scale is Type 1: You expect to enjoy yourself and you do (a day at the beach). At the other end of the scale is Type 3: not even remotely fun, catastrophically bad, something never to be repeated (shipwrecked). Somewhere between those extremes is the perfect fun, the kind of fun that pushes you past yourself and (hopefully) delivers you back to yourself in better condition — stronger, happier, full of fresh gratitude for comfort and organization.”.

Sources indicate that type 2 fun is the stuff of memories. When we tell a great story about travel or adventure — one that’s worth retelling throughout life — there is usually an edge to it. There are barriers overcome, there is a sketchy or frightening moment, there are lessons learned.

It has been revealed that I think about Type 2 fun all the time. As a distance runner and cyclist and outdoors person who remembers the first time they got hypothermia fondly (it’s a good story!), I embrace such “fun” and try to bring my kids into it. As a dad, I know that summers, with the kids out of school and the weather cooperating is a great time to go after it.

So, as we stare down Labor Day, I wonder to myself, how’d I do?

Sources indicate that this summer, if you are to look at my 8-year-old’s skinned knees, I think some memories were made. We daily took to the trails and roads and pump track to bike. There were falls, tears, and an awesome amount of getting back on the bike with a chin held high. One of his favorite stories to tell was actually from last summer when we were mountain biking together, attached, tandem-style. It was hot, buggy, and we had already had a minor crash (or two) along the rocky trail. At one point, there was a ledge that required you to walk your bike, single file, over a small cliff. I asked my son to go to the other side and wait, the better for him to watch as I awkwardly pushed the long tandem bike along the thin ledge, lost my balance and, rather than fall 20 feet to the forest floor, tossed the bike and leaned into the rock. I steadied myself as the bike crashed below. Thirty minutes later, we had were back up top and on the trail again — with a story to tell.

For my older child, I might have gone a little hard on the Type 2 fun this summer. I offered to pick up my teen and their best friend from overnight camp and take them on their first real backpacking trip this year. I marked the maps, packed the food, and neatly stored our tents, stoves, water purifiers, headlamps, and sleeping bags for a three-night, four day trip on The Long Trail in Vermont. The more serious ascent was to happen on day 1, leaving the rest of the trip for a rolling hike, out and back, to give them a pleasant taste for one of my favorite pastimes.

It has been revealed that the Gods of Type 2 fun had other intends. First of all, the parking lot on the map simply wasn’t where it should have been, so we wound our way through country roads to the next lot, miles away and downhill from the planned start. In the upcoming parking lot, a sign informed us that a shelter had moved a few miles further. The short of it: A good hike became a formidable trek. Three days, 18.34 miles, and 4,698 feet (up!) later, the kids refused to camp a third night in the woods, demanding to hike straight to the car and go get a hotel. We did just that. I stopped for milkshakes on the way, but somehow, years from now, I don’t think the truck stop shakes are what they’re going to remember about their time on The Long Trail.

According to recent reports, this weekend, I think I’m going to take the family to Coney Island. The kids will grab hot dogs, we’ll all ride on the Wonder Wheel, walk down the beach and share the breeze. We’ve made enough memories this summer — and everyone needs a little forgettable fun too.

Industry observers note that she’s been writing forever, and professionally for three years. According to recent reports, you’ve booked your tickets. You’ve planned your itinerary. You’ve figured out the My Disney Experience App (you think.) You’re as ready as you can be for your family’s first trip to Disney World. Then it dawns on you: What do you need to pack? Shopping for essentials for your first family trip to Disney World is an art – it’s about knowing your family and what you all need to thrive on one of the most exciting, most magical, and yes, sometimes stressful family vacations.

A little online searching will promptly convince you you'll need to buy extra luggage just to pack park essentials, but don’t stress. As an easily-overwhelmed mom who recently braved Disney World for the first time, I've got some hard-won advice to help guide your vacation prep and inform your packing list. Plus, I've scoured the internet for top picks of the most-used sanity-saving products to make the happiest place on earth live up to its name for you and your family.

It has been revealed that for many parents, taking the kids to Disney World at least once during their childhood is a bucket list goal. When that dream is finally realized, there is a mix of idyllic anticipation and anxious uncertainty. It’s not surprising that many parents find planning for a trip to Disney World to be a stressful experience.

When it comes to Disney World, there are two types of parents: those who have fond memories of their own childhood Disney vacation, and those who hope to give their own kids the trip they didn’t get to experience growing up. Whichever type you are, the goal is the same: To give your kids a core-memory-making family vacation they’ll cherish forever. Of course, a love of Disney also evokes childhood nostalgia that is so fun to share with your own children. The legacy of classic and modern Disney characters, movies, and parks is a special thing to pass on to the next generation and something that carries a lot of weight for many.

In a recent development, along with all the hopes and expectations wrapped up in a family trip to Disney World, the cost of the vacation only adds to the pressure to make it the best trip ever. For budget travelers, the average weeklong Disney World vacation for a family of four can cost $6,000 or more, according to NerdWallet, so ensuring you get your money’s worth is a huge factor. Not only that, but with so much to see, do, and experience in the parks, a vacation to Disney World is a complex trip to plan. Some families even turn to Disney vacation planners and travel agents to help with the sheer volume of logistical planning involved.

It has been revealed that as tempting as it may be, you don’t need to add-to-cart every single item you see on ‘Must Have Disney Essentials’ lists. Before you start shopping, it pays to think through what will help your family enjoy your trip the most. The best travel products for families will vary, so evaluate these factors before you start shopping:.

In a recent development, of course, start with the makeup of your family. How old will your kids be on the trip, and what needs and preferences correspond with their ages? Strollers are a substantial decision for many, and there are lots of pros and cons to consider: Will it help or hurt to have a stroller for airports? Is it worth it to lug a stroller to the parks? Would renting Disney World strollers be a better option? The answer will be different for every family, so don’t listen to advice that insists on a right answer. Our youngest was six on our trip and I seriously considered taking or renting a stroller. She ended up walking the parks like a champ and I was glad we didn’t have to deal with a stroller! Had she been a year younger, though, I am sure a stroller would have been our saving grace.

According to recent reports, what are your kids most looking forward to in the parks? How will they handle long lines? Will you need to anticipate an afternoon nap each day? Should you stock up on a few fun toys ahead of time so your kiddos aren’t pining for the theme park loot, or do you just need to upgrade your child’s luggage? A Disney World vacation will look very different depending on the ages of your kids, so narrow your list of essentials based on them.

According to recent reports, A surefire way to preemptively ruin your first trip to Disney World is to forget your own needs in the process. For parents, Disney World is fun, sure, but there’s also a lot of planning, incessant crowds, unrelenting heat, not to mention the never-ending soundboard of the kids' needs and wants. Take a moment and think about what essentials you need to make the most of the trip, and perhaps even a few indulgent spa day gifts to help melt stress away at the end of a non-stop Disney World day.

A travel-size umbrella that offers heavy-duty weather protection.

Weather is a massive factor in whether Disney World lives up to being “the happiest place on earth.” You likely know to expect warmer temperatures year-round, and extreme heat in the summer. But surprise rain showers are also a common occurrence in Orlando. Luckily, the Repel Compact Umbrella can help on both fronts. Not only will you be happy you have it if you get caught in a shower, but it will also filter UV rays when the sun is beating down. In fact, Repel even offers a UPF 50+ UV protection version of the umbrella to block out 99% of UV rays.

Industry observers note that the umbrella's double-vented canopy is designed to withstand winds up to 85 MPH, so you won’t have to worry about it inverting. It is a heavy-duty umbrella packed into a compact travel size, opens and collapses with a push of a button, and is definitely worth tossing in your park bag. Reviewers say it performs as advertised – one even said the umbrella “loves wind” – with just a few saying the only matter they’ve had is closing it. (And yes, Disney World does allow umbrellas!).

This microfiber towel will save the day in all sorts of ways when you’re out and about, and packs into its own travel bag.

It has been revealed that when you’re at the parks from sun up to sun down, unexpected needs are bound to arise, and the Rainleaf Microfiber Towel will be a lifesaver for many of them. Kid drop Dole Whip down their shirt? Want to dry off a wet seat? Need to add more sun shade to the stroller? Chances are you’ll be reaching for this towel all day long. Not only is it compact and made for travel, but it also absorbs five times its own weight and dries incredibly fast. If it’s super hot, drench the towel in cold water to help you cool off, then drape it over your backpack or stroller as you walk around to let it air dry.

Running from $9 to $20 a piece, depending on the size, it’s worth giving each family member their own, or grabbing a few to designate for certain purposes – one for clean up, one for shade and sweat, and one as a picnic blanket for parades or just a quick rest.

This compact travel charger keeps your devices topped up all day long.

Industry observers note that between taking a million pictures and using the Disney app to do everything from making meal orders and reservations to finding the next ride (or nearest restroom!), you’ll be using your phone a lot in the parks. The Anker Portable Charger ensures your devices stay charged up all day long. It has a universal USB-C cable and delivers 10,000mAh (milliamp hours), delivering the equivalent of two full smartphone charges. At 30W charging speed, you can expect it to fully charge a phone in about an hour – which is how long you’ll be lining for some rides anyway.

In a recent development, the charger is just a tad bigger than a credit card, and weighs about as much as a phone. It can charge three devices at once (you just need extra charging cables) and the cable connector stores in the battery pack for safekeeping between uses. Coming in under $30, it’s well worth the peace of mind so you don’t miss a single picture-perfect moment, even as the last firework illuminates the night sky.

One tip I got from a Disney World cast member is to take screenshots of the QR codes, order confirmations, lightning lane arrival windows, and anything else you may need for reference from the My Disney Experience App so you aren’t constantly having to access the app, which can drain your phone battery.

Take a rest whenever you need to with this super practical compact folding stool.

In a recent development, the Boreeman Folding Stool is as close as it gets to realizing the idea of pants that turn into a chair, but arguably way more practical. If your back just isn’t what it used to be, or you’ve got a kiddo who you know will complain about standing in line, this folding stool will single-handedly save your Disney World trip. The collapsible seat locks into place at various heights up to 17.72 inches. It packs down into a disc that is 9.84 inches by 2.36 inches with a carrying strap for added convenience. Use it in ride lines, waiting for parades or reveals, or just whenever you need to take a load off. It also comes in handy to help little ones with bathroom needs.

According to recent reports, the stool is highly rated with 4.4 stars from over 8,000 reviewers, but some say it’s not super comfortable, while others warn theirs broke while sitting on it. Still, other reviewers say they still use theirs often over a year later. It comes in tons of fun colors and can slide into bags, backpacks, or stroller compartments. It’s also light enough at 2.5 pounds for many kids to carry it through a ride line themselves.

Make any moment magical with these Disney-themed bubble wands.

The struggle to not buy every cute thing you see in Disney World is real, and the Little Kids Disney Light and Sound Musical Bubble Wand is here to help. Light-up bubble wands are all the rage in the parks, and they come with a hefty price tag. If you’re looking to save money where you can on your trip, surprise your little one with a pre-bought bubble wand for a fraction of the cost of the park varieties, which cost upwards of $35.

Recent findings suggest that these wands are themed with all their favorite characters, including Mickey Mouse, Tiana, Elsa, Moana, and more. They light up, play music, and come with extra bubbles so your kiddo can join in the bubble wand fun all day long. Some reviewers were not satisfied with the durability and quality of the wand, while others say it was perfect for their Disney Parks trip.

Outsmart unpredictable weather with this family pack of reusable ponchos.

In a recent development, my family didn’t end up needing the Lingito Rain Ponchos Family Pack for rain, but we were so glad we used them on Tiana’s Bayou Adventure! We got in one of the first virtual queue time slots of the morning, and without the ponchos, we would have been utterly soaked for the rest of the day. This family pack gets the job done at keeping your family (and your backpacks) dry, whether the water is weather or ride-related. The adult ponchos have drawstrings, and while I understand they might pose a hazard for kids, I wish the kid ponchos could tighten for a better fit. My kids held theirs closed just under their chins when we dropped down the log flume.

According to recent reports, they come compactly packed in small disposable bags, and you’ll be hard-pressed to fold them back in after you open them. The Amazon listing describes these ponchos as both reusable and disposable, which is accurate. While they can be dried out and used again on a trip, they might be too much trouble to save for your next adventure (however, one reviewer reports their family has used their set again and again). Still, at $10 for a pack of four (two adult and two kid-sized ponchos), they are well worth throwing in your bag every day in case you get caught in one of those notorious surprise Orlando rain showers – or just so you stay dry on wet rides.

This wearable fan rests around your neck for hands-free cooling wherever you go.

If you're worried about the relentless Orlando heat more than any other part of your Disney trip, do yourself a favor and pack the FrSara Portable Neck Fan. It’s encased blade vents blow air all the way around the back of the neck and out the ends to keep you noticeably cooler without having to worry about hazards like tangling hair. With a noise level of 25 dB – the equivalent of the ambient noise of a ‘silent’ PC – you can even keep it running indoors through those winding ride lines without being a nuisance to yourself or others …though it’s worth noting that some reviewers find it too loud.

Recent findings suggest that the fan's working time ranges from four to 16 hours, and its USB-C charging port means you can recharge on the go with a portable device charger. With three speeds and 360-degree surround airflow, it might not quite make you forget you’re in Orlando, but it can certainly take the edge off the heat.

This lightweight travel stroller folds down easily and has four recline positions with tons of storage.

It has been revealed that to pack a stroller or not to pack a stroller, that is the question for families making the pilgrimage to Disney World. If you decide to bring your own, the Summer Infant 3Dlite Stroller is our pick for Disney World for a few reasons. First, the stroller complies with Disney World’s list of prohibited items regarding stroller size, and reviewers do confirm that they used this stroller in Disney World. Second, the price is right at under $100, though it’s worth noting that single-stroller rentals at Disney World go for $15 per day, and $13 per day for multi-day rentals.

The stroller is lightweight, has four recline positions for napping on the go, a pop out weather canopy, and tons of extra storage, including a cup holder, close-top bag, and large storage compartment underneath the seat. Reiewers agree that this is a great, budget-friendly stroller for travel, and is highly rated at 4.6 stars with over 7,000 reviews. Plus, it has a weight capacity of 50 pounds, which is on the upper end for most travel strollers. So if you have an older kid who might not be able to last the entire day on foot, this stroller can be a lifesaver.

Take it from me, even anxious, stressed-out parents can make the most of their family’s first trip to Disney World. Resolve to manage your stress level by taking good care of yourself, setting yourself up for success by planning based on what will make it magical for your family, and packing essentials that will help everyone enjoy the trip.

The key is managing expectations, especially your own. Knowing that a vacation with kids is still parenting, just in a different location – and understanding that parenting in Disney World isn’t always a walk in the park – can help you make this trip every bit as magical for your kiddos as you hoped, though it likely won’t feel like it to you. So make sure you stop and take in their sweet faces when they meet their favorite characters, when they go on the ride they were so excited for, and as they watch as fireworks illuminate the night. You’ll experience the magic, guaranteed!

Menopause Is Hurting Women at Work. Something Has To Change.

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (908 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scarymommy

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that brain fog, hot flashes, no sleep...
  • I distinctly remember sitting in AP English class as a junior in high school with such horrible period cramps that it must've shown on my face.
  • It was the first time in my life that I hadn’t felt well and advocated for myself, albeit only after being nudged.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that brain fog, hot flashes, no sleep... and zero workplace support. Here’s what women can actually do about it.

I distinctly remember sitting in AP English class as a junior in high school with such horrible period cramps that it must've shown on my face. I kept staring at the clock, and eventually, my very strict, no-nonsense teacher came to my desk and asked if I was OK.

“Can I go home early?” I asked.

It was the first time in my life that I hadn’t felt well and advocated for myself, albeit only after being nudged.

According to recent reports, then, in my 20s, I was severely nauseous with my first pregnancy but kept suffering through it at work because I wanted to save up my PTO for maternity leave. Now, I work from home, but as I’m hitting my late 30s, I wonder if I’d be any better at advocating for my needs in the workplace if I had perimenopause symptoms.

Industry observers note that truthfully, I’m not sure I would be — and I’m far from the only one. In a latest study, Womea surveyed more than 830 employed U.S. women ages 45 and older about how perimenopause or menopause symptoms affect their experiences at work.

Of those surveyed, 60% mentioned no one at work knew they were experiencing symptoms. Meanwhile, 90% said their employers have no menopause or midlife health policies in place. An alarming 87% said their symptoms affected their job performance in the past year, and 17% believed their symptoms cost them a promotion, raise, or high-visibility project.

Sources indicate that so what’s a woman to do when she finds her perimenopause or menopause symptoms interfering with her career? And what can we reasonably expect our employers to do about it?

Perimenopause is the hormonal transition that leads us on the lovely path to menopause. It can begin in a woman’s 30s, although it more commonly starts in her 40s. “Fun” symptoms include brain fog, sleep disruption, mood changes, hot flashes, and irregular periods.

Dr. Gillian Goddard, a board-certified endocrinologist and author of The Hormone Loop, says disrupted sleep can leave a woman feeling physically and mentally sluggish. Declining estrogen levels also affect dopamine activity, making it harder to concentrate. Research also suggests that learning latest information can become more difficult during this period.

That helps explain why half of the women in the Womea survey reported experiencing brain fog or losing their train of thought during a meeting, client call, or presentation.

Women in this stage might not feel like themselves physically and emotionally, says Lauren Tetenbaum, LCSW, JD, PMH-C, MSCP, a New York-based women’s reproductive mental health expert and the author of Millennial Menopause: Preparing for Perimenopause, Menopause, and Life’s Next Period.

As a psychotherapist, Tetenbaum says many of her clients are ambitious and dedicated to their careers, but are “caught off guard by the symptoms… they were never warned about.” Not even by their own healthcare providers!

Rather than recognizing that they may need medical care or additional rest, some women catastrophize what they’re going through, she states, worrying that brain fog could be a sign of early dementia or that they’re no longer capable of meeting their own high standards. “The performance is often not the issue; it’s the self-perception,” Tetenbaum says.

Still, it’s not easy for women navigating midlife at work.

Women can feel pushed out of the workforce during major life transitions, Tetenbaum says, from matrescence to perimenopause, because they're presented with a false choice: “Sacrifice your health or wellbeing or values to work here, or leave, and don’t you dare show ‘weakness’ by asking for help.”.

According to recent reports, we shouldn’t have to choose between our health and our careers... nor should we feel obligated to disclose personal medical details to our managers just to get support.

Industry observers note that instead, Tetenbaum encourages women to familiarize themselves with their workplace benefits, such as health insurance coverage, PTO, and possible accommodations. (Sometimes, especially in competitive fields, employees can worry that taking PTO makes them look noncommitted. But taking care of ourselves shouldn't be seen as professional weakness. After all, we can’t bring our best selves to work if we're not feeling our best.).

Tetenbaum also strongly urges women to seek medical care rather than assume they have to push through their symptoms.

Employers have to do their part, too.

Goddard states several workplace conditions can make this phase of life more difficult for women, including insufficient restrooms, unpredictable or long hours, limited opportunities for breaks, and confined workspaces. Addressing some of these conditions could make a difference.

Employers can also review their health insurance policies to make sure menopause-related care is covered, such as menopause specialists, behavioral and psychological health care, and other relevant services, adds Tetenbaum, as well as look at ways to implement flexible schedules, remote work options, temperature controls, and uniforms that don’t exacerbate symptoms.

It has been revealed that of course, every individual and workplace is different. So employers should never be afraid to ask employees what would help them, she says.

As for women thinking about leaving their jobs or reducing their hours because of symptoms, Tetenbaum cautions, “Try not to make long-term decisions during a moment you feel overwhelmed.”.

And the best decision we can make of all? Learning to advocate for our needs... in every stage of our careers and bodies.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Are parents doomed to a lifetime of chasing after good sleep?

Industry observers note that on a tip from a savvy movie critic, I took my 7-year-old out to see his second ever Marvel movie the other day (he's a substantial fan of Norse mythology so he's seen Thor: Ragnarok and sorta liked it). We sat back, donning our 3D glasses (he was very into the novelty of this) and took in The Fantastic Four: First Steps. What a pleasant surprise. The movie is, in fact, as my movie critic colleague promised, The Best Marvel Movie for Families.

For the kids, there’s a lot to love. There are the action montages, a bright retro futuristic setting, a visual style that is gee-whiz superhero cool, but in a comic way — shiny and light and not over the top. The movie is just more palatable for kids than most other Marvel movies, emotionally and cognitively. The superheroes are relatable as family but they also play the part of role models well, interacting with and caring deeply about the public they serve. The villain, too, is not so much motivated by evil but by an unstoppable appetite (for planets, granted) that he is actively trying to rid himself of. A little sympathy goes a long way to take the teeth out of a monster. But most importantly there’s Franklin, the baby.

The Fantastic Four are a family and have arguments and issues that are familiar to all kids. One significant one is the strain (and joys) that having a baby puts on, well, everyone. I especially loved seeing Reed Richards and Sue Storm, superheroes with doctorates who no doubt have seen their share of sleep debt, complain about tiredness. Even genius superheroes can’t face the superheroic task that is getting baby to bed. It’s a tension that gets the screen time it deserves. Just ask any parent.

Sleep has been on my mind a lot lately. I always thought that I would crush sleep once my baby grew up, but some 6 years later I realize maybe it wasn’t the baby? I’ve never met someone who doesn’t have a tenuous relationship with sleep. When I was in physical prime either during my senior high school years as a soccer player and middle distant runner or during my marathon-happy thirties, I slept so very soundly. At least that’s how I remember it.

It has been revealed that now that I’m older I juggle more — so much more — work out a little less and do a lot more staring at the ceiling in the middle of the night. With age, I maybe need to admit, I need an assist.

It has been revealed that I’ve only just started to give sleep tracking a fair shake. I’ve been pairing up a new Samsung Galaxy 8 watch with a Samsung Galaxy Ring (I’ve been a Samsung man since I converted to their Flip phone, which pairs seamlessly together, requiring no third-party apps).

So what have I found? That data is in fact motivating. I won’t get too into the weeds but I will tell you that late night snacks, screens, night caps, and work are bad for my sleep. Evening walks, reading, and days with lighter fare and more quality workouts lead to more quality sleep.

It’s all fairly obvious stuff, but what the tracking does is force the attention. Good sleep matters and is, for those of us without babies, a fairly controllable thing. We can create habits that help sleep. We can choose to prioritize our health and well being. Stats don’t tell us what to do, but they do show what our current priorities.

When my son was a sleepless baby (he really was the worst) the only two priorities I had were to keep him healthy (alive) and to find sleep. My world is a little easier now and my list of priorities has grown immensely. I want to be outdoors more, to find newly introduced fitness, to take on new passions (birding is kind of fun, everyone), to embrace a new phase of marriage, to learn new skills, and meet my kids where they are. But sometimes you have to remember the basics. Without good sleep, everything is more difficult. Only a superhero can defeat the eater of worlds on a new parent’s sleep schedule. The rest of us need all the help we can get.

From A to Z (or in this case, Alan to Zenith).

In a recent development, if you’re a parent who lives to visit the next national park on their must-see list — the kind everyone turns to when they need to borrow camping supplies, who has probably seriously considered #vanlife at least once — of course you’re leaning toward nature-inspired baby names for your newly introduced little one. Whether you live in an arid region or they’re your favorite places to visit, these desert baby names will remind you of golden sands and endless blue skies.

Mojave asters are perennial flowering shrubs covered in beautiful purple blooms. This is a beautiful name choice if you like the idea of an earthy girl name, but floral names often strike you as too feminine. It gets bonus points for also meaning “star” in Greek.

Industry observers note that A canyon is a deep, narrow valley with steep, rocky sides, and usually there is a river at the bottom that has carved all that rock away over time. It would make a strong boy’s name, and subtly remind him to persevere, like water against stone.

Joshua Tree National Park connects the Mojave and Colorado deserts, and is known for its iconic bristled trees. While many desert baby names feel a little woo woo and whimsical, Joshua is a classic that’ll fly under the radar when you need it to.

This name means “fire”, if you’re drawing from the Arabic roots, or “my light” if you’re referencing the Turkish version. Something about it gives cool girl, yet grounded, and all of its meanings tie back to the heat and brightness of the desert.

Do any of these names sound just right for your the newly introduced baby in your nature-loving family?

Latest Update: The Real Reason We Struggle With Screen Time

📅 09 Sep 2025 | ⏱️ 4 min read (744 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fatherly

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that how should we all tackle phone use and screen time?
  • Does anyone have a truly healthy relationship with their phone?
  • I don’t see much evidence of it out there.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that how should we all tackle phone use and screen time? An ancient Eleusinian mystery may hold the answer.

Does anyone have a truly healthy relationship with their phone?

I don’t see much evidence of it out there. Personally, the phone is undeniably useful but still feels like a foreign object in my hand — a feeling that was brought into stark relief the second my kids were old enough to pick up a screen. To them, a tablet or phone offers an enticing, comforting, and even productive space. Not healthy, exactly, but familiar. For me, it’s alien — and ground zero for a cultural battle against brain rot, attention loss, and reality itself. Phones stress me out.

I ran into a much needed perspective on this dilemma in a long, thoughtful essay by Karl Ove Knausgaard, the brilliant Norwegian writer with an uncanny ability to see the world as it is, in meticulous detail. My struggle, as he helped me to see, comes from those most influential years in my life — the years before the smartphone. “To understand a man, you have to know what was happening in the world when he was twenty, Napoleon is supposed to have remarked,” writes Knausgaard in Harper’s Magazine. “The quotation is probably apocryphal, but that doesn’t mean it’s not true.”.

My Napoleonic prime was in the 2000s — shortly after the advent of Facebook, but right before the iPhone was in everyone’s hands. For Knausgaard, who is 56 years old, the internet barely existed in his twenties. He admits that he has been ignoring the fundamental influences of such technological advances since. “Not once in those forty years have I turned my attention to technology and tried to understand it,” Knausgaard writes, “how it works in itself, how it works in me. It’s as if I had moved to a foreign country and not bothered to learn its language, as if I am content with not understanding what is happening around me and just settling for my own little world. This lately feels like serious neglect.”.

It has been revealed that this resonates. While I spend considerable time trying to understand and control the impacts of screen time on my kids' developing brains, I hardly pay attention to my own use. What am I doing when I check for emails, Slack messages, and texts with lab rat-like repetition, or scroll Reddit News and The Latest York Times at every down moment, or get lost in Instagram and YouTube rabbit holes? More importantly, what should I do about it?

Knausgaard found his technological insight by heading out to Athens, Greece to talk to James Bridle, an author and artist with a specialty in nonhuman ways of thinking (and what orangutans can teach us about politics). In a sense, Bridle sees technology as getting in the way of experience. Sounding like a free range parenting proselytizer, he says that “the only thing you can do is experience it and do it yourself. You have to do it, you have to experience it, it has to happen to you. Bodily, physically — because you’re part of the world.”.

Recent findings suggest that bridle takes this deeper, offering the example of an ancient Eleusinian cult in which initiates were led into a dark room, shown a “whirlwind of impressions, without anyone telling them what they were seeing or what it meant” and being left to interpret that on their own. The next year, they were shown the initiation from the outside, “and you could say that only then, when the gaze from within was complemented by the gaze from without, was the initiation completed.”.

According to recent reports, this metaphor for the digital world made it all click for me. We’re all too often inside looking at the whirlwind of the internet with little control and understanding. There are more of us now trying to step outside of this world — to see the puppet masters at play in order to walk away from it all.

Sources indicate that we’re not going back to 2006, that innocent year before the iPhone was introduced. And I don’t think that should be the goal. The technology that has been introduced since my childhood is incredible, powerful, and a massive piece of human progress. But it’s no replacement for the real world lessons I get when I put down the phone and experience life, unfiltered.
